q: Rosa and Theo agree to open a bike shop. Rosa will invest $50,000 and stay out of daily operations; Theo will run the shop. They sign a written agreement calling Rosa a "limited partner" and Theo the "general partner," but they never file a certificate of limited partnership. The shop later defaults on a $90,000 supplier contract. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Rosa may be treated as a general partner and held personally liable for the shop's debts.
Rosa is not liable, because she took no part in running the shop.
Rosa is liable only up to her $50,000 investment, because the written agreement makes her a limited partner.
Rosa is liable only if the supplier knew she had invested in the shop.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. With no certificate on file, no LP was formed. Rosa and Theo are co-owners carrying on a business for profit, which is a general partnership whatever they called themselves (RUPA § 202(a)), and general partners are personally liable for partnership obligations (§ 306(a)).
Staying out of management is what a limited partner does, but Rosa never became one. Without a filed certificate, two co-owners running a business for profit are general partners.
A limited partnership exists only once a certificate is filed with the state. A private agreement cannot give Rosa a limited partner's shield against outsiders.
Partners' liability for partnership obligations comes from their status, not from the creditor's knowledge of who they are.
A is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — LP formed without a filing

q: Harmon Paper Co. makes Lucia its regional sales manager, a post whose holders in the paper industry customarily grant volume discounts of up to 15%. Harmon's president privately tells Lucia not to grant any discount above 5%. Lucia grants a long-time customer, Crestview Printing, a 12% discount. Crestview knows nothing of the 5% cap. Is Harmon bound to the 12% discount?
o: No, because Lucia lacked actual authority to grant more than 5%.
No, because Lucia told Crestview nothing about her authority.
Yes, but only if Harmon later ratifies the discount.
Yes, because by placing Lucia in a position whose holders customarily grant such discounts, Harmon manifested that she had that authority.
Yes, because a sales agent always has the power to bind her principal to whatever discount she grants, whatever the custom of the trade and whatever the principal has privately told her.
oe: Lack of actual authority is only the first step. Harmon can still be bound through apparent authority.
Apparent authority does not depend on the agent's statements. It comes from the principal's manifestation, and placing an agent in a position is such a manifestation.
Ratification is another route, but Harmon is already bound without it.

Correct. A principal that puts an agent in a position makes a manifestation that the agent has the authority customarily held there, and a third party need not inquire into undisclosed limits (R3d § 3.03 cmt. b; Lind v. Schenley).
Too broad. The authority reaches what is customary for the position; a discount far outside custom would not be reasonably believed.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Position as a manifestation

q: Under the RUPA (1997), which of the following may be a partner in a general partnership?
o: A limited liability company.
A trust.
Another general partnership.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A partnership is an association of two or more "persons," and the definition of person includes entities such as corporations and LLCs.
True. A trust (acting through its trustee) is also a person that may be a partner.
True. A partnership is itself a person and may be a partner in another partnership.
Incomplete. A trust may also be a partner.
Correct. Natural persons, corporations, LLCs, trusts, and other partnerships are all "persons" that may associate as partners.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Who can be a partner

q: Which of the following statements about the duties a principal owes its agent is true?
o: The principal owes the agent the same fiduciary duty of loyalty that the agent owes the principal.
The principal's duties are contractual: to act in good faith, compensate and reimburse the agent as agreed or contemplated, and indemnify losses from carrying out its instructions.
The principal owes no duties at all to a gratuitous agent.

The principal must pay the agent reasonable compensation in every agency relationship, even when the parties never discussed or contemplated any payment, because the agent's services always have value.
None of the above.
oe: The relationship is not symmetrical. The agent is the fiduciary; the principal's duties are contractual.

Correct. A principal owes the duties set by contract and good faith and fair dealing, including reasonable compensation if pay was contemplated, reimbursement of expenses, indemnity, cooperation, and warning of known risks (R3d §§ 8.14–8.15).
Even an unpaid agent is entitled to indemnity for losses suffered in carrying out the principal's instructions, and to warnings about known risks.
Compensation is owed only if the parties agreed to it or contemplated it. Gratuitous agencies are common (Gorton v. Doty).
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Principal's duties to the agent

q: Under the UPA (1914), which of the following does NOT cause the dissolution of a partnership?
o: The death of a partner.
The admission of a new partner with the consent of all existing partners.
A partner's express will to withdraw from a partnership at will.
The bankruptcy of a partner.
A court decree on a partner's application, where another partner's misconduct makes it impracticable to carry on the business with him.
oe: Death dissolves a UPA partnership (§ 31(4)); it is not wrongful.
Correct: this does not dissolve. Under the UPA a departing partner dissolves the firm, but adding a partner does not.
Under the aggregate theory, any partner's departure dissolves the firm, rightfully if it is at will (§ 31(1)(b)).
A partner's bankruptcy dissolves a UPA partnership (§ 31(5)).
Court-ordered dissolution is available under UPA § 32 (Owen v. Cohen).
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — UPA dissolution events

q: Four partners are drafting a buyout agreement. They want a price that is cheap to apply but that will not leave a departing partner's estate with far less than the business is really worth. Which pricing method best fits both goals?
o: The departing partner's capital account balance.
An agreed price that the partners update each year, with a fallback appraisal if they fail to update it.
The price the departing partner (or the estate) names at the time of departure, which the remaining partners must then accept.
Whatever price the remaining partners, acting in good faith, decide is fair at the time the departing partner leaves.
A full independent appraisal of the business, by an appraiser the partners choose together, every time a buyout is triggered.
oe: Cheap to apply, but capital accounts are kept at book value (cost), not market value, so the estate may get far less than the interest is worth (G & S Investments v. Belman).

Correct. An annually agreed price is cheap to apply and tracks real value as long as the partners keep it current; a fallback appraisal protects against a stale figure. Price methods include book value, appraisal, formula, and an annual agreed price.
That favors the departing partner and invites overreaching; it is not a shotgun clause, which lets the other side choose to buy or sell at the named price.
That leaves the departing partner (or estate) at the mercy of the buyers, the opposite of the second goal.
Accurate, but expensive and slow, and it invites a battle of appraisers. It does not meet the cost goal.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Price terms in a buyout agreement

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ava, Bram, and Cleo are partners in Lantern Hill Vineyard, a general partnership that grows grapes and runs a tasting room. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "The partnership shall last for twelve years." "No partner may buy equipment costing more than $25,000 without the consent of all partners." "Any partner may be expelled at any time by the unanimous vote of the other partners." Bram runs the vineyard crew; Cleo runs the tasting room; Ava keeps the books.

Bram signs a contract on the partnership's behalf to buy a $40,000 grape press from Valley Equipment, which does not know about the $25,000 limit in the agreement. Ava and Cleo never consented. Is the partnership bound to pay Valley Equipment?
o: No, because the agreement validly limited Bram's authority to buy equipment, which ends the inquiry.
No, because no reasonable seller would believe that one partner could commit a vineyard to a $40,000 purchase.
Yes, because the limit in the agreement is void; a partnership cannot restrict a partner's authority.
Yes, because the limit restricts Bram's actual authority but not his apparent authority, and Valley neither knew nor had notice of it.
None of the above.
oe: The limit removes Bram's actual authority but does not bind an outsider who neither knew of it nor had notice of it.
Buying a grape press is apparently carrying on a vineyard's business in the ordinary course. Nothing about the price makes Valley's belief unreasonable.
The limit is valid between the partners and makes Bram answerable to them. It just doesn't bind a third party without notice.

Correct. A partner's act apparently carrying on in the ordinary course binds the partnership unless the partner lacked authority and the third party knew or had notice of that (RUPA § 301(1)). A private limit in the agreement is not notice to outsiders (RNR Investments).
D is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Ordinary course and apparent authority

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ava, Bram, and Cleo are partners in Lantern Hill Vineyard, a general partnership that grows grapes and runs a tasting room. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "The partnership shall last for twelve years." "No partner may buy equipment costing more than $25,000 without the consent of all partners." "Any partner may be expelled at any time by the unanimous vote of the other partners." Bram runs the vineyard crew; Cleo runs the tasting room; Ava keeps the books.

While pouring wine at a crowded tasting, Cleo carelessly knocks over a patio heater, which burns a guest, Dev. Dev's damages are $200,000; the partnership's assets are worth $80,000. Which of the following statements best describes the liability of the partnership and the partners?
o: Only Cleo is liable, because she alone was negligent.
The partnership is liable, but Ava and Bram are not personally liable because they did nothing wrong.
The partnership and all three partners are jointly and severally liable, but Dev generally must exhaust the partnership's assets before collecting from Ava's or Bram's personal assets.
Ava and Bram are liable only up to the value of their interests in the partnership.
None of the above.
oe: Cleo is liable for her own tort, but she is not alone. The partnership answers for a partner's tort in the ordinary course of its business (§ 305).
Partners are personally liable for partnership obligations because of their status (§ 306(a)), not their fault.

Correct. The tort occurred in the ordinary course, so the partnership is liable (§ 305); all partners are jointly and severally liable (§ 306(a)); and the exhaustion rule (§ 307(d)) makes Dev go after partnership assets before levying on a partner's own property. Dev may of course sue Cleo directly as the tortfeasor.
Liability capped at one's investment describes a limited partner or an LLC member, not a general partner.
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Partners' liability for a partner's tort

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ava, Bram, and Cleo are partners in Lantern Hill Vineyard, a general partnership that grows grapes and runs a tasting room. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "The partnership shall last for twelve years." "No partner may buy equipment costing more than $25,000 without the consent of all partners." "Any partner may be expelled at any time by the unanimous vote of the other partners." Bram runs the vineyard crew; Cleo runs the tasting room; Ava keeps the books.

In Year 5, Bram leaves Lantern Hill to start his own winery. Which of the following statements best describes his responsibility for partnership obligations and losses?
o: Bram remains liable for partnership obligations incurred while he was a partner, and he may also be liable for damages the partnership suffers because he left early.
Bram is liable only for partnership obligations he knew or had reason to know of before he left, and he owes nothing for leaving, because every partner may withdraw.
Bram is liable for every obligation the partnership ever incurs, including those incurred after he leaves, and he owes damages for leaving.
Bram owes nothing to anyone, because every partner always has the right to leave.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Dissociation does not discharge liabilities incurred while he was a partner (§ 603(c)), and leaving a term partnership early by express will is wrongful, so he owes damages caused by his dissociation (§ 602(b)(2)(A), (c)). They are offset against his buyout price (§ 701(c)).
Knowledge is not the test for liability on obligations incurred while he was a partner, and leaving a term partnership early is wrongful.

A dissociated partner is generally not liable for obligations incurred after dissociation (§ 703(a)), except for two years to third parties who reasonably believe he is still a partner and lack notice (§ 703(b)).
Every partner has the power to leave (§ 602(a)), but not always the right; and leaving does not wipe out existing liabilities.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — A departing partner's responsibilities

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ava, Bram, and Cleo are partners in Lantern Hill Vineyard, a general partnership that grows grapes and runs a tasting room. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "The partnership shall last for twelve years." "No partner may buy equipment costing more than $25,000 without the consent of all partners." "Any partner may be expelled at any time by the unanimous vote of the other partners." Bram runs the vineyard crew; Cleo runs the tasting room; Ava keeps the books.

Ava repeatedly complains that the tasting room loses money and demands that it be closed. Bram and Cleo disagree, grow tired of the complaints, and vote to expel Ava. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Ava has not been dissociated, because a partner in a term partnership cannot be expelled before the term ends.
Ava has been dissociated, but Bram and Cleo breached their fiduciary duties by expelling her without cause.
Ava has been dissociated, but because this is a partnership for a twelve-year term, her expulsion before the term ends is a wrongful dissociation that entitles her to damages from Bram and Cleo.
Ava has been dissociated under the agreement, and Bram and Cleo did not breach any fiduciary duty by expelling her.
None of the above.
oe: The agreement expressly permits expulsion by unanimous vote of the other partners, and expulsion under the agreement is a dissociation event (§ 601(3)).
Courts enforce no-cause expulsion clauses as written; expelling a partner under a bargained-for clause is not itself a breach, so long as nothing owed to her is wrongfully withheld (Lawlis; Bohatch).
Expulsion under the agreement is not on the § 602(b) list of wrongful dissociations. Only a judicial expulsion is.

Correct. The agreement allows expulsion by unanimous vote of the others, so Ava is dissociated (§ 601(3)). A clause like this is enforced as written, and partners may part ways when trust breaks down (Lawlis v. Kightlinger & Gray; Bohatch v. Butler & Binion).
D is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Expulsion under the agreement

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ava, Bram, and Cleo are partners in Lantern Hill Vineyard, a general partnership that grows grapes and runs a tasting room. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "The partnership shall last for twelve years." "No partner may buy equipment costing more than $25,000 without the consent of all partners." "Any partner may be expelled at any time by the unanimous vote of the other partners." Bram runs the vineyard crew; Cleo runs the tasting room; Ava keeps the books.

Assume Ava has been validly expelled and Bram and Cleo continue the vineyard. Ava makes a written demand for payment. Under the RUPA's default rules, which of the following statements is true?
o: Ava receives the greater of the partnership's liquidation value or its going-concern value without her, measured on the date of her dissociation, plus interest.
Ava must wait until the twelve-year term expires before she can be paid.
If the partners do not agree on a price within 120 days after Ava's written demand, the partnership must pay her its own estimate of the buyout price.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: True. That is the § 701(b) buyout price, and interest runs from the date of dissociation (§ 701(c)).
False. Deferral applies only to a partner who wrongfully dissociates before the end of a term (§ 701(h)); expulsion under the agreement is not wrongful.
True. § 701(e) requires the partnership to pay its estimate, with interest, if no agreement is reached within 120 days of a written demand.

Correct. Ava is paid the greater of liquidation or going-concern value plus interest, and the partnership must pay its estimate within the 120-day window if no agreement is reached. She need not wait for the end of the term, because her dissociation was not wrongful.
B is false; only a wrongful dissociator from a term partnership must wait.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Buyout after a rightful dissociation

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Mrs. Okafor, recovering from surgery, asks her nephew Jalen to sell her car for her. She tells him, "Get at least $12,000, and don't let anyone else drive it." Jalen is not paid. With his aunt's permission, Jalen asks his friend Marcus, who works at a used-car lot, to help him find a buyer. While Jalen has the car, he keeps it at his apartment and shows it to prospective buyers.

Mrs. Okafor argues that Jalen cannot be her agent because she is not paying him and they signed nothing. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Jalen is not her agent, because an agency requires consideration.
Jalen is not her agent, because an agency to sell a car must be created in writing.
Jalen is her agent, because she consented to his acting for her, he agreed, and she kept control by setting the price and the rule about who may drive.
Jalen becomes her agent only if she later pays him a reasonable commission, because an unpaid helper who is doing a relative a favor is a volunteer, not an agent.
None of the above.
oe: Consideration is not required. Agency rests on consent and control, not on a bargain.
A writing is generally not required. Selling a car is not a land transaction, and the equal dignities rule does not apply.

Correct. Agency arises when the principal manifests assent that the agent will act on her behalf and subject to her control, and the agent consents (R3d § 1.01). Like the teacher who named the driver in Gorton v. Doty, Mrs. Okafor's conditions show control, and payment is unnecessary.
Compensation is not an element. A gratuitous agent is still an agent (R3d § 1.04(3)).
C is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Gratuitous agency

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Mrs. Okafor, recovering from surgery, asks her nephew Jalen to sell her car for her. She tells him, "Get at least $12,000, and don't let anyone else drive it." Jalen is not paid. With his aunt's permission, Jalen asks his friend Marcus, who works at a used-car lot, to help him find a buyer. While Jalen has the car, he keeps it at his apartment and shows it to prospective buyers.

Marcus finds a buyer and handles some of the paperwork. Which of the following statements about Marcus is true?
o: Marcus is Mrs. Okafor's subagent, so he owes fiduciary duties to her as well as to Jalen, and Jalen remains answerable to her for Marcus's conduct.
Marcus owes duties only to Jalen, because Mrs. Okafor never dealt with him.
Marcus is a coagent, so Jalen has no responsibility for anything Marcus does.
Marcus cannot be an agent at all, because Jalen had no power to involve anyone else.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A subagent is a person an agent appoints, with authority to do so, to perform functions the agent has agreed to perform for the principal. The subagent is the principal's fiduciary, and the appointing agent remains responsible to the principal for the subagent's conduct (R3d §§ 1.04(8), 3.15).
A subagent appointed with the principal's permission is an agent of both the appointing agent and the principal, and owes duties to both.
Coagents are agents the principal appoints directly. Marcus was appointed by Jalen, which makes him a subagent, and Jalen stays answerable for him.
Mrs. Okafor gave permission, so Jalen had actual authority to appoint him.
A is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Subagents

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Mrs. Okafor, recovering from surgery, asks her nephew Jalen to sell her car for her. She tells him, "Get at least $12,000, and don't let anyone else drive it." Jalen is not paid. With his aunt's permission, Jalen asks his friend Marcus, who works at a used-car lot, to help him find a buyer. While Jalen has the car, he keeps it at his apartment and shows it to prospective buyers.

While driving a prospective buyer on a test drive, Jalen carelessly runs a red light and injures a pedestrian, Nell. Nell sues Mrs. Okafor. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Mrs. Okafor cannot be liable, because Jalen is unpaid and is only doing his aunt a family favor, and only a paid employee can make a principal vicariously liable for a tort.
Mrs. Okafor is liable only if she was negligent in choosing Jalen, for example because she knew he had a poor driving record.
Mrs. Okafor may be vicariously liable, because she had the right to control how Jalen used the car for her errand, and he was acting within the scope of that errand.
Mrs. Okafor is liable only if she ratifies the test drive after the accident.
Only Nell's own insurer can pay, because Jalen is liable for his own tort.
oe: Gratuitous service does not relieve the principal of liability. Gorton v. Doty imposed liability for an unpaid driver.
Negligent selection is one route to direct liability, but it is not the only one. Vicarious liability does not require any fault on her part.

Correct. A principal who controls or has the right to control the manner and means of the agent's work is liable for torts within the scope of that work, even if the agent is unpaid (R3d § 7.07(3); Gorton v. Doty). Her rule that no one else may drive shows control over the car's use.
She authorized test drives as part of selling the car; nothing needs ratifying.
Jalen is liable for his own tort (R3d § 7.01), but that does not shield the principal.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Gratuitous servant's tort

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Mrs. Okafor, recovering from surgery, asks her nephew Jalen to sell her car for her. She tells him, "Get at least $12,000, and don't let anyone else drive it." Jalen is not paid. With his aunt's permission, Jalen asks his friend Marcus, who works at a used-car lot, to help him find a buyer. While Jalen has the car, he keeps it at his apartment and shows it to prospective buyers.

A buyer offers Jalen $14,500 for the car. Instead, Jalen arranges for his roommate to buy it for $12,000, planning to resell it to the first buyer for $14,500 and split the profit. Mrs. Okafor learns the truth. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Jalen did nothing wrong, because he got the $12,000 his aunt asked for.
Jalen owes a lower duty of loyalty than a paid agent, so the arrangement is permissible.
Jalen breached his duty of loyalty by secretly dealing as or for an adverse party and taking a benefit from his position.
Mrs. Okafor may recover the $2,500 profit from Jalen even if she cannot prove any other loss.
C and D.
oe: The $12,000 was a floor, not a ceiling. An agent must act loyally for the principal's benefit, not divert a better deal to himself.
Compensation can affect the standard of care (R2d § 379), but the duty of loyalty applies in full to gratuitous agents.
True. An agent may not deal with the principal as or on behalf of an adverse party without disclosure and consent (R3d § 8.03), and may not acquire a material benefit through his position (§ 8.02).
True. Disgorgement of an agent's secret profit does not require proof of a separate loss (Reading v. Regem; General Automotive v. Singer).
Correct. Jalen breached his duty of loyalty, and his aunt may make him give up the profit.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Loyalty of an unpaid agent

q: A customer signs an order for a new boat at Bayline Marine. The salesperson signs too, but the form states that it "is not binding until accepted in writing by the sales manager." No manager ever sees the order. When the manufacturer raises its prices, the customer insists that Bayline ratified the order by failing to object to it. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Bayline ratified the order, because its salesperson accepted the customer's deposit on Bayline's behalf.
There is no contract, because no manager knew of the order, so Bayline could not ratify it.
Bayline ratified the order, because silence by a principal always amounts to ratification once a reasonable time has passed after the agent acts.
There is a contract, because the salesperson had apparent authority to accept orders on the showroom floor.
None of the above.
oe: The salesperson's acceptance is the unauthorized act itself; it cannot also be the principal's ratification of that act. Ratification must come from the principal.

Correct. Silence can ratify only when the principal knows of the transaction. As Ercanbrack v. Crandall-Walker Motor Co. put it, ratification of an act about which the principal knows nothing is inherently impossible (R3d § 4.06).
Silence ratifies only where the principal knows the facts and would be expected to object. Passage of time alone is not enough.
The order form itself told the customer that only a manager could accept it, so the customer could not reasonably believe the salesperson had that authority.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Silence without knowledge

q: Wanda sells her entire interest in a RUPA partnership to the two remaining partners, who agree to take over its debts. A year later, the partnership discovers that a former bookkeeper embezzled funds during Wanda's time as a partner, and it recovers $50,000 from the bank that honored the forged checks. Wanda claims a third of the recovery. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Wanda is entitled to a third of the recovery, because the embezzlement occurred while she was a partner and the losses were partly hers.
Wanda is entitled to a third of the recovery, because as a partner she co-owned the partnership's claims as a tenant in partnership.
Wanda is not entitled to any of the recovery, because a partner owns an interest in the partnership, not in its specific assets, and she sold that whole interest.
Wanda is entitled to the recovery only if the remaining partners knew of the embezzlement when they bought her interest.
None of the above.
oe: The claim belonged to the partnership, not to Wanda, and she sold her entire interest in the partnership, including claims no one yet knew about.

Tenancy in partnership was the UPA (1914) idea, and even under the UPA it gave a partner no separate interest to keep after selling out. Under the RUPA a partner is not a co-owner of partnership property at all (§ 501).
Correct. This is Putnam v. Shoaf: the claims against the banks were partnership property, and a partner who conveys her whole partnership interest conveys everything, including unknown claims.
Knowledge might matter to a fraud claim, but nothing suggests the buyers knew. On these facts the recovery belongs to the partnership.
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Selling the whole interest

q: In Arguello v. Conoco, Inc., customers sued Conoco under federal civil-rights laws for racist treatment by a clerk at a store Conoco owned and by staff at independently owned stations that sold Conoco-brand gas. Which of the following statements is consistent with the court's holding?
o: Conoco could be liable for its own clerk's conduct during a sale, but the branded stations' staff were not its agents.
Conoco was liable for both groups, because every station displayed the Conoco brand and sold Conoco gasoline.
Conoco was liable for neither group, because agency principles do not apply to claims under federal civil-rights statutes.
Conoco ratified the clerk's conduct by counseling her afterward instead of firing her.
Conoco was liable for the branded stations, but not for its own clerk, because the clerk's racist abuse served only her own purposes.
oe: Correct. The independently owned stations were not Conoco's agents, because Conoco did not control their daily operations or staff. Its own clerk's abuse, committed while making a sale, could be within the scope of employment, which was a jury question.
Brand display and fuel supply are the trademark and supply ties that do not, by themselves, show control of daily operations. That reasoning would make every franchisor liable for every franchisee.
The court applied ordinary agency and scope-of-employment principles to the statutory claims.
The court held that counseling the clerk was not ratification of her conduct.
That reverses the holding. The owned store's clerk could be within scope; the branded stations were not agents at all.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Owned vs. branded outlets (Arguello)

q: Three members form Tidal Kayak Tours, LLC by filing a certificate of organization under the ULLCA. For three years they never hold a meeting, never keep minutes, and never adopt a written operating agreement. A customer injured on a tour, through no fault of any member, wins a judgment against the LLC that exceeds its assets. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The members are personally liable for the unpaid judgment, because the LLC ignored the formalities that keep its shield in place.
The members are personally liable, because without a written operating agreement the LLC is treated as a general partnership.
The members are personally liable only in proportion to their contributions to the LLC.
The members are not personally liable, because the judgment is solely the LLC's obligation.
None of the above.
oe: ULLCA § 304(b): a failure to observe formalities is not a ground for imposing liability on members or managers.
An LLC exists once the certificate is filed (§ 201). An operating agreement need not be written, and the act supplies default rules when there is none.
Members are not liable for company obligations solely because they are members (§ 304(a)), so there is nothing to apportion.
Correct. An LLC's debts are its own (§ 304(a)), and § 304(b) rejects informality as a ground for member liability. Veil piercing remains the main exception, and nothing here suggests fraud or abuse.
D is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — LLC shield and formalities

q: Ira retired from a law partnership and receives a pension from it. After he retires, the managing partners approve a merger that turns out badly, and the firm collapses, ending his pension. Ira sues the managing partners for negligently approving the merger. Under Bane v. Ferguson, which of the following statements is true?
o: Ira wins, because partners owe one another the utmost good faith for as long as any of them receives money from the firm.
Ira loses, because partners owe their fiduciary duties to current partners rather than former ones.
Ira loses, because even a current partner could not recover for the managing partners' merely negligent business decision.
Ira wins, because the managing partners owed him a duty of ordinary care in managing the firm on which his pension depended.
B and C.
oe: Bane held that partners' fiduciary duties run to current partners, not to retired ones. A pension makes Ira a creditor of sorts, not a partner.
True. Ira was no longer a partner when the merger was approved.

True. The business judgment rule shields ordinary negligence, and under the RUPA a partner's duty of care is only to refrain from gross negligence, recklessness, intentional misconduct, or knowing violations of law (§ 409(c)).
The duty of care does not reach ordinary negligence, and it is owed to current partners.
Correct. Bane rejected the claim on both grounds: no duty to a former partner, and no liability for mere negligence.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — To whom partners owe duties (Bane)

q: Which of the following is LEAST relevant when founders choose a business form?
o: The color scheme and logo the business will use.
How the business and its owners will be taxed.
How easily an owner can exit the business and cash out.
Who will have the right to manage and how money will be raised.
Whether the owners will be personally liable for the business's debts.
oe: Correct. Branding has nothing to do with the choice of entity. The selection factors are formation complexity, management rights, raising money, filings, personal liability, tax treatment, exit, and which fiduciary duties apply.
Tax treatment (entity-level tax versus pass-through) is a core factor.
The ability to exit and cash out promptly is a listed selection factor.
Management rights and the ability to raise money are both selection factors.
Avoiding personal liability is a central selection factor.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Entity-selection factors

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Brightline Solar Corp. manufactures solar panels. SunPath Installers, Inc., a small installation company, buys almost all of its panels from Brightline. When SunPath falls behind on its bills, Brightline extends it a growing line of credit. In return, SunPath agrees that Brightline may approve any SunPath contract over $10,000, may station one of its engineers in SunPath's office to run the job schedule, may audit SunPath's books at any time, and may veto any dividend or any change in SunPath's officers. Brightline's regional manager calls SunPath every day with instructions about which jobs to take, and SunPath writes up its jobs on order forms printed with Brightline's logo, which Brightline supplies. Their written agreement says, "SunPath is not the agent of Brightline for any purpose." SunPath collapses owing $900,000 to roofing subcontractors and to homeowners who paid deposits.

SunPath's unpaid subcontractors sue Brightline. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Brightline is not liable, because a creditor that merely lends money and buys or sells goods can never become its debtor's principal.
Brightline is likely liable as SunPath's principal, because its control over SunPath's daily business went beyond protecting a loan.
Brightline is liable only if it signed SunPath's contracts with the subcontractors.
Brightline is not liable, because SunPath's subcontractors never knew that Brightline was involved.
Brightline is liable only for the homeowners' deposits, because those were paid on Brightline forms.
oe: A creditor that only protects its loan is not a principal, but a creditor that takes over the debtor's management can become one (R2d § 14O).

Correct. Like Cargill, Brightline approved contracts, ran the schedule, audited the books, vetoed dividends and officer changes, gave daily instructions, and supplied its own forms. A creditor that assumes de facto control over the debtor's business becomes a principal liable for the debtor's acts (A. Gay Jenson Farms v. Cargill).
A principal is bound on contracts its agent makes on its behalf; it need not sign them itself.
An undisclosed or unknown principal can still be liable on its agent's authorized contracts. The farmers in Cargill dealt with the elevator, not with Cargill.
If Brightline is SunPath's principal, it answers for the contracts SunPath made for it generally, not only those written on its forms.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Creditor as principal

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Brightline Solar Corp. manufactures solar panels. SunPath Installers, Inc., a small installation company, buys almost all of its panels from Brightline. When SunPath falls behind on its bills, Brightline extends it a growing line of credit. In return, SunPath agrees that Brightline may approve any SunPath contract over $10,000, may station one of its engineers in SunPath's office to run the job schedule, may audit SunPath's books at any time, and may veto any dividend or any change in SunPath's officers. Brightline's regional manager calls SunPath every day with instructions about which jobs to take, and SunPath writes up its jobs on order forms printed with Brightline's logo, which Brightline supplies. Their written agreement says, "SunPath is not the agent of Brightline for any purpose." SunPath collapses owing $900,000 to roofing subcontractors and to homeowners who paid deposits.

Brightline points to the clause in the agreement stating that "SunPath is not the agent of Brightline for any purpose." How will a court most likely treat the clause?
o: As decisive, because parties to a contract are free to decide whether an agency relationship exists between them.
As decisive against the subcontractors only, because they were not parties to the agreement and cannot rely on its terms.
As irrelevant, because a written agreement between a creditor and a debtor is never admissible on the question of agency.
As relevant evidence, but not controlling, because agency turns on what the parties actually did.
None of the above.
oe: Parties can decide whether to enter the relationship, but if they do the things that make up agency, their label does not change the legal result.
Third parties do not need to rely on the agreement. They rely on the facts showing consent and control.
The clause is admissible and informative; it just does not decide the question.

Correct. Whether a relationship is an agency is determined by the law, and the parties' characterization is not controlling (R3d § 1.02). Courts look at actual practices (MJ & Partners v. Zadikoff; Cargill).
D is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Labels don't control

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Brightline Solar Corp. manufactures solar panels. SunPath Installers, Inc., a small installation company, buys almost all of its panels from Brightline. When SunPath falls behind on its bills, Brightline extends it a growing line of credit. In return, SunPath agrees that Brightline may approve any SunPath contract over $10,000, may station one of its engineers in SunPath's office to run the job schedule, may audit SunPath's books at any time, and may veto any dividend or any change in SunPath's officers. Brightline's regional manager calls SunPath every day with instructions about which jobs to take, and SunPath writes up its jobs on order forms printed with Brightline's logo, which Brightline supplies. Their written agreement says, "SunPath is not the agent of Brightline for any purpose." SunPath collapses owing $900,000 to roofing subcontractors and to homeowners who paid deposits.

Suppose Brightline's only rights had been the ones listed below. Which, standing alone, would be most consistent with Brightline's being a protected lender rather than a principal or partner?
o: The right to choose which jobs SunPath takes each day.
The right to have its engineer schedule all of SunPath's crews.
The right to inspect SunPath's books and to veto unusually risky transactions.
The right to approve every SunPath contract over $10,000, which covers nearly all of its jobs.
The right to name SunPath's officers.
oe: Choosing the debtor's business each day is running the business, the kind of control that made Cargill a principal.
Running the debtor's operations day to day goes beyond protecting a loan.

Correct. Information rights and a veto over speculative deals are reasonable protections for a large, risky loan. In Martin v. Peyton the lenders could veto but could not initiate transactions or bind the firm, so they were not partners.
Approving nearly every contract shades into running the business. In Cargill, approval of major decisions was one of the control factors.
Controlling who manages the debtor is management control, not loan protection.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Lender protections (Martin v. Peyton)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Brightline Solar Corp. manufactures solar panels. SunPath Installers, Inc., a small installation company, buys almost all of its panels from Brightline. When SunPath falls behind on its bills, Brightline extends it a growing line of credit. In return, SunPath agrees that Brightline may approve any SunPath contract over $10,000, may station one of its engineers in SunPath's office to run the job schedule, may audit SunPath's books at any time, and may veto any dividend or any change in SunPath's officers. Brightline's regional manager calls SunPath every day with instructions about which jobs to take, and SunPath writes up its jobs on order forms printed with Brightline's logo, which Brightline supplies. Their written agreement says, "SunPath is not the agent of Brightline for any purpose." SunPath collapses owing $900,000 to roofing subcontractors and to homeowners who paid deposits.

The subcontractors also argue that Brightline and SunPath were partners. Which of the following statements best evaluates that argument?
o: It is weak, because Brightline neither shared SunPath's profits nor co-owned its business.
It is strong, because Brightline's control over SunPath is enough by itself to make the two companies partners.
It is strong, because a partnership is formed whenever two businesses deal with each other continuously for profit.
It is weak, because two corporations can never be partners in a general partnership.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A partnership requires an association to carry on a business as co-owners for profit (RUPA § 202(a)). Profit sharing raises a presumption, but Brightline received the price of goods and repayment of a debt, which raise none (§ 202(c)(3)). Agency, not partnership, is the subcontractors' better theory.
Control is relevant to agency, but partnership requires co-ownership of a business, usually shown by sharing profits. Control alone does not make a lender or buyer a partner.
Continuous dealing for profit between a buyer and a seller is ordinary commerce, not co-ownership of one business.
Corporations are persons and can be partners. The argument fails on the facts, not for that reason.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — No profit share, no partnership

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Brightline Solar Corp. manufactures solar panels. SunPath Installers, Inc., a small installation company, buys almost all of its panels from Brightline. When SunPath falls behind on its bills, Brightline extends it a growing line of credit. In return, SunPath agrees that Brightline may approve any SunPath contract over $10,000, may station one of its engineers in SunPath's office to run the job schedule, may audit SunPath's books at any time, and may veto any dividend or any change in SunPath's officers. Brightline's regional manager calls SunPath every day with instructions about which jobs to take, and SunPath writes up its jobs on order forms printed with Brightline's logo, which Brightline supplies. Their written agreement says, "SunPath is not the agent of Brightline for any purpose." SunPath collapses owing $900,000 to roofing subcontractors and to homeowners who paid deposits.

A homeowner, Lily, paid SunPath a $15,000 deposit. She claims Brightline is bound because SunPath's salesperson told her, "Brightline stands behind every one of our jobs." Which fact best supports a claim that SunPath had apparent authority to act for Brightline?
o: The salesperson's statement that Brightline stood behind every job.
Lily's sincere belief that Brightline would protect her deposit.
The fact that SunPath was in financial trouble when Lily paid her deposit.
The fact that Brightline later learned of Lily's deposit.
Lily signed an order form bearing Brightline's logo that Brightline had supplied.
oe: An agent's own statements cannot create apparent authority. The manifestation must be traceable to the principal (R3d § 2.03).
A third party's belief must be reasonable and traceable to the principal's manifestation; sincerity alone is not enough.
SunPath's finances say nothing about whether Brightline held SunPath out as acting for it.
Learning about a transaction after the fact might bear on ratification, but it is not a manifestation that created Lily's belief when she paid.

Correct. Apparent authority must rest on the principal's own manifestation to the third party. By supplying forms bearing its logo, Brightline itself communicated something to the people who received them.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Whose manifestation?

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Marisol owns Fuego, a taco truck, as a sole proprietor. When her cook, Dev, asks for a raise, Marisol instead signs a document with him titled "Partnership Agreement." It provides that Dev keeps his $800 weekly wage and will also receive 20% of the truck's net profits "if the business can afford it"; that Marisol keeps sole ownership of the truck and sole control of the menu, hiring, and spending; and that Dev bears no share of any losses. Dev's duties do not change. The truck's registration, bank account, and tax returns all remain in Marisol's name alone.

A state agency claims Marisol owes unemployment taxes on Dev's wages. Marisol argues that Dev is her partner, not her employee. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Dev is a partner, because he and Marisol signed a document titled "Partnership Agreement."
Dev is an employee, because his profit share was a form of wages and he had no ownership, control, or exposure to losses.
Dev is a partner, because anyone who receives a share of a business's profits is presumed to be a partner, and the presumption cannot be rebutted.
Dev is a partner for tax purposes but an employee for all other purposes.
None of the above.
oe: The parties' label does not control; what matters is whether they carry on a business as co-owners.

Correct. In Fenwick v. Unemployment Compensation Commission, a receptionist made a "partner" on paper was still an employee: she contributed no capital, had no control, bore no losses, and kept the same job. Profits received as wages do not raise a presumption of partnership (RUPA § 202(c)(3)).
Profit sharing raises a presumption, but not when the profits are received as wages, and the presumption is rebuttable.
Partnership status is decided on one set of factors; there is no such split here.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Profit share as wages (Fenwick)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Marisol owns Fuego, a taco truck, as a sole proprietor. When her cook, Dev, asks for a raise, Marisol instead signs a document with him titled "Partnership Agreement." It provides that Dev keeps his $800 weekly wage and will also receive 20% of the truck's net profits "if the business can afford it"; that Marisol keeps sole ownership of the truck and sole control of the menu, hiring, and spending; and that Dev bears no share of any losses. Dev's duties do not change. The truck's registration, bank account, and tax returns all remain in Marisol's name alone.

At a food show, Marisol introduces Dev to a meat supplier as "my partner." Dev stands beside her and says nothing. Relying on Dev's being a partner, the supplier sells Fuego $6,000 of meat on credit, which Marisol does not pay. Is Dev liable to the supplier?
o: No, because Dev is not actually a partner, so he cannot be liable for Fuego's debts.
No, because Dev never said anything to the supplier, so he made no representation.
Yes, because he consented to being held out as a partner, and the supplier relied on it.
Yes, because Dev receives 20% of Fuego's profits, which makes him a partner for all purposes.
None of the above.
oe: Liability under § 308 does not depend on actually being a partner. It attaches to a person who is represented as one with his consent.
Liability reaches a person who consents to being represented by another as a partner. Standing by silently while being introduced as a partner is strong evidence of consent.
Correct. A purported partner is liable to a person who enters into a transaction with the partnership in reliance on the representation (RUPA § 308(a); UPA § 16).
Dev's profit share is wages (Fenwick); his liability here rests on estoppel, not on actual partnership.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Partner by estoppel (§ 308)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Marisol owns Fuego, a taco truck, as a sole proprietor. When her cook, Dev, asks for a raise, Marisol instead signs a document with him titled "Partnership Agreement." It provides that Dev keeps his $800 weekly wage and will also receive 20% of the truck's net profits "if the business can afford it"; that Marisol keeps sole ownership of the truck and sole control of the menu, hiring, and spending; and that Dev bears no share of any losses. Dev's duties do not change. The truck's registration, bank account, and tax returns all remain in Marisol's name alone.

A customer who got sick from a Fuego taco sues Dev, claiming he is liable as Marisol's partner. The customer never heard anyone describe Dev as a partner. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Dev is liable, because once he let himself be called a partner at the food show, he became liable as a partner to everyone who deals with Fuego.
Dev is liable, because a customer harmed by a business may sue anyone who has ever been described as an owner of it.
Dev is liable, because tort victims do not need to show reliance in order to hold a purported partner liable.
Dev is not liable as a partner, because the customer did not rely on any representation that Dev was a partner.
None of the above.
oe: A representation made privately reaches only those who relied on it. A public representation can reach more people, but even then the claimant must have relied on it.
Being described as an owner creates liability only to those who acted in reliance on that description.
Partnership by estoppel always requires reliance on the representation. That is why the investors in Young v. Jones lost their claim against the U.S. firm.
Correct. Under § 308 and Young v. Jones, liability as a purported partner runs only to those who relied on the representation, and Dev is not an actual partner.
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Estoppel needs reliance (Young v. Jones)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Marisol owns Fuego, a taco truck, as a sole proprietor. When her cook, Dev, asks for a raise, Marisol instead signs a document with him titled "Partnership Agreement." It provides that Dev keeps his $800 weekly wage and will also receive 20% of the truck's net profits "if the business can afford it"; that Marisol keeps sole ownership of the truck and sole control of the menu, hiring, and spending; and that Dev bears no share of any losses. Dev's duties do not change. The truck's registration, bank account, and tax returns all remain in Marisol's name alone.

Assume instead that Dev had put $15,000 of his own borrowed money into a second truck, that he and Marisol split all of the business's profits and losses equally, and that Marisol's books still listed Dev as an employee. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Dev is likely a partner, because he contributed capital and shared all profits and losses.
Dev is an employee, because the business's books and records control the question of partnership status.
Dev is a lender, because the $15,000 he put in was money he borrowed from someone else.
Dev is a partner only if Marisol intended to form a partnership with him.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. As in Zajac v. Harris, a person who puts in capital and shares in all of the profits is a co-owner, and one-sided bookkeeping that calls him an employee does not change that.
Records are evidence, not a decision. In Zajac the other partner's books treated the plaintiff as an employee, and the court still found a partnership.
Where Dev got the money doesn't matter. He contributed it to the business as capital, not as a loan to Marisol.
Intent to be partners is not required; a partnership forms "whether or not the persons intend to form a partnership" (§ 202(a)).
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Capital and shared profits (Zajac)

q: Peak Fitness fires Theo, a personal trainer, but for months he keeps wearing Peak shirts and using Peak's sign-up forms. Peak's manager learns that Theo is selling "Peak training packages" to gym members and does nothing. Ella, a member, pays Theo $900 for a package he never delivers. Ella sues Peak on an estoppel theory. Which of the following must Ella show?
o: That Peak intentionally or carelessly caused her belief, or knew of it and failed to take reasonable steps to correct it.
That she justifiably relied on the belief and changed her position to her detriment.
That Theo still had actual authority to sell packages when she paid him.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Estoppel rests on the principal's conduct, including a failure to correct a belief it knows others hold (R3d § 2.05).
True. Estoppel protects only a third party who was induced to make a detrimental change in position; Ella paid $900.
False. If Theo had actual authority, Ella would not need estoppel. Estoppel fills the gap when there is no authority at all.
Correct. Under R3d § 2.05, Ella must show Peak's intentional or careless conduct (or its knowing failure to correct her belief) and her justifiable, detrimental reliance.
C is wrong; estoppel does not require actual authority.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Estoppel after the agency ends

q: Hal and Ivy are limited partners in Westgate Storage, L.P., and also the officers of Westgate GP, Inc., its only general partner. Acting as officers of the corporation, they sign a supply contract that the LP later breaches. The supplier knew it was dealing with a limited partnership whose general partner was a corporation. Under Frigidaire Sales Corp. v. Union Properties, Inc., which of the following statements is true?
o: Hal and Ivy are personally liable, because limited partners who take part in control of the business lose their shield.
Hal and Ivy are personally liable, because using a corporation as general partner is a sham designed to evade liability.
Hal and Ivy are not personally liable, because they acted only as officers of the corporate general partner.
Hal and Ivy are personally liable only up to the value of their shares in Westgate GP, Inc.
None of the above.
oe: Frigidaire held that the two did not take part in control as individuals; they acted as officers of the corporate general partner. And ULPA (2001) § 303 has since largely eliminated the control rule anyway.
Using a corporate general partner is a common, legitimate structure. Its purpose is to give everyone in the LP limited liability.

Correct. They acted only as officers of the corporate general partner, and the supplier knew it was dealing with the corporation. If the corporation is undercapitalized, the remedy is to pierce its veil, not to treat the limited partners as general partners.
Shareholders of the corporate general partner risk only what they put into it; no rule makes them liable up to that amount for the LP's debts.
C is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Corporate general partner (Frigidaire)

q: Lia, a partner in a RUPA landscaping partnership, stops by the firm's equipment yard after hours to drop off a mower and brings her six-year-old son. While she loads the mower, she carelessly leaves a trimmer running, and it injures a visiting client. The client sues the partnership, which then seeks indemnity from Lia. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The partnership can recover from Lia, because a partner must indemnify the partnership for any harm her negligence causes.
The partnership is liable, and it cannot shift the loss to Lia, whose conduct was at most ordinary negligence.
The partnership is not liable, because Lia's errand was partly personal, since she brought her son along.
The partnership is liable, but only Lia, and not the other partners, can be held personally liable to the client.
None of the above.
oe: The statute points the other way. A partnership must indemnify a partner for liabilities incurred in the ordinary course (§ 401(c)); it does not give the partnership indemnity from a partner who was merely negligent.

Correct. As in Moren v. Jax Restaurant, the partnership is liable for a partner's tort in the ordinary course of business (§ 305), and indemnity runs from the partnership to the partner, not the reverse. Ordinary negligence is not a breach of the duty of care (§ 409(c)).
Mixed personal and business purposes do not take the act outside the ordinary course. Dropping off equipment is partnership business.
All partners are jointly and severally liable for partnership obligations (§ 306(a)), including those arising from one partner's tort.
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Indemnity runs to the partner (Moren)

q: Mara sells insurance for Harbor Agency. Her non-compete expired years ago. Harbor's customer and policy-expiration lists are kept in an unlocked file that any employee may consult, and insurance buyers in town routinely compare agencies at renewal. Mara quits, joins a competitor, and calls the Harbor customers she remembers. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Mara is not liable, because Harbor's lists were not trade secrets and nothing else bars her from competing.
Mara is liable, because customer lists are always trade secrets.
Mara is liable, because a departing agent may never solicit her former principal's customers.
Mara is not liable, because an agent's fiduciary duties end the moment she quits, so she may use anything she learned on the job.
Mara is liable only if she calls more than half of Harbor's customers.
oe: Correct. As in Corroon & Black-Rutters & Roberts v. Hosch, widely accessible lists of insurance buyers who shop around are not trade secrets, and without a non-compete a departing agent may solicit former clients.
Whether a list is a trade secret depends on the circumstances. Lists open to every employee, of customers who shop around anyway, may not qualify.
After leaving, an agent may compete and may solicit customers, so long as she does not use trade secrets or confidential information.
Some obligations survive: she still may not use trade secrets or confidential information after leaving (R2d § 396; R3d § 8.05).
No numerical rule decides the question; the issue is whether she used protected information.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Leaving without a non-compete (Corroon & Black)

q: Two majority partners in a shopping-center partnership exclude the minority partner from management. A court orders the partnership dissolved and its property sold. The majority partners want to bid at the sale. Under Prentiss v. Sheffel, which of the following statements is true?
o: They may never bid, because a fiduciary may not buy partnership property at a sale it helped cause.
They may bid only if the minority partner consents.
They may bid only if they first pay the minority partner damages for the exclusion.
They may bid, absent a showing of a bad-faith plan to freeze out the minority partner.
They may bid, but they must pay at least twice the appraised value of the property.
oe: Prentiss rejected a flat bar. Partners' bids can help the minority by raising the price.
Prentiss allowed the bid without the minority partner's consent.
Nothing in Prentiss conditioned the bid on paying damages.

Correct. In Prentiss, the court let the majority partners bid at the judicial sale because there was no showing that they excluded the minority partner in bad faith to grab the property, and their bid increased the minority partner's share.
There is no such rule. The sale price is set by the bidding.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Insiders bidding at a judicial sale (Prentiss)

q: Which of the following business forms gives all of its owners limited liability without any filing with the state?
o: A limited liability partnership.
A limited partnership.
A limited liability company.
A general partnership.
None of the above.
oe: An LLP must file a statement of qualification (RUPA § 901). Until it does, its partners are general partners with unlimited liability.
An LP must file a certificate of limited partnership, and even then its general partners are personally liable.
An LLC comes into existence only when its certificate of organization is filed (ULLCA § 201).
A general partnership needs no filing, but its partners are personally liable for its obligations (RUPA § 306(a)).
Correct. Every form that limits owners' liability requires a filing with the state. The form that requires no filing, the general partnership, gives no shield at all.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — No filing, no shield

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Nell, Omar, and Pia are equal partners in Tidewater Charters, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that runs fishing and sightseeing charters from a marina. They have no written partnership agreement. The firm owns two charter boats, which are its main assets. Omar books the charters, Pia captains the larger boat, and Nell handles maintenance, fuel, and weather planning.

Omar and Pia vote to give a corporate client a 20% discount on a season of weekly charters. Nell objects that the discount is too steep. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The discount is valid, because a majority of the partners approved it.
The discount is invalid, because any partner may veto a decision she believes is unwise.
The discount is invalid, because any change in prices requires the consent of all partners.
The discount is valid, but Omar and Pia breached their duty of care by overruling Nell.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Pricing charters is in the ordinary course of the firm's business, and an ordinary-course difference may be decided by a majority (RUPA § 401(k)). Two of the three partners agreed.
Each partner has equal management rights (§ 401(h)), but that does not give a single partner a veto over ordinary-course decisions.
Unanimity is required for acts outside the ordinary course and for amending the agreement, not for routine pricing.
Outvoting a partner on a business judgment is not a breach. The duty of care reaches only gross negligence, recklessness, intentional misconduct, or knowing violations of law (§ 409(c)).
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Ordinary course: majority rules

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Nell, Omar, and Pia are equal partners in Tidewater Charters, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that runs fishing and sightseeing charters from a marina. They have no written partnership agreement. The firm owns two charter boats, which are its main assets. Omar books the charters, Pia captains the larger boat, and Nell handles maintenance, fuel, and weather planning.

Without telling Nell or Omar, Pia signs a contract selling the larger charter boat to Shoreline Tours for $300,000. Shoreline believes Pia speaks for the firm. Nell and Omar object. Is the partnership bound?
o: Yes, because every partner is an agent of the partnership and can bind it to any transaction with a third party who lacks notice of a limit.
Yes, because Shoreline reasonably believed that Pia was acting for the partnership.
No, unless Nell and Omar authorized the sale.
No, because a partner can never sell partnership property.
None of the above.
oe: That rule covers acts apparently carrying on the partnership's business in the ordinary course. Selling one of the firm's two boats is not.
Belief alone is not enough for an act outside the ordinary course; the other partners must have authorized it.
Correct. An act that is not apparently for carrying on the partnership's business in the ordinary course binds the partnership only if the other partners authorized it (RUPA § 301(2)).
Any partner may sign a conveyance of partnership property when the partnership is bound (§ 302); the problem here is authority, not the power to sign.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Outside the ordinary course

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Nell, Omar, and Pia are equal partners in Tidewater Charters, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that runs fishing and sightseeing charters from a marina. They have no written partnership agreement. The firm owns two charter boats, which are its main assets. Omar books the charters, Pia captains the larger boat, and Nell handles maintenance, fuel, and weather planning.

Assume instead that the partners had filed a statement of partnership authority stating that "Nell is authorized to sell any vessel of the partnership." Later, Omar and Pia tell Nell privately not to sell the smaller boat, but she sells it to Harbor Cruises, which pays $120,000 without knowing of their instruction. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The partnership is not bound, because Omar and Pia withdrew Nell's authority before she sold the boat.
The partnership is bound, because Harbor Cruises gave value in reliance on the filed grant.
The partnership is bound only if Harbor Cruises actually read the filed statement before buying.
The partnership is not bound, because a statement of authority can only limit a partner's authority, never grant it.
None of the above.
oe: Withdrawing actual authority privately does not affect a buyer who gives value in reliance on a filed grant without knowledge to the contrary.

Correct. RUPA § 303 makes a filed grant of authority conclusive in favor of a person who gives value in reliance on it, unless that person knows of a contrary limit. Nell may owe the partnership damages for disobeying her partners.
A filed grant protects a person who gives value in reliance on it, and the statement is on the public record. The question here is Harbor's lack of knowledge of the private instruction.
A statement of partnership authority may grant or limit authority (§ 303).
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Filed grant of authority

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Nell, Omar, and Pia are equal partners in Tidewater Charters, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that runs fishing and sightseeing charters from a marina. They have no written partnership agreement. The firm owns two charter boats, which are its main assets. Omar books the charters, Pia captains the larger boat, and Nell handles maintenance, fuel, and weather planning.

Omar secretly owns a fuel dock, and he has the partnership buy all of its fuel there at the dock's ordinary prices. Nell and Pia learn about it a year later. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Omar's sales to the partnership fall within the duty to refrain from dealing with the partnership as a person with an adverse interest.
Omar has a defense if he proves that the purchases were fair to the partnership.
Omar could have avoided any claim by disclosing all material facts and obtaining the authorization of all the partners in advance.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Selling to the firm from his own business is dealing with the partnership on behalf of a person with an adverse interest (§ 409(b)(2)).
True. Fairness to the partnership is a defense to a claim under § 409(b)(2) (§ 409(g)).
True. All the partners may authorize or ratify, after full disclosure, a specific transaction that would otherwise violate the duty of loyalty (§ 409(f)).
Incomplete. C is also true.
Correct. The transactions implicate the duty of loyalty, fairness is a defense, and full disclosure plus the consent of all partners would have protected Omar.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — A partner selling to the firm

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Nell, Omar, and Pia are equal partners in Tidewater Charters, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that runs fishing and sightseeing charters from a marina. They have no written partnership agreement. The firm owns two charter boats, which are its main assets. Omar books the charters, Pia captains the larger boat, and Nell handles maintenance, fuel, and weather planning.

Nell misreads a storm forecast and cancels a booked charter that could safely have sailed. The firm loses an $8,000 fee. Omar and Pia sue Nell for breaching her duty of care. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Nell is liable, because a partner must manage the partnership's affairs with the care of a reasonably prudent person.
Nell is liable, because any partner whose decision causes a loss must reimburse the partnership.
Nell is not liable, because ordinary negligence is not a breach of a partner's duty of care.
Nell is not liable, because partners owe one another no duty of care at all.
None of the above.
oe: That is not the RUPA standard. The partner's duty of care is much narrower.
Partners are not insurers of their business decisions. Liability requires a breach of duty.

Correct. A partner's duty of care is to refrain from grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law (RUPA § 409(c)). Misreading a forecast is at most ordinary negligence.
Partners do owe a duty of care (§ 409(a), (c)); it just does not reach ordinary negligence.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Negligence is not a breach

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: The Velvet Room, a nightclub, employs Grant as a bouncer. His job is to check IDs at the door, keep the entrance clear, and remove disorderly patrons. The club's written rules forbid bouncers to strike anyone except in self-defense. When it hired Grant, the club knew that he had two convictions for assault arising from bar fights, but it did not look into them further.

Rick, a patron, plants himself in the club's doorway and keeps shoving people who try to enter. When Grant tells him to move, Rick shoves Grant too. Grant, angry, punches Rick, breaking his jaw. Rick sues the Velvet Room. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The club is not liable, because its rules forbade Grant to strike anyone except in self-defense.
The club may be vicariously liable, because Rick was interfering with Grant's job.
The club is not liable, because an intentional tort can never fall within the scope of employment.
The club is liable only if it ratified the punch afterward.
Only Grant can be liable, because he acted out of anger rather than to serve the club.
oe: Forbidden acts can still be within the scope of employment (R2d § 230). A rule against the conduct does not end the inquiry.

Correct. As in Manning v. Grimsley, an employer may be liable when an employee's assault responds to the plaintiff's conduct that is presently interfering with the employee's job. Keeping the door clear was Grant's job, and force by a bouncer is not unexpectable.
Intentional torts can be within scope; R2d § 228(1)(d) asks only whether the use of force was not unexpectable.
Ratification is one route to direct liability, but vicarious liability for a tort within the scope of employment needs no ratification.
Anger does not by itself take the act outside scope. The conduct need be actuated only in part by a purpose to serve the employer.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Force while doing the job (Manning)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: The Velvet Room, a nightclub, employs Grant as a bouncer. His job is to check IDs at the door, keep the entrance clear, and remove disorderly patrons. The club's written rules forbid bouncers to strike anyone except in self-defense. When it hired Grant, the club knew that he had two convictions for assault arising from bar fights, but it did not look into them further.

After his shift ends, Grant follows a patron who had flirted with Grant's girlfriend inside the club to a diner three blocks away and beats him up. Is the club vicariously liable under respondeat superior?
o: No, because Grant was engaged in an independent course of conduct that served no purpose of the club.
Yes, because the club knew Grant had a history of violence.
Yes, because Grant met the patron at work, so the attack grew out of his employment.
No, because bouncers are independent contractors, not employees.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under R3d § 7.07(2), an act is outside the scope of employment when it occurs within an independent course of conduct not intended by the employee to serve any purpose of the employer. A personal grudge pursued off duty and off premises is the classic example (compare Bushey's example of a sailor shooting his wife's lover).
That knowledge bears on direct liability for negligent hiring or retention, not on whether this attack was within the scope of employment.
A workplace connection is not enough when the later attack serves only the employee's own ends.
Nothing suggests Grant is an independent contractor; the club controls how he does his job.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Purely personal violence

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: The Velvet Room, a nightclub, employs Grant as a bouncer. His job is to check IDs at the door, keep the entrance clear, and remove disorderly patrons. The club's written rules forbid bouncers to strike anyone except in self-defense. When it hired Grant, the club knew that he had two convictions for assault arising from bar fights, but it did not look into them further.

Which of the following theories could make the Velvet Room liable for Grant's punch of Rick in the doorway?
o: Respondeat superior, because the punch was within the scope of Grant's employment.
Direct liability for negligently hiring or retaining Grant, given what the club knew about his record.
Liability under a nondelegable duty, because a nightclub may never delegate door work to an employee.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. As in Manning, force used to deal with someone interfering with the job can be within scope.

True. A principal is directly liable for harm caused by its own negligence in selecting, retaining, or supervising an agent (R3d § 7.05). The club knew of two assault convictions and did not look into them.
False. A nondelegable duty concerns attempts to shift responsibility to an independent contractor; Grant is the club's own employee.
Correct. The club may be vicariously liable for a tort within the scope of employment and directly liable for its own negligent hiring or retention.
C is wrong; nondelegable duties are not the issue when the actor is an employee.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Direct and vicarious liability

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: The Velvet Room, a nightclub, employs Grant as a bouncer. His job is to check IDs at the door, keep the entrance clear, and remove disorderly patrons. The club's written rules forbid bouncers to strike anyone except in self-defense. When it hired Grant, the club knew that he had two convictions for assault arising from bar fights, but it did not look into them further.

Defending against Rick's claim, which argument gives the Velvet Room its best chance under Restatement (Second) of Agency § 228?
o: Grant punched Rick during his shift, at the club's door.
Removing disorderly patrons is part of a bouncer's job.
Bouncers sometimes have to use force on patrons.
Grant acted solely out of personal anger at being shoved, not to serve the club.
None of the above.
oe: That fact helps Rick: the punch was within the authorized time and space limits.
That also helps Rick: the conduct was of the kind Grant was employed to perform.
That helps Rick as well: the use of force was not unexpectable by the employer.

Correct. The club's best argument goes to the purpose prong: conduct is within scope only if actuated, at least in part, by a purpose to serve the master (§ 228(1)(c)). If Grant acted purely from personal rage, the club can argue he left its business, though Manning suggests a jury could still find a mixed motive.
D is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — The club's best § 228 argument

q: The Ridge Runners, an unincorporated hiking club, has no assets. At a meeting, members Ana and Ben vote to rent a mountain lodge for the club's retreat and direct the treasurer to sign the rental contract; member Cal votes no; member Dee is absent. The club cannot pay the $8,000 rent. Under Karl Rove & Co. v. Thornburgh, who is personally liable to the lodge?
o: Every member of the club, because members of an unincorporated association are always liable for its debts.
Ana and Ben, because they authorized the contract, and the treasurer signed it as their agent.
Only the treasurer, because she signed the contract.
No one, because an association with no assets cannot enter a binding contract.
Ana, Ben, and Cal, because each attended the meeting where the contract was approved.
oe: Membership alone is not the test. A member is bound by contracts he authorized, assented to, or ratified.

Correct. A member of an unincorporated association is personally bound by contracts that he authorizes, assents to, or ratifies, personally or through an agent (Karl Rove & Co. v. Thornburgh). Cal objected and Dee took no part.
The treasurer may also be liable as a party, but Ana and Ben are bound because the treasurer acted as their agent.
Lack of assets does not void the contract; it means the lodge will look to those who authorized it.
Attending a meeting and voting no is not authorizing, assenting to, or ratifying the contract.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Members of an unincorporated association (Karl Rove)

q: Owen owns a rental house. He tells his property manager, Rae, "Get the roof fixed before winter." Rae hires a roofer. The night before the roofer arrives, a storm hits, and Rae buys $300 of tarps from a hardware store, on Owen's account, to cover the exposed attic. Owen refuses to pay for the tarps. Is Owen bound?
o: Yes, because Rae had implied actual authority to buy the tarps.
No, because an agent may never buy goods on the principal's credit without express permission.
Yes, but only because Owen ratified the purchase by owning the house the tarps protected.
