No, because Owen authorized Rae only to hire a roofer, and he said nothing about buying supplies.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Implied actual authority covers acts incidental or reasonably necessary to the agent's express duties, and emergencies are a recognized source of implied authority (compare Mill Street Church: the job could not be done without help).
An agent authorized to accomplish a result may make purchases reasonably necessary to it, and emergencies widen implied authority.
Owning the property is not an affirmance of the purchase. Owen is bound without ratification.
Express authority is not the limit of actual authority. An agent also has implied authority to do what is incidental or reasonably necessary to accomplish the express task.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Incidental authority

q: A law firm organized as a general partnership gives some lawyers the title "income partner." They receive fixed salaries and bonuses, share in no profits or losses, cannot vote on firm matters, and get back their small capital accounts without gain when they leave. A malpractice plaintiff sues the income partners personally as partners. Which of the following statements is true?
o: They are partners, because the firm publicly calls them partners, and title controls partnership status.
They are partners, because they made capital contributions to the firm.
They are not partners, and so they are not vicariously liable as partners for the firm's malpractice.
They are partners for liability purposes, but employees for all other purposes.
None of the above.
oe: Titles do not control. Partnership status turns on co-ownership: sharing profits and losses and having a say in management.
A small contribution returned without gain is not the kind of capital stake that makes someone a co-owner, and they share no profits or losses.

Correct. In Davis v. Loftus, income partners who received fixed pay, shared no profits or losses, and could not vote were not partners under the UPA, so they were not vicariously liable. (A claimant who relied on their being held out as partners might still try partnership by estoppel.)
Partnership status is decided on one set of factors; there is no rule that makes a person a partner only for liability.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Nonequity "partners" (Davis v. Loftus)

q: Under the ULLCA, the operating agreement of Ridge Coffee, LLC states that the company is "manager-managed" and names Sam as its manager. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Matters in the ordinary course of the company's activities are decided by the manager.
A majority of the members may remove Sam as manager at any time, without notice or cause.
Sam may amend the operating agreement on his own, because he controls the company's management.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. In a manager-managed LLC, matters relating to the company's activities and affairs are decided exclusively by the manager or managers, except as the act provides (§ 407(c)(1)).
True. A manager may be removed at any time by a majority of the members without notice or cause (§ 407(c)(4)).
False. Amending the operating agreement requires the consent of all members, even in a manager-managed LLC (§ 407(c)(3)).
Correct. The manager decides ordinary-course matters, and a majority of the members may remove the manager without cause. Acts outside the ordinary course and amendments still need all the members.
C is false; amendments need every member's consent.

q: Nina and Owen form a UPA partnership to restore antique furniture, agreeing to split profits equally and saying nothing about losses. Nina contributes $40,000. Owen contributes $500 and all of the restoration work. The business fails, and $20,000 of Nina's capital is lost. In a jurisdiction that follows Kovacik v. Reed, which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Owen owes Nina nothing, because Owen contributed his labor, and a partner who contributes services is never liable for capital losses.
Owen must share the capital loss with Nina as the statute provides, because he made a capital contribution.
Owen owes Nina nothing, because they never agreed to share losses.
Owen must repay all of Nina's lost capital, because he controlled the restoration work that caused the losses.
None of the above.
oe: The Kovacik rule applies only to a partner who contributed services alone. Owen contributed some capital, so the exception does not fit.

Correct. Kovacik is a narrow exception to UPA § 18(a), and courts do not apply it when the service partner made any capital contribution, even a nominal one, or was paid a salary. The statute's rule applies: losses are shared like profits.
Silence on losses brings in the default rule that losses are shared like profits (UPA § 18(a)); Kovacik is the only exception, and it does not apply here.
No rule makes the managing partner bear all losses; losses are shared like profits.
B is correct.
topic: 11 · Loss sharing (Kovacik) — Kovacik's limits

q: Compared with a corporation, which of the following is an advantage of a general partnership?
o: It can be formed without any filing or formality.
Its income is taxed only once, at the owners' level.
Its owners are not personally liable for its obligations.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A general partnership is the default form for two or more people carrying on a business as co-owners; no filing is required.
True. A partnership has no entity-level income tax; profits pass through to the partners.
False. That is the main drawback of a general partnership; partners are personally liable (RUPA § 306(a)).
Correct. Simplicity and a single layer of tax are a general partnership's advantages; unlimited personal liability is its chief disadvantage.
C is false.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — General partnership: pros

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), brothers Hugo and Ivan are equal partners in Suds City, a laundromat. They have no written agreement and never discussed how long the partnership would last, though both hoped the business would someday earn enough to repay a loan from Hugo. Hugo lent the partnership $60,000, payable on demand, to buy machines; each brother also contributed $5,000 in capital. The laundromat lost money for six years. This year a large apartment complex opened next door, and the business turned a profit for the first time. Hugo immediately announces that he is dissolving the partnership. Ivan suspects that Hugo wants to buy the business cheaply at a forced sale and keep the new profits for himself.

Ivan argues that the brothers formed a partnership for a term that lasts until Hugo's loan is repaid from profits, so Hugo cannot dissolve it now. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Ivan is right, because every partnership implicitly lasts until the partners recoup their investments.
Ivan is right, because once a business turns profitable, a partner can no longer dissolve it.
Ivan is wrong; a shared hope of repayment from profits does not create a term.
Ivan is wrong, because under the UPA a term must always be stated in writing.
None of the above.
oe: A general hope of recouping an investment is not enough to imply a term; otherwise nearly every partnership would be one for a term.
Turning a profit does not take away the power or right to dissolve an at-will partnership.

Correct. In Page v. Page, a mere expectation that a loan would be repaid from profits did not create a partnership for a term. Contrast Owen v. Cohen, where the parties' understanding that a loan would be repaid from profits implied a term.
A term may be implied from clear evidence of an understood duration or undertaking; it need not be written.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — At will or for a term (Page v. Page)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), brothers Hugo and Ivan are equal partners in Suds City, a laundromat. They have no written agreement and never discussed how long the partnership would last, though both hoped the business would someday earn enough to repay a loan from Hugo. Hugo lent the partnership $60,000, payable on demand, to buy machines; each brother also contributed $5,000 in capital. The laundromat lost money for six years. This year a large apartment complex opened next door, and the business turned a profit for the first time. Hugo immediately announces that he is dissolving the partnership. Ivan suspects that Hugo wants to buy the business cheaply at a forced sale and keep the new profits for himself.

Assume the partnership is at will. Which of the following statements best describes Hugo's power to dissolve it?
o: Hugo may dissolve it, but only in good faith, not to freeze Ivan out.
Hugo may not dissolve the partnership while it is profitable.
Hugo may dissolve the partnership for any reason, because fiduciary duties do not limit a partner's power to dissolve a partnership at will.
Hugo may dissolve the partnership only with Ivan's consent.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Page v. Page held that a partner in an at-will partnership may dissolve it, but the power must be exercised in good faith; a partner may not dissolve to appropriate the business's new prosperity for himself.
Profitability does not end a partner's right to dissolve an at-will partnership.
Fiduciary duties continue to govern how a partner exercises the power to dissolve (Page v. Page).
Under the UPA, any partner may dissolve an at-will partnership by his express will (§ 31(1)(b)).
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Good faith limits dissolution

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), brothers Hugo and Ivan are equal partners in Suds City, a laundromat. They have no written agreement and never discussed how long the partnership would last, though both hoped the business would someday earn enough to repay a loan from Hugo. Hugo lent the partnership $60,000, payable on demand, to buy machines; each brother also contributed $5,000 in capital. The laundromat lost money for six years. This year a large apartment complex opened next door, and the business turned a profit for the first time. Hugo immediately announces that he is dissolving the partnership. Ivan suspects that Hugo wants to buy the business cheaply at a forced sale and keep the new profits for himself.

Assume Hugo dissolves the partnership in good faith. Which of the following statements about winding up under the UPA is true?
o: Either brother may insist that the partnership's assets be sold and the net proceeds paid to the partners in cash.
Hugo may keep running the laundromat himself and pay Ivan the book value of his interest.
After dissolution, each brother's authority to bind the partnership is generally limited to acts appropriate for winding up.
A and C.
None of the above.
oe: True. After a dissolution that violates no agreement, each partner may have the partnership property applied to discharge its liabilities and the surplus paid in cash (UPA § 38(1)).
False. That buy-out option belongs to the innocent partners after a wrongful dissolution (§ 38(2)). In a rightful dissolution, either partner can force a liquidation.
True. Dissolution begins winding up, not termination, and a partner's authority is limited to winding up, subject to rules protecting third parties without notice (UPA §§ 30, 33, 35).
Correct. Either partner may force a liquidation after a rightful dissolution, and authority shrinks to winding-up acts.
D is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Rightful dissolution under the UPA

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), brothers Hugo and Ivan are equal partners in Suds City, a laundromat. They have no written agreement and never discussed how long the partnership would last, though both hoped the business would someday earn enough to repay a loan from Hugo. Hugo lent the partnership $60,000, payable on demand, to buy machines; each brother also contributed $5,000 in capital. The laundromat lost money for six years. This year a large apartment complex opened next door, and the business turned a profit for the first time. Hugo immediately announces that he is dissolving the partnership. Ivan suspects that Hugo wants to buy the business cheaply at a forced sale and keep the new profits for himself.

While the business is being wound up, the landlord offers Hugo a new ten-year lease of the laundromat space. Hugo signs it in his own name, planning to reopen the laundromat alone. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Hugo did nothing wrong, because once a partnership dissolves the partners owe one another no further duties.
Hugo did nothing wrong, because the new lease begins after the old partnership's lease ends.
Hugo breached his duty of loyalty by taking the partnership's opportunity during winding up.
Hugo breached only a duty of care, because he negligently failed to offer the lease to Ivan.
None of the above.
oe: Fiduciary duties continue until winding up is complete.
The renewal grew out of the partnership's business, as in Meinhard v. Salmon. When it begins does not change that.
Correct. As in Monin v. Monin, partners' fiduciary duties continue until winding up is complete, and a partner may not grab the firm's key asset or opportunity for himself during that period.
Taking a partnership opportunity is a loyalty problem, not a question of careless management.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Duties during winding up (Monin)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), brothers Hugo and Ivan are equal partners in Suds City, a laundromat. They have no written agreement and never discussed how long the partnership would last, though both hoped the business would someday earn enough to repay a loan from Hugo. Hugo lent the partnership $60,000, payable on demand, to buy machines; each brother also contributed $5,000 in capital. The laundromat lost money for six years. This year a large apartment complex opened next door, and the business turned a profit for the first time. Hugo immediately announces that he is dissolving the partnership. Ivan suspects that Hugo wants to buy the business cheaply at a forced sale and keep the new profits for himself.

The laundromat's assets sell for $100,000. The partnership owes outside creditors $30,000 and still owes Hugo his $60,000 loan. How is the $100,000 distributed under UPA § 40(b)?
o: Outside creditors $30,000; then Hugo $60,000 on his loan; then $5,000 of capital to each brother; nothing is left as profit.
Outside creditors $30,000; then $5,000 of capital to each brother; then Hugo $60,000 on his loan.
Outside creditors and Hugo's loan are paid pro rata, then the rest is split equally as profit.
The $100,000 is split equally between the brothers, who must then pay the creditors themselves.
Hugo $60,000 on his loan first; then the outside creditors $30,000; then $5,000 of capital to each brother.
oe: Correct. UPA § 40(b) pays (1) outside creditors, (2) partners' loans and advances, (3) partners' capital, and (4) profits. That leaves $10,000 for capital ($5,000 each) and nothing for profits. Hugo receives $65,000 and Ivan $5,000.
Partner loans come before capital under § 40(b).
The UPA ranks partner loans behind outside creditors, rather than paying them together. (RUPA § 806 is the statute that pays partner-creditors with outside creditors.)
Creditors come first; partners take nothing until the partnership's liabilities are paid.
Outside creditors come before partners' loans.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — UPA § 40(b) payout order

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Leah is the purchasing director of Pinecrest Hotels, a regional hotel chain, at a salary of $120,000 a year. She chooses the vendors for linens, cleaning supplies, and furniture. Without telling Pinecrest, Leah accepts two free Caribbean vacations from Crisp Linen Co., which wins all of Pinecrest's linen business. Crisp's prices and quality are as good as any competitor's, and Pinecrest loses no money on its linen contracts.

Pinecrest discovers the vacations and demands that Leah account for their value. Leah responds that Pinecrest lost nothing. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Leah may keep the vacations, because Pinecrest suffered no loss.
Leah must account to Pinecrest for the value of the vacations.
Leah may keep the vacations, because accepting gifts from vendors is a matter of company policy, not fiduciary duty.
Leah must account for the vacations only if Crisp's prices were higher than a competitor's.
None of the above.
oe: An agent's duty to account for benefits obtained through her position does not depend on any loss to the principal.

Correct. An agent may not acquire a material benefit from a third party in connection with actions taken for the principal (R3d § 8.02). As in Reading v. Regem, a servant who uses his position to obtain a gain must account for it, even if the employer lost nothing.
Secret benefits from a vendor in exchange for business are a core loyalty problem, whatever the company's gift policy.
Fair prices do not cure the secret benefit; the duty is not to profit from her position without consent.
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Benefits from position (Reading v. Regem)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Leah is the purchasing director of Pinecrest Hotels, a regional hotel chain, at a salary of $120,000 a year. She chooses the vendors for linens, cleaning supplies, and furniture. Without telling Pinecrest, Leah accepts two free Caribbean vacations from Crisp Linen Co., which wins all of Pinecrest's linen business. Crisp's prices and quality are as good as any competitor's, and Pinecrest loses no money on its linen contracts.

A convention group asks Pinecrest for 300 custom embroidered bathrobes. Leah believes Pinecrest's own suppliers cannot fill the order in time, so without telling anyone she sends the order to her cousin's embroidery shop and takes a $9,000 commission. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Leah breached her duty of loyalty and must disgorge the commission, because she had to let Pinecrest decide.
Leah did nothing wrong, because the convention group received its robes and was satisfied.
Leah breached only her duty of obedience, because nobody had told her what to do with orders like this one.
Leah did nothing wrong, because Pinecrest could not have filled the order anyway.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In General Automotive Manufacturing Co. v. Singer, a manager who sent orders he thought his employer could not fill to other shops and kept the profit had to disgorge it. A fiduciary must disclose the opportunity and let the principal decide.
The customer's satisfaction does not answer whether Leah was loyal to Pinecrest.
The core problem is loyalty and disclosure: she diverted business and took a secret profit.
Whether Pinecrest could fill the order was Pinecrest's decision to make, not Leah's.
A is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Orders the principal can't fill (General Automotive)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Leah is the purchasing director of Pinecrest Hotels, a regional hotel chain, at a salary of $120,000 a year. She chooses the vendors for linens, cleaning supplies, and furniture. Without telling Pinecrest, Leah accepts two free Caribbean vacations from Crisp Linen Co., which wins all of Pinecrest's linen business. Crisp's prices and quality are as good as any competitor's, and Pinecrest loses no money on its linen contracts.

Leah quits and goes to work for Crisp Linen. She has memorized the confidential prices and contract terms Pinecrest negotiated with each of its vendors, and she uses them to help Crisp outbid those vendors. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Leah may freely use the information, because she took no documents and relied only on her memory.
Leah may not use the pricing information, but she may use her general skill and knowledge.
Leah may freely use the information, because her duties to Pinecrest ended completely when she quit.
Leah may not work for any of Pinecrest's vendors, because she owes Pinecrest a continuing duty not to compete.
None of the above.
oe: Under the Restatement (Third), using confidential information is a breach whether it is carried away on paper or in memory (R3d § 8.05 & illus.).

Correct. After the agency ends, a former agent may compete and use general knowledge and skill, but not the principal's confidential information, even if it was memorized (R3d § 8.05(2); compare R2d § 396).
The duty not to use or disclose the principal's confidential information survives the end of the agency (R3d § 8.05(2)).
Without a non-compete agreement, a former agent may compete with the former principal or join its vendors.
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Confidential information after leaving

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Leah is the purchasing director of Pinecrest Hotels, a regional hotel chain, at a salary of $120,000 a year. She chooses the vendors for linens, cleaning supplies, and furniture. Without telling Pinecrest, Leah accepts two free Caribbean vacations from Crisp Linen Co., which wins all of Pinecrest's linen business. Crisp's prices and quality are as good as any competitor's, and Pinecrest loses no money on its linen contracts.

Which of the following remedies may Pinecrest pursue against Leah?
o: Disgorgement of the vacations' value and the $9,000 commission, even without proof of loss.
Forfeiture of compensation for the period in which Leah was disloyal.
An injunction against further use of Pinecrest's confidential information.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Secret profits belong to the principal; disgorgement removes the incentive to breach (Reading; General Automotive).
True. Withholding or recovering compensation for a period of intentional disloyalty is a recognized remedy.
True. Injunctive relief protects against continuing misuse of confidential information (compare Town & Country v. Newbery).
Incomplete. An injunction is also available.
Correct. A principal may seek disgorgement, forfeiture of compensation, damages, an accounting, a constructive trust, and an injunction against a disloyal agent.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Remedies against a disloyal agent

q: On the last day before the statute of limitations runs, attorney Nash hires a courier service to file a client's complaint. The courier arrives after the clerk's office closes, and the claim is lost. The client sues Nash, who argues that the courier was an independent contractor. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Nash is not liable, because a principal is never liable for the negligence of an independent contractor.
Nash is not liable, because he chose a reputable courier service.
Nash may be liable only if he controlled the details of how the courier drove to the courthouse.
Nash may be liable, because his duty to the client is nondelegable.
The client's only claim is against the courier service.
oe: The general rule has exceptions, and a nondelegable duty is one of them.
Careful selection defeats a claim of negligent selection, but not liability for breach of a nondelegable duty.
Retained control is a separate exception. Liability for a nondelegable duty does not depend on it.

Correct. As in Kleeman v. Rheingold, some duties are so important that the person who owes them cannot escape responsibility by hiring an independent contractor (R3d § 7.06). A lawyer's duty to see that the client's action is properly commenced is one of them.
The client may sue the courier, but Nash remains answerable for his nondelegable duty.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — A nondelegable duty

q: The board of the Lakeshore Homeowners' Association appoints Judge Park, a retired judge, to hear disputes between neighbors. Under the association's bylaws, the board cannot instruct Park, overrule his rulings, or remove him during his three-year term. A homeowner sues the association over one of Park's rulings, claiming Park acted as its agent. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Park is not the association's agent in deciding disputes, because the association has no right to control how he does it.
Park is the association's agent, because the association appointed him and pays his fee.
Park is the association's agent for all purposes, because an agent for one purpose is an agent for every purpose.
Park is the association's agent only if the bylaws call him one.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Control is an element of agency. As in Rose v. Giamatti, someone given exclusive, independent authority that the appointing body cannot control acts more like an arbitrator than an agent, at least for that function.
Appointment and payment are not enough; the principal must have the right to control the undertaking.
A person may be an agent for some purposes and not others (Rose v. Giamatti).
Labels do not control either way (R3d § 1.02); what matters is consent and the right to control.
A is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — No control, no agency (Rose v. Giamatti)

q: Vanya, a partner in a RUPA partnership, transfers her entire transferable interest to her daughter as a gift. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The daughter becomes a partner with full management and voting rights.
The daughter receives only Vanya's distributions, and the others may expel Vanya by unanimous vote.
Vanya is automatically dissociated by the transfer.
The transfer is void, because a partner's interest cannot be transferred without the consent of all partners.
The daughter becomes a co-owner of specific partnership property.
oe: A transferee does not become a partner. She has no right to take part in management or to inspect the books.

Correct. A transferee is entitled only to the distributions the transferor would receive. Vanya remains a partner, but the other partners may expel her by unanimous vote because she has transferred all of her transferable interest (RUPA § 601(4)(B)).
A transfer of a transferable interest is not, by itself, an event of dissociation.
A transferable interest may be transferred without the others' consent; what cannot be transferred alone is the status of partner.
A partner is not a co-owner of partnership property (§ 501), so there is no such interest to transfer.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Transferring an interest

q: A partnership agreement forbids each partner from offering "wired broadband service" in the partnership's territory, and defines that term narrowly. One partner begins offering a new satellite internet service there. The other partners sue, arguing that the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing should extend the noncompete to cover the new service. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The partners win, because the implied covenant bars any conduct that frustrates the purpose of a partnership agreement.
The partners lose, because a court will not use the implied covenant to expand a precise, unambiguous noncompete.
The partners win, because every partner owes a duty not to compete that the agreement cannot narrow.
The partners lose, because the implied covenant does not apply to partnership agreements.
None of the above.
oe: The implied covenant is a narrow gap-filler. It does not override or expand express, unambiguous terms.

Correct. In Cincinnati SMSA L.P. v. Cincinnati Bell Cellular Systems Co., the Delaware Supreme Court refused to use the implied covenant to broaden a narrowly drawn noncompete. Compare Nemec v. Shrader: the covenant does not override what the contract expressly addresses.
A partnership agreement may identify activities that do not violate the duty of loyalty, if not manifestly unreasonable, and the parties drew this line themselves.
The covenant applies to partnership agreements; it simply does not rewrite clear terms.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Implied covenant and a narrow noncompete

q: A public limited partnership's agreement eliminates the general partner's default fiduciary duties and provides instead that any conflict transaction is approved if the general partner's conflicts committee approves it "in good faith," meaning that the committee members subjectively believe it is in the partnership's best interests. The committee approves a sale of assets to the general partner's parent company. A unitholder sues. Under Delaware law, which of the following statements is true?
o: The court applies the default fiduciary duty of loyalty, because fiduciary duties can never be eliminated in a Delaware limited partnership.
The court reviews whether the price was entirely fair to the limited partners, regardless of what the agreement says.
The unitholder automatically wins, because any sale to an affiliate of the general partner is void.
The court asks whether the committee met the contractual standard of subjective good faith that the agreement chose.
None of the above.
oe: Delaware lets an LP agreement eliminate default fiduciary duties and substitute contractual standards; only the implied covenant cannot be eliminated.
Entire-fairness review is a default fiduciary standard that the agreement displaced here.
Affiliate transactions are not void; the agreement set a procedure for approving them.

Correct. In In re El Paso Pipeline Partners, the court applied the contractual standard the parties chose; investors in Delaware alternative entities may get only the protections the contract gives them. (A later trial on a second sale found the committee had breached that standard.)
D is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Contractual standards (El Paso)

q: A federal statute covers only employers with 15 or more employees. A medical practice has 13 staff members and four physician-owners who manage the practice, hire and fire staff, set its rules, and share its profits and losses. Under Clackamas Gastroenterology Associates v. Wells, how should a court decide whether the physicians count as employees?
o: By applying the common-law control test, guided by the EEOC's factors.
By asking whether the physicians receive salaries, since anyone on a payroll is an employee.
By looking at the physicians' titles, such as "shareholder" or "director."
By deferring to how the practice is organized under state law, because state-law form controls federal coverage.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Clackamas adopted the common-law control test, guided by the EEOC's six factors. Owners who run the business and share its profits and losses look like employers, not employees.
Receiving a salary is one fact, but the test turns on control over the organization.
Titles are not decisive; the inquiry looks at control.
Clackamas looked past the corporate form to the actual relationship.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Owner-physicians as employees (Clackamas)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Quinn, Ross, Sela, and Tom are partners in Summit Physical Therapy, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says that the partnership will continue for fifteen years and that profits are shared equally; it says nothing about what happens when a partner dies. In Year 2, the partnership signed a ten-year lease for its clinic. In Year 4, Ross dies. His will leaves everything to his widow, Una, who is also the executor of his estate.

What is the immediate effect of Ross's death on the partnership?
o: The partnership automatically dissolves, because the death of a partner always dissolves a partnership.
Ross is dissociated, and the firm continues unless at least half of the others vote within 90 days to wind up.
Ross's estate becomes a partner in his place, with all of his management rights.
Ross is dissociated, and his estate owes the partnership damages for his wrongful dissociation before the end of the term.
None of the above.
oe: That was the UPA (1914) rule. Under the RUPA, death dissociates the partner but does not by itself dissolve the firm.

Correct. Death is a dissociation event (§ 601(7)(A)). In a term partnership, dissociation by death leads to dissolution only if, within 90 days, at least half of the remaining partners agree to wind up (§ 801(2)(A)); otherwise the business continues and Ross's interest is bought out (§ 701).
An estate succeeds only to the deceased partner's transferable interest, not to the status of partner.
Death is not on the § 602(b) list of wrongful dissociations.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Death in a term partnership

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Quinn, Ross, Sela, and Tom are partners in Summit Physical Therapy, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says that the partnership will continue for fifteen years and that profits are shared equally; it says nothing about what happens when a partner dies. In Year 2, the partnership signed a ten-year lease for its clinic. In Year 4, Ross dies. His will leaves everything to his widow, Una, who is also the executor of his estate.

Seventy-five days after Ross's death, Sela tells her partners that she wants to wind up the business. Quinn and Tom want to continue. What is the result?
o: The partnership dissolves, because any remaining partner may force a dissolution after a partner dies.
The partnership dissolves, because Sela acted within 90 days of Ross's death.
The partnership continues, because a term partnership can be dissolved before its term ends only by unanimous consent.
The partnership continues, because only one of the three remaining partners wants to wind up.
None of the above.
oe: § 801(2)(A) requires the vote or consent of at least half of the remaining partners, not just one.
Acting within 90 days is necessary but not sufficient; at least half of the remaining partners must agree.
Unanimous consent is one route (§ 801(2)(B)), but the 90-day vote after a death is another.
Correct. At least half of the remaining partners must vote or consent to wind up within 90 days (§ 801(2)(A)). One of three is not enough, so the partnership continues and buys out Ross's interest.
D is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Counting the remaining partners

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Quinn, Ross, Sela, and Tom are partners in Summit Physical Therapy, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says that the partnership will continue for fifteen years and that profits are shared equally; it says nothing about what happens when a partner dies. In Year 2, the partnership signed a ten-year lease for its clinic. In Year 4, Ross dies. His will leaves everything to his widow, Una, who is also the executor of his estate.

Assume the partnership continues. Una, as executor, demands that the partners auction off the clinic's equipment and patient contracts so that Ross's estate can receive its share of a "true market price." Which of the following statements is true?
o: Una can force a sale of all partnership assets, because a deceased partner's estate is always entitled to a liquidation.
Una can force a sale, but only of the assets Ross himself contributed.
Una cannot force a sale; the estate is entitled to the § 701 buyout price.
Una cannot force a sale, and the estate must wait until the fifteen-year term ends to be paid.
None of the above.
oe: Under the RUPA, a dissociation that does not cause dissolution leads to a buyout, not a liquidation.
The estate has no claim to specific partnership property; a partner is not a co-owner of it (§ 501).

Correct. When the business continues, the partnership must buy out the dissociated partner's interest at the § 701(b) price, plus interest. As in Creel v. Lilly, winding up is not the same as a fire sale; a good-faith valuation and payment protect the estate.
Deferred payment applies only to a partner who wrongfully dissociates before the end of a term (§ 701(h)); death is not wrongful.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — No forced fire sale (Creel)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Quinn, Ross, Sela, and Tom are partners in Summit Physical Therapy, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says that the partnership will continue for fifteen years and that profits are shared equally; it says nothing about what happens when a partner dies. In Year 2, the partnership signed a ten-year lease for its clinic. In Year 4, Ross dies. His will leaves everything to his widow, Una, who is also the executor of his estate.

Which of the following statements best describes the liability of Ross's estate?
o: The estate remains liable on the Year 2 clinic lease, but not on obligations the partnership incurs after Ross's death.
The estate is released from the clinic lease, because a partner's death automatically ends his liability for partnership obligations.
The estate is liable for every obligation the partnership incurs for the rest of the fifteen-year term.
The estate is liable on the clinic lease only if the landlord first sues Ross's estate before suing the partnership.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Dissociation does not discharge liability for obligations incurred while Ross was a partner; he can be released only by agreement with the creditor or by a material alteration of the obligation without his consent (§ 703(c), (d)). He is not liable for obligations incurred after dissociation (§ 703(a)), and a deceased partner cannot be reasonably believed to be acting as a partner.
Death does not discharge pre-dissociation liabilities.
A dissociated partner is generally not liable for obligations incurred after dissociation (§ 703(a)).
The exhaustion rule runs the other way: a creditor generally must exhaust partnership assets before levying on a partner's (or former partner's) personal assets (§ 307(d)).
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — A deceased partner's liabilities

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Quinn, Ross, Sela, and Tom are partners in Summit Physical Therapy, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says that the partnership will continue for fifteen years and that profits are shared equally; it says nothing about what happens when a partner dies. In Year 2, the partnership signed a ten-year lease for its clinic. In Year 4, Ross dies. His will leaves everything to his widow, Una, who is also the executor of his estate.

Una, as executor, wants to review the partnership's books to check the buyout figure. Which of the following statements is true under the RUPA?
o: Una has no right to any partnership information, because Ross is no longer a partner.
Una may inspect all of the partnership's records, including those created after Ross's death, on demand.
Una may get information from Ross's time as a partner by a good-faith demand in a record.
Una may see the records only by suing for an accounting.
None of the above.
oe: A person dissociated as a partner keeps a limited right of access to information (§ 408(e)), which a legal representative may exercise (§ 408(h)).
Access is limited to information pertaining to the period during which Ross was a partner.

Correct. RUPA § 408(e) gives a person dissociated as a partner access, on 10 days' demand in a record, to information to which he was entitled while a partner if it pertains to that period and is sought in good faith; § 408(h) lets a legal representative exercise the right.
No lawsuit is needed; § 408(e) provides a demand procedure.
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Information after dissociation

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Fairway Hills Country Club, Inc. hires Doug as its general manager. Managers of private clubs in the region customarily book entertainment, order supplies, and sign vendor contracts of up to about $25,000. Fairway's board privately tells Doug that he may not sign any contract over $10,000 without the board's approval. For three years Doug has rented golf carts for club tournaments from CartCo, signing as "General Manager, Fairway Hills," and Fairway has always paid CartCo's invoices.

Doug signs an $18,000 contract with a jazz band to play at Fairway's annual gala. The band knows nothing of the board's $10,000 limit. When the board refuses to pay, the band sues. Is Fairway bound?
o: No, because Doug lacked actual authority to sign any contract over $10,000.
Yes, because Fairway held Doug out as having a club manager's customary authority.
No, because the band should have asked the board whether Doug could sign the contract.
Yes, but only because Doug told the band he had authority to sign the contract.
None of the above.
oe: Lack of actual authority does not end the analysis. Fairway can still be bound through apparent authority.

Correct. Placing an agent in a position is a manifestation that he has the authority customary for it. Booking entertainment within the customary range binds the club to a third party without notice of a secret limit (compare Kidd v. Thomas A. Edison, Inc.).
A third party need not inquire into undisclosed limits on the authority customarily held by an agent in that position (R3d § 3.03 cmt. b).
An agent's own statements cannot create apparent authority; the manifestation must come from the principal.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Customary authority of a manager

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Fairway Hills Country Club, Inc. hires Doug as its general manager. Managers of private clubs in the region customarily book entertainment, order supplies, and sign vendor contracts of up to about $25,000. Fairway's board privately tells Doug that he may not sign any contract over $10,000 without the board's approval. For three years Doug has rented golf carts for club tournaments from CartCo, signing as "General Manager, Fairway Hills," and Fairway has always paid CartCo's invoices.

Fairway fires Doug and tells its staff, but not CartCo. A week later, Doug calls CartCo, rents twenty carts for the club's tournament "as usual," and signs as general manager. CartCo delivers the carts to the club. Is Fairway bound on the rental?
o: No, because Doug's actual authority ended when he was fired.
No, because Fairway announced Doug's firing to its staff.
Yes, because Fairway's prior course of dealing led CartCo to reasonably believe Doug still had authority, and Fairway never told CartCo otherwise.
Yes, because a former agent can always bind his former principal for one year after he leaves.
None of the above.
oe: Ending actual authority does not automatically end apparent authority. It lingers until the third party has notice.
Telling its own staff gives no notice to CartCo.

Correct. Apparent authority continues until it is no longer reasonable for the third party to believe the agent has authority (R3d § 3.11). Three years of paying CartCo's invoices was a manifestation by Fairway, and CartCo had no notice that it had ended.
There is no fixed period. Apparent authority lasts only as long as the third party's belief remains reasonable.
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Lingering apparent authority

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Fairway Hills Country Club, Inc. hires Doug as its general manager. Managers of private clubs in the region customarily book entertainment, order supplies, and sign vendor contracts of up to about $25,000. Fairway's board privately tells Doug that he may not sign any contract over $10,000 without the board's approval. For three years Doug has rented golf carts for club tournaments from CartCo, signing as "General Manager, Fairway Hills," and Fairway has always paid CartCo's invoices.

Assume CartCo's rental did not bind Fairway when Doug signed it. Fairway's new manager sees the CartCo carts arriving, learns that Doug ordered them, and uses them for the tournament anyway. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Fairway is bound, because by knowingly accepting the benefits of the rental it ratified Doug's unauthorized act.
Fairway is not bound, because a principal cannot ratify an act done by someone who was no longer its agent.
Fairway may ratify the rental of ten carts and reject the rest.
Fairway is not bound, because ratification must be in writing.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A principal ratifies by knowingly accepting the benefits of a transaction done on its behalf (R3d § 4.01). Once ratified, the act has the same effect as if it had been authorized from the start.
Ratification applies to acts done or purportedly done on the principal's behalf, including those of a person who had no authority at all.
No partial ratification: a principal must affirm the entire transaction or none of it (R3d § 4.07).
Ratification may be express or implied from conduct, such as accepting benefits.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Ratification by keeping benefits

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Fairway Hills Country Club, Inc. hires Doug as its general manager. Managers of private clubs in the region customarily book entertainment, order supplies, and sign vendor contracts of up to about $25,000. Fairway's board privately tells Doug that he may not sign any contract over $10,000 without the board's approval. For three years Doug has rented golf carts for club tournaments from CartCo, signing as "General Manager, Fairway Hills," and Fairway has always paid CartCo's invoices.

Assume Fairway neither is bound on CartCo's rental nor ratifies it. Which of the following statements about Doug's liability to CartCo is true?
o: Doug is liable to CartCo for the loss it suffers because Fairway is not bound.
CartCo's recovery from Doug may include the benefit it expected from the rental.
If Fairway later ratified the rental, Doug would no longer be liable to CartCo on the warranty.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A person who purports to make a contract on behalf of a principal, without the power to bind it, impliedly warrants his authority and is liable for the resulting loss (R3d § 6.10).
True. Liability under the implied warranty includes the benefit of the bargain that the third party expected from performance by the principal (§ 6.10).
True. Ratification gives the act the effect of actual authority and removes the basis for the warranty claim.
Incomplete. C is also true.
Correct. Doug is liable on the implied warranty of authority, CartCo may recover its expected benefit, and ratification by Fairway would end Doug's liability.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Implied warranty of authority

q: Ivo, a wine buyer, orders $30,000 of wine from Cask & Barrel, telling the seller he is buying "for a restaurant group I represent, which prefers to stay anonymous." The wine is delivered, and no one pays. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Only the restaurant group is liable, because Cask & Barrel knew Ivo was acting as an agent.
Ivo is a party to the contract, because the seller never learned who his principal was.
Only Ivo is liable, because a principal whose identity is not disclosed can never be bound.
No one is liable, because Cask & Barrel agreed to sell without knowing who the buyer was.
None of the above.
oe: Knowing that an agent is acting for someone is not enough to release the agent. The seller did not know who the principal was.

Correct. When the third party knows the agent acts for a principal but does not know the principal's identity, the principal is unidentified (partially disclosed), and the agent is a party to the contract unless the parties agree otherwise (R3d § 6.02; Atlantic Salmon A/S v. Curran).
An unidentified principal that authorized the deal is bound once identified.
Choosing to deal with an anonymous principal through an agent is exactly why the law makes the agent a party.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Partially disclosed principal

q: Which of the following is the best example of a special agent rather than a general agent?
o: A store manager who runs a shop's daily operations for its owner.
A purchasing director who buys supplies for a hotel chain year after year.
A real estate broker hired to sell one particular house.
A resident manager who collects rents and arranges repairs for an apartment building.
None of the above.
oe: A store manager conducts a continuous series of transactions, which makes her a general agent.
Ongoing purchasing is a continuous series of transactions, so this is a general agent.
Correct. A special agent is authorized to conduct a single transaction or a series of transactions not involving continuity of service (R2d § 3). A broker hired for one sale fits.
Managing a building over time is a continuous series of transactions, which makes this a general agent.
C is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — General vs. special agent

q: Ann and Bo are equal partners in a RUPA window-washing partnership with no written agreement. Ann wants to hire a third washer; Bo says no. Ann hires one anyway, pays him $6,000 out of her own pocket, and asks the partnership to reimburse her. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Ann is not entitled to reimbursement, because one of two equal partners is not a majority and Bo never agreed to the hire.
Ann is entitled to reimbursement, because she spent the money for the partnership's benefit.
Ann is entitled to reimbursement, because each partner has equal rights in management and may make ordinary business decisions.
Ann is not entitled to reimbursement, because hiring employees is outside the ordinary course of a window-washing business.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In Summers v. Dooley, a partner who hired a worker over his equal partner's objection could not get reimbursement: business differences are decided by a majority, and one of two partners is not a majority. Compare National Biscuit v. Stroud, which protects outsiders, not a partner seeking reimbursement.
A partner is reimbursed for payments made in the course of partnership activities only if she complied with her duties in making them (RUPA § 401(b)); here the majority never approved the hire.
Equal management rights do not let one partner impose an expense over the other's objection, as between the partners themselves.
Hiring a worker is ordinary-course business; the problem is that no majority approved it.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Between the partners (Summers v. Dooley)

q: A limited partnership agreement gives the general partners "sole discretion" to sell partnership land, including to themselves. The general partners buy a parcel from the partnership at a price based on an appraisal that ignores a recent rezoning they know greatly increased the land's value. The limited partners sue. Under Jerman v. O'Leary, which of the following statements is true?
o: The general partners did nothing wrong, because the agreement allowed them to buy the land in their sole discretion.
The purchase is void, because general partners may never buy partnership property.
The clause permitted the purchase, but not at an unfair price without disclosure.
The limited partners lose, because limited partners have no standing to sue general partners.
None of the above.
oe: Jerman held that a permissive clause authorized the purchase but did not wipe out fiduciary duties in carrying it out.
The agreement permitted purchases by the general partners; the question is how they had to make them.

Correct. In Jerman v. O'Leary, the court read fiduciary obligations into the permissive clause: the general partners could buy, but had to pay a fair price and disclose material facts such as the rezoning. Contrast Delaware's contract-first approach in Sonet v. Plum Creek.
Limited partners may sue general partners for breach of fiduciary duty.
C is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — A permissive clause doesn't end duties (Jerman)

q: Three partners worry that if one of them runs into personal financial trouble, an outsider could end up with a claim on that partner's share of the business. Which trigger events should their buyout agreement include to address that risk?
o: A partner's bankruptcy.
A judgment creditor's seizure of, or charging order against, a partner's interest.
A partner's retirement at an agreed age.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Bankruptcy is a standard trigger, because a bankruptcy trustee would otherwise step into the partner's economic rights.
True. Creditor seizure is a listed trigger event; a buyout lets the firm cash out the interest instead of dealing with the creditor.
Retirement is a common trigger, but it does not address the risk of outsiders acquiring rights because of a partner's financial trouble.
Correct. Bankruptcy and creditor seizure are the triggers aimed at keeping a partner's financial trouble from bringing an outsider into the business.
C does not address this risk, though it is a sensible trigger for other reasons.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Triggers in a buyout agreement

q: Under the ULLCA, Fen contributed $80,000 to Riverside Pottery, LLC, and Gia and Hal contributed $10,000 each. The operating agreement says nothing about distributions. The members decide to distribute $30,000 before the company dissolves. How much does each member receive?
o: Fen receives $24,000 and Gia and Hal receive $3,000 each, in proportion to their contributions.
Each member receives $10,000, because the default rule calls for equal shares.
Fen receives the entire $30,000 until the others' contributions catch up to his.
Nothing, because members of an LLC have no right to any distribution before dissolution.
None of the above.
oe: The ULLCA's default is not proportional to contributions.

Correct. Unless the operating agreement provides otherwise, any distribution before dissolution must be in equal shares among members (ULLCA § 404(a)). Members who want contribution-based shares must say so in the operating agreement.
No such catch-up rule exists before dissolution. (In winding up, unreturned contributions are paid before the remaining surplus (§ 707(b)), but that is different.)
Members have no right to demand an interim distribution, but once the LLC decides to make one, the default sharing rule applies.
B is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — LLC distributions: equal shares by default

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Wren and Hollis open Second Stitch, a vintage-clothing store, as partners. Wren contributes $60,000 in cash and lives two hours away. Hollis contributes no money but agrees to run the store full time without a salary. They agree to split profits equally and say nothing about losses. After two years the store closes. Once all outside creditors are paid, $24,000 is left, so $36,000 of Wren's capital has been lost.

In a jurisdiction that follows Kovacik v. Reed, how is the $36,000 loss of Wren's capital borne?
o: Wren bears the entire capital loss and receives the remaining $24,000; Hollis owes her nothing.
Hollis must pay Wren $18,000, half of the capital loss.
Hollis must repay Wren the entire $36,000, because he ran the store when the money was lost.
Wren and Hollis each receive $12,000 of the remaining $24,000.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under Kovacik v. Reed, when one partner contributes money and the other only services, and they never agreed on losses, neither must reimburse the other: Wren loses her money and Hollis loses the value of his labor.
That is the statutory result (losses shared like profits), which Kovacik rejected for money-versus-services partnerships.
No rule makes the managing partner bear all capital losses.
Capital is returned before anything is treated as profit; nothing is left to split.
A is correct.
topic: 11 · Loss sharing (Kovacik) — Applying Kovacik

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Wren and Hollis open Second Stitch, a vintage-clothing store, as partners. Wren contributes $60,000 in cash and lives two hours away. Hollis contributes no money but agrees to run the store full time without a salary. They agree to split profits equally and say nothing about losses. After two years the store closes. Once all outside creditors are paid, $24,000 is left, so $36,000 of Wren's capital has been lost.

Assume instead that the partnership is governed by the RUPA, which rejects Kovacik. How is the loss handled?
o: Wren bears the entire capital loss, because Hollis contributed no capital.
Hollis must contribute $18,000, and Wren receives $42,000.
Hollis must contribute $36,000, so that Wren recovers her full $60,000.
Wren and Hollis split the remaining $24,000 equally, and neither owes the other anything.
None of the above.
oe: That is the Kovacik result. The RUPA applies its default loss rules even when a partner contributed no capital (§ 401 comment).

Correct. Losses are shared in the same proportion as distributions (§ 401(a)), so the $36,000 loss is split $18,000 each. Hollis must contribute $18,000, and Wren receives the $24,000 plus Hollis's $18,000, a total of $42,000. The RUPA's comment to § 401 says the default loss rule applies even to a partner who contributed no capital.
Hollis bears only his share of the loss, not all of it.
Unreturned contributions are repaid before any surplus is split (§ 806(b)), and partners must contribute to cover losses.
B is correct.
topic: 11 · Loss sharing (Kovacik) — The statutory result under the RUPA

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Wren and Hollis open Second Stitch, a vintage-clothing store, as partners. Wren contributes $60,000 in cash and lives two hours away. Hollis contributes no money but agrees to run the store full time without a salary. They agree to split profits equally and say nothing about losses. After two years the store closes. Once all outside creditors are paid, $24,000 is left, so $36,000 of Wren's capital has been lost.

Assume that after the store's assets are exhausted, Loom Supply, an outside creditor, is still owed $10,000. Loom sues Hollis personally. Hollis argues that, under Kovacik, a service partner bears no share of the losses. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Hollis is not liable, because under Kovacik a partner who contributed only services never bears any losses.
Hollis is liable only for half of Loom's claim, because partners share losses equally.
Hollis is not liable, because Loom dealt only with Wren, who signed the purchase orders.
Hollis and Wren are each personally liable to Loom for the full amount.
None of the above.
oe: Kovacik allocates losses between the partners. It does not limit partners' liability to outside creditors.
Partners' liability to creditors is joint and several, not divided by loss shares.
A partnership obligation is every partner's obligation, whoever signed for the partnership.

Correct. Partners are personally liable for partnership obligations (UPA § 15; RUPA § 306(a)), whatever their internal loss-sharing rule. As between Wren and Hollis, any payment would then be allocated under the applicable loss rule.
D is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Kovacik doesn't bind creditors

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Wren and Hollis open Second Stitch, a vintage-clothing store, as partners. Wren contributes $60,000 in cash and lives two hours away. Hollis contributes no money but agrees to run the store full time without a salary. They agree to split profits equally and say nothing about losses. After two years the store closes. Once all outside creditors are paid, $24,000 is left, so $36,000 of Wren's capital has been lost.

When the store closes, Hollis demands a salary for the two years he ran it, plus pay for the three months he spends winding it up. Under the RUPA's default rules, which of the following statements is true?
o: Hollis is entitled to reasonable pay for both periods, because he worked full time while Wren did not.
Hollis is entitled to nothing for either period, because he agreed to work without a salary.
Hollis is entitled to reasonable pay for the winding-up work only, and to nothing for running the store.
Hollis is entitled to pay for both periods, but only out of profits, not out of Wren's capital.
None of the above.
oe: The default rule gives a partner no remuneration for services, however unequal the work.
The agreement covered his work running the store; the statute separately allows reasonable compensation for winding-up services.
Correct. A partner is not entitled to remuneration for services performed for the partnership, except reasonable compensation for services rendered in winding up its business (RUPA § 401(j)).
The default rule allows no pay for operating the business, whether out of profits or capital.
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — No salary by default

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Wren and Hollis open Second Stitch, a vintage-clothing store, as partners. Wren contributes $60,000 in cash and lives two hours away. Hollis contributes no money but agrees to run the store full time without a salary. They agree to split profits equally and say nothing about losses. After two years the store closes. Once all outside creditors are paid, $24,000 is left, so $36,000 of Wren's capital has been lost.

While the store is still open, Hollis learns that the landlord plans to raise the rent by 40% at the end of the year. Wren has not asked about the lease. Under the RUPA, which of the following statements is true?
o: Hollis need say nothing until Wren asks, because a partner's information duty arises only on demand.
Hollis must tell Wren without being asked, because the rent increase is information material to her rights and duties as a partner.
Hollis must tell Wren only if the partnership agreement requires it.
Hollis need not tell Wren, because she does not work at the store.
None of the above.
oe: Some information must be furnished without demand: information material to a partner's exercise of her rights and duties.

Correct. The partnership, and each partner who knows the information, must furnish without demand any information material to the proper exercise of a partner's rights and duties, unless the partner already knows it (RUPA § 408(c)(1), (d)). Other information must be furnished on demand (§ 408(c)(2)).
The information duty is a statutory default; no agreement is needed.
A partner who is not involved in daily operations has the same right to material information.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Information without demand

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Bean Street Coffee, Inc. franchises coffee shops. Its franchise agreement lets each franchisee hire, train, schedule, discipline, and pay its own employees. But Bean Street requires every franchisee to use Bean Street espresso machines, which Bean Street's own technicians install and service on a schedule Bean Street sets; franchisees are forbidden to adjust or repair the machines. Every shop displays Bean Street's name, colors, and logo, and nothing in the shops tells customers who owns them. Ridgeway Coffee LLC operates a Bean Street shop downtown.

Because Bean Street's technicians skip a scheduled service, the steam wand on Ridgeway's espresso machine bursts and burns a customer, Iris. Iris sues Bean Street. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Bean Street cannot be vicariously liable, because a franchisor never answers for a franchisee's operations.
Bean Street can be liable only if it controlled Ridgeway's hiring and supervision of employees.
Bean Street can be liable only if Iris knew that Bean Street serviced the machines.
Bean Street may be vicariously liable, because it controlled the machine maintenance that failed.
None of the above.
oe: Franchisors are not immune; under the majority rule they are liable when they control the aspect of the business that caused the harm.
Kerl's test asks about control over the specific aspect of the business that caused the harm, not control over everything.
Vicarious liability based on actual control does not depend on the plaintiff's knowledge.

Correct. Under Kerl v. Rasmussen, a franchisor is vicariously liable only if it controls or has the right to control the daily operation of the specific aspect of the franchisee's business that caused the harm. Bean Street controls machine service, and its own technicians skipped the service.
D is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Control of the specific aspect (Kerl)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Bean Street Coffee, Inc. franchises coffee shops. Its franchise agreement lets each franchisee hire, train, schedule, discipline, and pay its own employees. But Bean Street requires every franchisee to use Bean Street espresso machines, which Bean Street's own technicians install and service on a schedule Bean Street sets; franchisees are forbidden to adjust or repair the machines. Every shop displays Bean Street's name, colors, and logo, and nothing in the shops tells customers who owns them. Ridgeway Coffee LLC operates a Bean Street shop downtown.

A Ridgeway barista whom Ridgeway hired despite a history of violence assaults a customer during an argument over an order. The customer sues Bean Street for negligent hiring and supervision. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Bean Street is not liable, because it had no control or right to control Ridgeway's hiring or supervision of employees.
Bean Street is liable, because the shop displays Bean Street's name and logo.
Bean Street is liable, because it controls the espresso machines, and control over any part of the business makes it liable for the whole.
Bean Street is liable, because a franchisor must guarantee that its franchisees hire safe employees.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. As in Kerl v. Rasmussen, where the franchisor had no say over the franchisee's hiring or supervision, a franchisor is not vicariously liable for harm arising from an aspect of the business it does not control.
Brand display alone is not control over hiring. (A plaintiff who relied on the brand might try apparent agency, but that is a different theory.)
Under Kerl, control must be over the specific aspect that caused the harm.
There is no such guarantee; franchisors that leave hiring to franchisees are not answerable for it.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — No control over hiring

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Bean Street Coffee, Inc. franchises coffee shops. Its franchise agreement lets each franchisee hire, train, schedule, discipline, and pay its own employees. But Bean Street requires every franchisee to use Bean Street espresso machines, which Bean Street's own technicians install and service on a schedule Bean Street sets; franchisees are forbidden to adjust or repair the machines. Every shop displays Bean Street's name, colors, and logo, and nothing in the shops tells customers who owns them. Ridgeway Coffee LLC operates a Bean Street shop downtown.

Iris says she chose Ridgeway's shop because she trusts Bean Street's brand. Under the apparent-agency theory applied in Miller v. McDonald's Corp. (R2d § 267), which of the following must she show to hold Bean Street liable on that theory?
o: That Bean Street held out Ridgeway's shop as its own, for example through uniform branding with no sign of separate ownership.
That she relied on that appearance in choosing the shop.
That Bean Street controlled the daily operation of the shop as a whole.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. The principal's own representation, here the uniform branding Bean Street requires, is the first element.
True. Apparent agency in tort requires the plaintiff's reliance on the principal's representation, which is why Iris's reason for choosing the shop matters.
False. Actual control is the basis of the other theory (actual agency). Apparent agency rests on holding out and reliance instead.
Correct. In Miller, the uniform branding and the customer's reliance on McDonald's reputation raised a jury question on apparent agency, separate from the actual-agency question.
C is not required for apparent agency.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Apparent agency (Miller)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Bean Street Coffee, Inc. franchises coffee shops. Its franchise agreement lets each franchisee hire, train, schedule, discipline, and pay its own employees. But Bean Street requires every franchisee to use Bean Street espresso machines, which Bean Street's own technicians install and service on a schedule Bean Street sets; franchisees are forbidden to adjust or repair the machines. Every shop displays Bean Street's name, colors, and logo, and nothing in the shops tells customers who owns them. Ridgeway Coffee LLC operates a Bean Street shop downtown.

A customer slips on a wet floor at Ridgeway's shop and sues Bean Street. Which fact, standing alone, would be LEAST likely to make Bean Street liable for the fall?
o: Bean Street requires uniform signs, colors, and building plans and inspects shops periodically to protect its brand.
Bean Street's manual sets the exact schedule and method for mopping floors, and its field staff enforce it daily.
Bean Street's own employees clean the shop floors every morning.
Bean Street owns the shop, sets the hours, and may assign Ridgeway's manager "other duties" at will.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Brand standards and periodic inspections aimed at system-wide uniformity are not control over daily operations such as floor cleaning (Murphy v. Holiday Inns; Hoover v. Sun Oil).
Daily control over floor cleaning is control over the specific aspect that caused the fall (Kerl; compare Parker v. Domino's).
If Bean Street's employees did the cleaning, it would answer for their negligence directly.
Facts like these made the station operator a servant in Humble Oil v. Martin.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Brand standards aren't control (Murphy)

q: A furniture store uses Kip to deliver furniture to customers. Which of the following facts tend to show that Kip is the store's employee (servant) rather than an independent contractor?
o: The store pays Kip by the hour and tells him which routes to drive and in what order.
Kip drives a truck the store owns and wears the store's uniform.
Kip also runs his own moving company, has his own customers, and is paid a flat fee per delivery.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Payment by time rather than by the job and control over the details of the work point toward employment (R2d § 220(2)).
True. Who supplies the tools and instrumentalities is a § 220 factor; the employer's truck and uniform point toward employment.
False. A distinct business of his own and payment by the job point toward independent-contractor status.
Correct. Hourly pay, control over routes, and the store's truck and uniform are § 220 factors suggesting a servant relationship; the facts in C point the other way.
C points toward independent-contractor status.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Employee or independent contractor (R2d § 220)

q: Two construction companies agree to build a single highway bridge together. Each contributes equipment and crews, they make decisions on the project jointly, and they will split the profit equally when the bridge is finished. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: They have formed a joint venture, to which partnership law, including partners' fiduciary duties, generally applies.
They have formed no business association at all, because the project will end when the bridge is done.
They have formed a corporation, because both participants are corporations.
They have formed a joint venture, and the venturers owe each other no fiduciary duties because the relationship is temporary.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A joint venture is a partnership for a limited undertaking. Its elements are contributions, joint proprietary interest and mutual control, an agreement to share profits, and an express or implied contract (Sandvick v. LaCrosse), and partnership law generally governs it.
A business association can exist for a single project; that is what makes it a joint venture.
A corporation is formed only by filing articles of incorporation.
Joint venturers owe fiduciary duties like partners do; Meinhard v. Salmon itself involved a joint venture.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Joint ventures

q: Kai and Liv orally agree to build a data-analytics business as equal partners. After a year, Liv changes the passwords, locks Kai out, incorporates the business in her own name, and raises money from investors. Kai sues. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Kai has no claim, because an oral partnership agreement is unenforceable.
Kai has no claim, because Liv was free to dissolve an at-will partnership at any time.
Kai's claims may proceed, because Liv cannot dissolve in order to take the business.
Kai's only remedy is to start a competing business of his own.
None of the above.
oe: Partnerships need no writing; they arise from conduct (RUPA § 202(a)).
A partner may dissolve an at-will partnership, but may not use dissolution to take the business without accounting to her partner.

Correct. In Second Measure, Inc. v. Kim, the court let the claims go forward: partners' duties continue through winding up, and a partner cannot dissolve in order to appropriate the business (compare Page v. Page).
Kai has claims for breach of fiduciary duty and an accounting.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — No freeze-out by incorporation (Second Measure)

q: Under the UPA (1914), two companies form a partnership whose agreement calls it "permanent." One partner contributed licenses to its patents for the partnership's use. That partner then announces that it is ending the partnership. Under Pav-Saver Corp. v. Vasso Corp., which of the following statements is true?
o: The dissolution is wrongful, and the innocent partner may continue the business using the patents.
The patent-contributing partner may take back its patents immediately, because they remain its property.
The dissolution is rightful, because a partner always has the right to end a partnership.
The dissolution is wrongful, so the partnership must be liquidated and the patents sold at auction.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under UPA § 38(2), after a wrongful dissolution the innocent partners may continue the business, use the partnership property, and pay the wrongdoer the value of its interest, excluding goodwill and less damages. Pav-Saver applied this to the contributed patents.
In Pav-Saver the court let the innocent partner continue the business and keep using the patents.
A partner always has the power to dissolve, but not always the right; ending a "permanent" partnership breaches the agreement.
Wrongful dissolution gives the innocent partner the option to continue, not just a liquidation.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Wrongful dissolution under the UPA (Pav-Saver)

q: Ruth hires Sol to ship her antique clock to an auction house and tells him, "Insure it for its full $20,000 value." Sol decides insurance is too expensive and ships it uninsured. The clock is destroyed in transit. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Sol is not liable, because he used his own business judgment in good faith.
Sol is liable to Ruth for the loss, because he disobeyed her instruction.
Sol is liable only if he was paid for shipping the clock.
Sol is not liable, because the carrier, not Sol, destroyed the clock.
None of the above.
oe: An agent must obey the principal's reasonable, lawful instructions; good-faith disagreement does not excuse disobedience.

Correct. An agent has a duty to act within the scope of actual authority and to comply with the principal's reasonable instructions, and is liable for losses caused by breaching that duty (R3d § 8.09; R2d §§ 383, 385).
Even a gratuitous agent who undertakes to act must obey the principal's reasonable instructions.
The loss would have been covered had Sol followed instructions; his disobedience caused Ruth's loss.
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Duty of obedience

q: Lena runs a bakery by herself under the trade name "Sweet Rise," without forming any entity. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Lena may do business under the trade name "Sweet Rise."
The bakery's creditors cannot reach Lena's personal savings.
Lena has full control of the business but may find it hard to raise money.
A and C.
None of the above.
oe: True. A sole proprietor may use a trade name.
False. A sole proprietorship does not separate the owner's personal assets from the business's liabilities.
True. Full control and difficulty raising capital are both features of the sole proprietorship.
Correct. Lena may use a trade name and has full control, but she is personally liable for the business's debts and may struggle to raise money.
D is correct.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Sole proprietorships

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Copperline Coffee Roasters, LLC is formed under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). Its members are Dara (50%), Eitan (30%), and Fumi (20%). The operating agreement states that the company is "managed by managers" and names Dara as its sole manager; it says nothing about distributions, withdrawal, or members' authority. Copperline has filed no statement of authority. It owns a roasting plant and owes $400,000 on a bank loan.

Fumi signs a contract with a coffee-bean importer, purporting to commit Copperline to a year of purchases. The importer knows that Fumi is a member of Copperline but nothing else about her role. Is Copperline bound?
o: Yes, because every member of an LLC is an agent of the company for its ordinary business.
Yes, because the importer reasonably believed that a member could bind the company.
No, unless agency law gives Fumi authority to bind it.
No, because an LLC can act only through a filed statement of authority.
None of the above.
oe: That is the rule for general partners, not LLC members. A member is not an agent of an LLC solely by reason of being a member (ULLCA § 301(a)).
Apparent authority must rest on the LLC's manifestations, not merely on the third party's assumption about members.

Correct. Under ULLCA § 301(a), membership alone confers no agency power. Copperline is bound only if ordinary agency principles (actual or apparent authority) or a filed statement of authority supply it, and as a non-manager member of a manager-managed LLC, Fumi has none here.
A statement of authority is one source of authority; ordinary agency law is another.
C is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — No agency power as a member

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Copperline Coffee Roasters, LLC is formed under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). Its members are Dara (50%), Eitan (30%), and Fumi (20%). The operating agreement states that the company is "managed by managers" and names Dara as its sole manager; it says nothing about distributions, withdrawal, or members' authority. Copperline has filed no statement of authority. It owns a roasting plant and owes $400,000 on a bank loan.

Dara causes Copperline to distribute $200,000 to the members. Afterward the company cannot pay its debts as they come due, and it defaults on the bank loan. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The distribution was proper, because the members have a right to share in the company's profits.
The bank may sue all three members personally for its loan, because the distribution forfeited their liability shield.
Dara may be personally liable to Copperline for the excess, if she failed her duties in consenting.
Only Eitan and Fumi can be liable, because they received the money and Dara merely approved it.
None of the above.
oe: Members have no right to interim distributions, and no distribution may be made if it leaves the company unable to pay its debts as they come due (ULLCA § 405(a)(1)).
