The improper distribution does not pierce the shield. The remedy runs to the company for the excess, not to creditors on the debt itself.

Correct. A manager who consents to a distribution made in violation of § 405 and, in doing so, fails to comply with § 409 is personally liable to the company for the excess (ULLCA § 406(a)). Members who knowingly received an improper distribution may also have to return it (§ 406(b)).
The manager who consented is the primary target of § 406(a); recipients' liability depends on their knowledge.
C is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Improper distributions

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Copperline Coffee Roasters, LLC is formed under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). Its members are Dara (50%), Eitan (30%), and Fumi (20%). The operating agreement states that the company is "managed by managers" and names Dara as its sole manager; it says nothing about distributions, withdrawal, or members' authority. Copperline has filed no statement of authority. It owns a roasting plant and owes $400,000 on a bank loan.

Fumi's personal creditor, which has nothing to do with Copperline, wins a $90,000 judgment against her. What may the creditor do?
o: Obtain a charging order that requires Copperline to pay the creditor any distributions that would otherwise go to Fumi.
Seize and sell a fifth of the roasting plant, since Fumi owns 20% of the company.
Step into Fumi's place as a member and vote on company matters.
Force Copperline to dissolve and liquidate so that Fumi's share can be paid out.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A charging order is a lien on the judgment debtor's transferable interest and is the exclusive remedy by which a member's judgment creditor may satisfy the judgment from that interest (ULLCA § 503). A purchaser at a foreclosure sale gets only the transferable interest and does not become a member.
Members do not own the LLC's property; the company does, and a member's creditor cannot reach it.
A charging creditor or transferee gets economic rights only, not membership or management rights.
A member's creditor has no power to dissolve the company; the charging order is its remedy.
A is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Charging order

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Copperline Coffee Roasters, LLC is formed under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). Its members are Dara (50%), Eitan (30%), and Fumi (20%). The operating agreement states that the company is "managed by managers" and names Dara as its sole manager; it says nothing about distributions, withdrawal, or members' authority. Copperline has filed no statement of authority. It owns a roasting plant and owes $400,000 on a bank loan.

Eitan, tired of disputes with Dara, gives Copperline written notice that he is withdrawing as a member immediately. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Eitan cannot withdraw, because the operating agreement does not mention withdrawal.
Eitan is dissociated, and Copperline must buy his interest at its fair value.
Eitan is dissociated, his withdrawal is rightful because the agreement is silent, and he keeps all of his rights as a member.
Eitan is dissociated, wrongfully, and keeps his interest only as a transferee.
None of the above.
oe: A member always has the power to dissociate by express will (ULLCA § 601(a)).
Unlike a RUPA partnership, an LLC has no mandatory buyout of a dissociated member.
Withdrawal by express will before winding up is complete is wrongful (§ 601(b)(2)(A)), and a dissociated member loses management rights.

Correct. A member may withdraw at any time, but withdrawal by express will before the company's winding up is complete is wrongful (§ 601(b)(2)(A)), and he is liable for damages it causes (§ 601(c)). He gets no buyout; his transferable interest is held solely as a transferee (§ 603(a)(3)).
D is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Withdrawing from an LLC

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Copperline Coffee Roasters, LLC is formed under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). Its members are Dara (50%), Eitan (30%), and Fumi (20%). The operating agreement states that the company is "managed by managers" and names Dara as its sole manager; it says nothing about distributions, withdrawal, or members' authority. Copperline has filed no statement of authority. It owns a roasting plant and owes $400,000 on a bank loan.

Dara causes Copperline to sell a spare roasting machine to her husband's company for half its value. Eitan wants to sue Dara over the sale. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Eitan may sue directly, because any harm to the company is also a harm to every member.
Eitan's claim is derivative, so he must make a demand or show futility.
Eitan has no claim, because a manager owes duties only to the company, not to members.
Eitan has no claim, because a manager's sale of company property is a business judgment.
None of the above.
oe: A direct action requires an injury that is not solely the result of an injury to the company (ULLCA § 801(b)).

Correct. The underpriced sale harmed Copperline, and Eitan's loss flows from that harm, so his claim is derivative. He must make a demand on the manager, or show futility, before suing (§ 802). Since Dara is the manager and the interested party, a demand on her may well be futile.
The claim belongs to the company, but a member may enforce it derivatively.
Selling company property to the manager's family at half price is self-dealing, a loyalty issue, not a protected business judgment.
B is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Direct or derivative?

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Nora plans to open Greenleaf Bakery. On March 1, before any company has been formed, she signs a three-year lease of a storefront from Pell Properties, signing "Greenleaf Bakery, LLC, by Nora, Manager." Pell does not check the state's records. Greenleaf Bakery, LLC is formed on April 15, with Nora and her brother Otto as its only members and Nora as its manager. The LLC moves into the storefront, pays rent for a year, and then stops paying.

Pell sues Nora personally for the unpaid rent. Nora argues that she signed only as the LLC's manager. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Nora is not liable, because she signed in a representative capacity.
Nora is liable, because she contracted for a principal that did not yet exist.
Nora is not liable, because Pell could have checked the state's records and discovered that the LLC did not exist.
Nora is liable only for the rent that came due before the LLC was formed on April 15.
None of the above.
oe: Signing as an agent does not protect a person who purports to act for a principal that does not exist.

Correct. A person who makes a contract with a third party purportedly on behalf of a principal that does not exist or lacks capacity becomes a party to the contract, unless the third party agrees otherwise (R3d § 6.04).
The third party has no duty to search public records (compare Atlantic Salmon v. Curran); the burden is on the agent.
Her liability as a party to the lease is not limited to the period before formation.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Agent for a nonexistent principal

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Nora plans to open Greenleaf Bakery. On March 1, before any company has been formed, she signs a three-year lease of a storefront from Pell Properties, signing "Greenleaf Bakery, LLC, by Nora, Manager." Pell does not check the state's records. Greenleaf Bakery, LLC is formed on April 15, with Nora and her brother Otto as its only members and Nora as its manager. The LLC moves into the storefront, pays rent for a year, and then stops paying.

Pell also sues Greenleaf Bakery, LLC for the rent. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The LLC ratified the lease when it moved in, so the lease binds it as of March 1.
The LLC is bound because it adopted the lease, not because it ratified it.
The LLC is not bound, because only Nora signed the lease.
The LLC is not bound, because Pell never agreed to substitute the LLC for Nora.
None of the above.
oe: Ratification relates back to the time of the act, and a principal may ratify only if it existed when the act was done (R3d § 4.04). The LLC did not exist on March 1.

Correct. Because the LLC did not exist on March 1, it cannot ratify (§ 4.04); but an entity formed later may adopt a contract made on its behalf, by express words or by accepting its benefits with knowledge. Adoption takes effect when it occurs and does not relate back.
An entity can become bound by adopting a contract signed on its behalf by its promoter.
Pell's consent is needed to release Nora, not to bind the LLC that adopted the lease.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Ratification needs an existing principal

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Nora plans to open Greenleaf Bakery. On March 1, before any company has been formed, she signs a three-year lease of a storefront from Pell Properties, signing "Greenleaf Bakery, LLC, by Nora, Manager." Pell does not check the state's records. Greenleaf Bakery, LLC is formed on April 15, with Nora and her brother Otto as its only members and Nora as its manager. The LLC moves into the storefront, pays rent for a year, and then stops paying.

After the LLC is formed, Nora orders $8,000 of flour from Mill Co. in her own name, without mentioning the LLC. The flour is used in the bakery. Mill Co. is not paid and later learns that Nora was buying for the LLC. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Mill Co. may hold Nora liable, because she contracted as a party.
Mill Co. may hold the LLC liable, because it is an undisclosed principal on whose behalf Nora acted with actual authority.
Mill Co. cannot hold the LLC liable, because it extended credit only to Nora.
A and B.
None of the above.
oe: True. An agent for an undisclosed principal is a party to the contract (R3d § 6.03).
True. An undisclosed principal is bound by contracts its agent makes with actual authority (R3d § 6.03).
False. The third party's ignorance of the principal does not shield an undisclosed principal from liability on an authorized contract.
Correct. Both the agent, as a party, and the undisclosed principal are liable to Mill Co.
D is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Undisclosed principal

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Nora plans to open Greenleaf Bakery. On March 1, before any company has been formed, she signs a three-year lease of a storefront from Pell Properties, signing "Greenleaf Bakery, LLC, by Nora, Manager." Pell does not check the state's records. Greenleaf Bakery, LLC is formed on April 15, with Nora and her brother Otto as its only members and Nora as its manager. The LLC moves into the storefront, pays rent for a year, and then stops paying.

Nora tells Pell's property manager, Quinn, that water is pouring through a crack in the storefront ceiling. Quinn never tells Pell. Months later, the ceiling collapses. Pell argues that it never knew about the crack. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Pell is treated as knowing about the crack, because notice to an agent about a matter within her duties is notice to the principal.
Pell is not treated as knowing, because Quinn never passed the information along.
Pell is treated as knowing only if Quinn was acting adversely to Pell when she received the notice.
Pell is not treated as knowing, because notice must be given in writing to the principal itself.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Notice given to an agent is effective as notice to the principal if it concerns a matter within the agent's actual authority (R3d § 5.02), and an agent's knowledge of material facts within the scope of her duties is imputed to the principal (§ 5.03).
The point of imputation is that the principal cannot escape notice because its agent failed to pass information along.
Adverse-interest conduct by the agent is a reason not to impute knowledge, not a requirement for imputation.
No such writing requirement applies; notice to an authorized agent suffices.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Notice to an agent

q: Without authority, Ward signs a contract on behalf of his employer, Hollis Corp., to sell a used forklift to Kemp for $9,000. Kemp learns that Ward lacked authority and, before Hollis says anything, writes to Hollis withdrawing from the deal. Hollis then announces that it ratifies the sale. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Hollis's ratification binds Kemp, because ratification relates back to the moment Ward signed the contract.
Hollis's ratification binds Kemp, because a principal may ratify its agent's act at any time.
Hollis's ratification binds Kemp only if Hollis ratified in writing.
Hollis's ratification binds Kemp, because Kemp had no right to withdraw from a signed contract.
None of the above.
oe: Relation back does not apply once the third party has withdrawn. Ratification is not effective if it comes after the third party's manifestation of intent to withdraw (R3d § 4.05).
There are limits on timing: a third party's withdrawal before ratification, or a material change in circumstances, cuts off the power to ratify (§ 4.05).
The form of ratification is not the problem. Even a written ratification comes too late after Kemp withdrew.
Until Hollis ratified, there was no binding contract on Hollis's side, so Kemp was free to withdraw.
Correct. Ratification is not effective when, before it occurs, the third party has manifested its intent to withdraw (R3d § 4.05). Kemp withdrew first, so Hollis's later ratification cannot bind him.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Too late to ratify

q: Members of a large family farming partnership governed by the UPA (1914) bought their interests at book value, understanding that the managing partner could end any partner's interest at will by paying its book value. The manager ends Ora's interest and tenders book value. Ora sues to force a liquidation so that she can share in the land's market value. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Ora wins, because the UPA gives every partner an unwaivable right to force a liquidation.
Ora loses, because the partners' agreement controls.
Ora wins, because a buyout at book value is always unconscionable when land has appreciated.
Ora loses, because she was never a partner at all.
None of the above.
oe: UPA rules on dissolution and distribution are largely defaults that partners can change by agreement.

Correct. In Frank v. R.A. Pickens & Son Co., the court held that the partners' agreement to buy and sell interests at book value controlled; the UPA's rules are defaults, so the expelled partner got book value and could not force a liquidation.
Courts enforce book-value terms as written (compare G & S Investments v. Belman), even when they produce harsh results.
Frank held that she was a partner; she lost because the agreement controlled her exit.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — The agreement controls (Frank v. Pickens)

q: Under the RUPA, which of the following may a partnership agreement validly do?
o: Identify specific types of activities that do not violate the duty of loyalty, if not manifestly unreasonable.
Prescribe the standards by which the duty of care is measured, if not manifestly unreasonable.
Relieve a partner of liability for intentional misconduct against the partnership.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. The agreement may identify specific types or categories of activities that do not violate the duty of loyalty, if not manifestly unreasonable (§ 105(d)).
True. The agreement may alter the duty of care, but may not authorize conduct involving bad faith, willful or intentional misconduct, or knowing violation of law (§ 105).
False. The agreement may not relieve or exonerate a person from liability for conduct involving bad faith, willful or intentional misconduct, or knowing violation of law (§ 105(c)).
Correct. The agreement may define permitted activities and alter the duty of care within limits, but it may not exculpate intentional misconduct.
C is outside what § 105 allows.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — What the agreement may do (§ 105)

q: Pine Hollow Cabins, LLC is a member-managed LLC under the ULLCA with three members and an operating agreement that is silent on management. Two members want to sell all of the company's cabins to a resort chain; the third objects. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The sale may proceed, because a majority of the members may decide any matter.
The sale may proceed, because each member is an agent of the company and may sell its property.
The sale may proceed only if the two members first buy out the third.
The sale requires the consent of all three members, because it is outside the ordinary course.
None of the above.
oe: Majority vote decides only differences on matters in the ordinary course of the company's activities (ULLCA § 407(b)(3)).
Members are not agents of the company solely by being members (§ 301(a)).
No such rule exists; the issue is consent, not a buyout.
Correct. In a member-managed LLC, an act outside the ordinary course of the company's activities requires the affirmative vote or consent of all members (ULLCA § 407(b)(4)(A)).
D is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Unanimity in a member-managed LLC

q: A partnership's buyout agreement provides that when a partner dies, the surviving partners "may, at their option, purchase" the deceased partner's interest at an appraised price. Ken dies, and the survivors decline to buy. Ken's estate demands that they buy his interest under the agreement. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The estate cannot force the purchase under the agreement.
The estate can force the purchase, but only at book value.
The estate can force the survivors to sell their interests to the estate instead.
The estate can force the purchase, because a buyout agreement always obligates the survivors to buy.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Drafters must decide whether a buyout is an obligation or an option and what happens if someone refuses to buy. Here the survivors have only an option, so the estate must look to the statute's default rules instead.
The agreement sets an appraised price, and it does not obligate the survivors to buy at any price.
Nothing in the agreement gives the estate a reverse option.
Buyout agreements may impose an obligation or merely grant an option; this one grants an option.
A is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Obligation or option?

q: Which of the following relationships is NOT an agency?
o: A lawyer retained to negotiate a settlement for a client.
A grain dealer that buys grain from farmers for resale on its own account and sets its own prices.
An employee who sells merchandise in a store for its owner.
A real estate broker hired to find a buyer for a house.
A nephew who agrees, without pay, to sell his aunt's car at a price she sets.
oe: Retaining a lawyer creates an agency: the lawyer acts for the client and subject to the client's control on the objectives of the representation.

Correct: this is not an agency. One who contracts to acquire property from a third person and convey it to another is that person's agent only if it agreed to act primarily for the other's benefit (R2d § 14K). An independent dealer buying for its own account is a supplier, not an agent (Cargill found Warren was not merely a supplier only because of Cargill's control).
An employee who acts for the employer and subject to its control is an agent.
A broker acts on the seller's behalf and subject to the seller's control over the terms, so the broker is an agent.
A gratuitous agent is still an agent (compare Gorton v. Doty).
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Not an agency

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Gus, Iris, and Jae are partners in Cedar & Pine Woodworks, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that builds custom furniture. They have no agreed term and share profits equally. Gus contributed $30,000 and Iris $10,000; Jae contributed only his skill as a craftsman. Gus also lent the partnership $20,000. Jae bought a lathe with his own money, titled in his own name, and lets the firm use it. Iris bought a planer with a partnership check, but the bill of sale names only her.

Jae's personal creditors claim the lathe. The partnership argues that the lathe is partnership property because the firm uses it every day. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The lathe is partnership property, because property used in the partnership's business belongs to the partnership.
The lathe is partnership property, because Jae contributed no money and so must have contributed the lathe.
The lathe is presumed to be Jae's separate property, though the firm uses it.
The lathe is owned by all three partners as tenants in partnership.
None of the above.
oe: Use in the business does not make property partnership property. The RUPA looks at how the property was acquired and titled.
Jae's contribution was his skill; nothing shows he transferred the lathe to the partnership.

Correct. Property acquired in a partner's name without an indication of the partner's capacity or of the partnership, and without partnership assets, is presumed to be separate property even if used for partnership purposes (RUPA § 204(d)).
Tenancy in partnership is a UPA (1914) concept; the RUPA treats property as owned by the entity or by a partner.
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Separate property used by the firm

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Gus, Iris, and Jae are partners in Cedar & Pine Woodworks, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that builds custom furniture. They have no agreed term and share profits equally. Gus contributed $30,000 and Iris $10,000; Jae contributed only his skill as a craftsman. Gus also lent the partnership $20,000. Jae bought a lathe with his own money, titled in his own name, and lets the firm use it. Iris bought a planer with a partnership check, but the bill of sale names only her.

Which of the following best describes the planer that Iris bought with a partnership check, titled in her own name?
o: It is Iris's separate property, because the bill of sale names only her.
It is presumed to be partnership property.
It is owned equally by Iris and the partnership, because each has a claim to it.
It belongs to whichever partner uses it most.
None of the above.
oe: Title in a partner's own name does not control when partnership funds paid for the property.
Correct. Property purchased with partnership assets is presumed to be partnership property, even if not acquired in the partnership's name (RUPA § 204(c)).
There is no such split ownership; the presumption assigns it to the partnership.
Use does not determine ownership under § 204.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Bought with partnership funds

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Gus, Iris, and Jae are partners in Cedar & Pine Woodworks, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that builds custom furniture. They have no agreed term and share profits equally. Gus contributed $30,000 and Iris $10,000; Jae contributed only his skill as a craftsman. Gus also lent the partnership $20,000. Jae bought a lathe with his own money, titled in his own name, and lets the firm use it. Iris bought a planer with a partnership check, but the bill of sale names only her.

Iris's personal creditor, which has a judgment against her for a car loan, tries to seize the planer. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The creditor may seize the planer, because it is titled in Iris's name.
The creditor may seize a third of the planer, matching Iris's share of the profits.
The creditor may seek a charging order, but may not seize the planer.
The creditor may force the partnership to dissolve so that Iris's share can be paid.
None of the above.
oe: The planer is presumed partnership property, and a partner's personal creditor cannot reach partnership property.
A partner is not a co-owner of partnership property and has no interest in it that can be transferred, voluntarily or involuntarily (RUPA § 501).

Correct. A partner's judgment creditor may obtain a charging order, a lien on the partner's transferable interest requiring the partnership to pay the creditor any distributions due to the partner (§ 504). It cannot levy on partnership property such as the planer.
A partner's creditor may not force a dissolution simply by having a claim against the partner. (A transferee may apply for dissolution in limited circumstances, § 801(5).)
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — A partner's creditor and firm property

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Gus, Iris, and Jae are partners in Cedar & Pine Woodworks, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that builds custom furniture. They have no agreed term and share profits equally. Gus contributed $30,000 and Iris $10,000; Jae contributed only his skill as a craftsman. Gus also lent the partnership $20,000. Jae bought a lathe with his own money, titled in his own name, and lets the firm use it. Iris bought a planer with a partnership check, but the bill of sale names only her.

Gus notifies Iris and Jae that he is withdrawing from Cedar & Pine. What is the result under the RUPA?
o: Gus's withdrawal is wrongful, and he owes damages to the partnership.
Gus is dissociated, and the partnership continues and must buy out his interest.
Nothing happens until Iris and Jae consent to Gus's withdrawal.
The partnership is dissolved, and its business must be wound up.
None of the above.
oe: Withdrawal from an at-will partnership breaches no term, so it is rightful unless it violates an express provision of the agreement (§ 602(b)).
That is the result when a dissociation does not cause dissolution. In an at-will partnership, a partner's express will to withdraw causes dissolution.
A partner may withdraw by express will at any time; no consent is needed.
Correct. In a partnership at will, the partnership's knowledge or notice of a partner's express will to withdraw dissolves it, and its business must be wound up (RUPA § 801(1)).
D is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Withdrawal from an at-will partnership

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Gus, Iris, and Jae are partners in Cedar & Pine Woodworks, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that builds custom furniture. They have no agreed term and share profits equally. Gus contributed $30,000 and Iris $10,000; Jae contributed only his skill as a craftsman. Gus also lent the partnership $20,000. Jae bought a lathe with his own money, titled in his own name, and lets the firm use it. Iris bought a planer with a partnership check, but the bill of sale names only her.

In winding up, the partnership's assets sell for $130,000. It owes outside creditors $40,000 and still owes Gus his $20,000 loan. How much does Gus receive in total under RUPA § 806?
o: None of the above.
oe: Correct. Creditors, including Gus as a creditor, are paid first: $40,000 + $20,000 = $60,000, leaving $70,000. Unreturned contributions come next: Gus $30,000 and Iris $10,000, leaving $30,000. The surplus is split equally, $10,000 each. Gus receives $20,000 + $30,000 + $10,000 = $60,000.
That total leaves out Gus's $10,000 share of the surplus.
That total overstates the surplus. After creditors and contributions are paid, $30,000 remains, not $40,000.
That total omits the repayment of Gus's $20,000 loan, which is paid with the creditors.
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — RUPA § 806 in numbers

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: The Town of Brookhaven hires SkyBurst Pyrotechnics, an independent fireworks company, to put on its Fourth of July show in a crowded riverside park. The contract pays SkyBurst a flat fee and states that "SkyBurst assumes all liability for the show." SkyBurst supplies its own shells, mortars, and licensed crew and decides how to set up and fire the show; a town official attends only to give the signal to start. Before signing, the town clerk learned that the state had suspended SkyBurst's license the year before for safety violations, but the town hired SkyBurst anyway because its bid was lowest.

A misfired shell lands in the crowd and injures a spectator, Lark. Lark sues the town, which argues that SkyBurst was an independent contractor. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The town is not liable, because a principal is never liable for an independent contractor's torts.
The town is not liable, because the town official only gave the signal to start and did not control the firing.
The town may be liable, because a hirer cannot shed the risks of such dangerous work by hiring out.
The town is liable only if the contract failed to require SkyBurst to carry insurance.
None of the above.
oe: The independent-contractor rule has exceptions, including inherently dangerous and abnormally dangerous work.
Lack of control establishes that SkyBurst is an independent contractor; it does not defeat the exceptions.

Correct. A principal who hires a contractor for inherently dangerous work, or for an abnormally dangerous activity, remains liable for the harm it causes (Restatement of Torts §§ 416, 427A; compare Majestic Realty, where demolition on a crowded block was inherently dangerous).
Insurance terms allocate costs between the town and SkyBurst; they do not determine the town's liability to Lark.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Abnormally dangerous work

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: The Town of Brookhaven hires SkyBurst Pyrotechnics, an independent fireworks company, to put on its Fourth of July show in a crowded riverside park. The contract pays SkyBurst a flat fee and states that "SkyBurst assumes all liability for the show." SkyBurst supplies its own shells, mortars, and licensed crew and decides how to set up and fire the show; a town official attends only to give the signal to start. Before signing, the town clerk learned that the state had suspended SkyBurst's license the year before for safety violations, but the town hired SkyBurst anyway because its bid was lowest.

Lark also argues that the town is liable because of how it chose SkyBurst. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The town may be directly liable for negligently selecting a contractor it knew had a suspended license for safety violations.
The town cannot be liable for its choice, because it accepted the lowest bid as the law requires.
The town can be liable for its choice only if it also controlled the firing of the show.
The town's choice is irrelevant, because only SkyBurst's conduct on the day of the show matters.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A principal is directly liable for harm resulting from its own negligence in selecting an agent or contractor that it knew, or should have known, was incompetent for the work (R3d § 7.05; one of the Majestic Realty exceptions).
A low bid does not excuse hiring a contractor the town knew was unsafe.
Negligent selection is a separate exception from retained control; it rests on the town's own carelessness in choosing.
Direct liability looks at the principal's own negligence, including in selection.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Negligent selection

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: The Town of Brookhaven hires SkyBurst Pyrotechnics, an independent fireworks company, to put on its Fourth of July show in a crowded riverside park. The contract pays SkyBurst a flat fee and states that "SkyBurst assumes all liability for the show." SkyBurst supplies its own shells, mortars, and licensed crew and decides how to set up and fire the show; a town official attends only to give the signal to start. Before signing, the town clerk learned that the state had suspended SkyBurst's license the year before for safety violations, but the town hired SkyBurst anyway because its bid was lowest.

A SkyBurst crew member is burned when a defective mortar explodes during setup. He collects workers' compensation from SkyBurst and then sues the town. Under Anderson v. Marathon Petroleum Co., which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The town is liable, because fireworks are dangerous, and anyone who hires out dangerous work is liable to everyone it injures.
The town is liable, because the crew member's workers' compensation award shows that someone was at fault.
The town is generally not liable, because workers' compensation covers the crew member.
The town is liable only if it chose the type of mortar SkyBurst used.
None of the above.
oe: Anderson explained why the dangerous-work exceptions protect neighbors and the public, not the contractor's own employees.
Workers' compensation is no-fault; the award does not establish anyone's tort liability.

Correct. Judge Posner reasoned in Anderson that the independent-contractor rule applies to the contractor's own workers, whose injuries are covered by the contractor's exclusive workers' compensation, a cost built into the contract price. The exceptions for dangerous work exist mainly to protect third parties.
Had the town retained control over equipment, that could matter, but these facts show none.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — The contractor's own employee (Anderson)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: The Town of Brookhaven hires SkyBurst Pyrotechnics, an independent fireworks company, to put on its Fourth of July show in a crowded riverside park. The contract pays SkyBurst a flat fee and states that "SkyBurst assumes all liability for the show." SkyBurst supplies its own shells, mortars, and licensed crew and decides how to set up and fire the show; a town official attends only to give the signal to start. Before signing, the town clerk learned that the state had suspended SkyBurst's license the year before for safety violations, but the town hired SkyBurst anyway because its bid was lowest.

The town argues that it cannot be liable to Lark because SkyBurst "assumes all liability for the show" under their contract. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The clause bars Lark's claim against the town, because the parties allocated all liability to SkyBurst.
The clause makes SkyBurst the town's agent, so the town is liable only for SkyBurst's intentional torts.
The clause is void, so the town cannot recover anything from SkyBurst.
The clause means that SkyBurst, not the town, must pay Lark if the town is found liable, so Lark must sue SkyBurst.
None of the above.
oe: Lark is not a party to the contract and is not bound by its allocation of risk.
An indemnity clause does not convert an independent contractor into an agent, and nothing limits liability to intentional torts.
Indemnity and risk-allocation clauses between contracting parties are generally enforceable between them.
Lark may sue whoever is liable to her; the clause affects who ultimately bears the loss, not whom she may sue.

Correct. The clause does not bind Lark, who may still sue the town under the dangerous-work and negligent-selection exceptions. It allocates the loss between the town and SkyBurst, so the town may seek indemnity from SkyBurst for what it pays.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Contract allocation vs. third parties

q: An unconscious crash victim is taken by ambulance to Metro Hospital's trauma center, which advertises "Metro's expert trauma surgeons." The surgeon who operates is an independent contractor. A disclaimer stating that doctors are not hospital employees appears only in a consent form the patient never saw or signed. The patient sues the hospital for the surgeon's negligence. Under Williams v. Dimensions Health Corp., which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The hospital may be vicariously liable as the surgeon's apparent principal.
The hospital cannot be liable, because its disclaimer told patients that doctors are not its employees.
The hospital cannot be liable, because the surgeon was an independent contractor.
The hospital may be liable only if the patient personally chose the surgeon.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Williams applied R2d § 267: a hospital that holds out its trauma center and its surgeons, where patients reasonably rely on the facility, may be liable for an apparent agent's negligence. The majority did not require proof of the unconscious patient's own subjective belief; the dissent would have.
A disclaimer the patient never saw, in a form she never signed, is not a meaningful notice that defeats apparent agency.
Apparent agency can make a principal vicariously liable for an independent contractor's negligence.
The patient's reliance is on the hospital, not on choosing a particular doctor; a patient brought in unconscious chooses no one.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Apparent agency in a hospital (Williams)

q: A law firm's partnership agreement gives an executive committee control over firm policy and allows a majority of partners to approve mergers. After a merger approved under that procedure, Pratt, a senior partner, loses his post as sole head of the firm's branch office, and the office moves. Pratt sues, claiming the other partners breached their fiduciary duties by not warning him that he would lose his post. Under Day v. Sidley & Austin, which of the following statements is true?
o: Pratt wins, because partners must disclose every change in the firm that could affect another partner.
Pratt wins, because a merger always requires the unanimous consent of all partners.
Pratt loses, because the agreement allowed the change and he suffered no cognizable injury.
Pratt loses, because partners in a law firm owe one another no fiduciary duties.
None of the above.
oe: Day held that fiduciary duty did not require disclosing internal changes that brought no profit to the others and no loss to the firm.
Unanimity is a default rule; this agreement let a majority approve a merger.

Correct. In Day v. Sidley & Austin, the agreement gave the executive committee control and let a majority approve the merger; partners may contract around default rules, and a "bruised ego" is not a claim.
Partners in law firms owe fiduciary duties; Day simply found no breach of them.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Bargained-for governance (Day v. Sidley)

q: Two partners in a motel partnership dissolve it before it has earned any profit. Instead of ordering the motel sold, the trial court lets one partner buy out the other. Under Disotell v. Stiltner, which of the following statements is true?
o: The court erred, because dissolution always requires a sale of the partnership's property.
A buyout is permitted, but only at a fair market value proven by evidence.
A buyout is permitted at any price the court considers fair, with or without evidence of value.
A buyout is permitted only if both partners consent to it.
None of the above.
oe: Disotell allowed a buyout instead of a forced sale; liquidation by sale is not the only option.

Correct. Disotell approved a buyout in place of liquidation, required that the price be the property's fair market value as shown by the evidence, and held that a partner must account for personal use of partnership property while winding up. The case reflects the shift toward buyouts now found in RUPA § 701.
The price must rest on evidence of fair market value.
The court ordered the buyout over objection; consent was not required.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Buyout instead of sale (Disotell)

q: The operating agreement of a member-managed LLC under the ULLCA provides: "No member may apply to a court to dissolve the company for any reason." Two members later use their control to divert company business to their own firm, directly harming the third member, Ula. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Ula may not seek judicial dissolution, because she agreed to the clause.
Ula may seek judicial dissolution, but only if all the members consent.
Ula may seek judicial dissolution only if the company's business is unlawful.
Ula may apply for judicial dissolution; the clause is unenforceable.
None of the above.
oe: The operating agreement may not vary the grounds for judicial dissolution (ULLCA § 105(c)(9)).
A court-ordered dissolution does not require the other members' consent.
Unlawful business is one ground, but not the only one.

Correct. The operating agreement cannot vary the court's power to dissolve (§ 105(c)), and a court may dissolve the company when those in control have acted in a manner that is oppressive and directly harmful to the applicant (§ 701(a)(4)(C)(ii)); the court may also order a lesser remedy.
D is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — What an operating agreement can't do

q: Vic, a real estate broker, has an exclusive contract to sell Wilma's vacant lot. Vic learns from a reliable source that the state will soon announce a new highway interchange next to the lot, which will sharply raise its value. Wilma has just accepted Vic's suggestion to list the lot at a low price. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Vic need not tell Wilma, because she did not ask about nearby development.
Vic must tell Wilma, because the information is material to his job.
Vic need not tell Wilma, because the information is not yet public.
Vic must tell Wilma only if he plans to buy the lot himself.
None of the above.
oe: The duty to provide information applies when the agent knows the principal would wish to have the facts or the facts are material, whether or not the principal asks (R3d § 8.11).

Correct. An agent has a duty to use reasonable effort to provide the principal with facts that the agent knows, has reason to know, or should know when the agent knows the principal would wish to have them or the facts are material to the agent's duties, unless a superior duty to another forbids it (R3d § 8.11).
There is no such exception. The information came from a reliable source and is plainly material.
Buying it himself would also raise adverse-dealing problems, but the duty to disclose exists regardless.
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Duty to disclose

q: Which of the following accurately distinguishes an LLC under the ULLCA from a general partnership under the RUPA?
o: An LLC member is not an agent of the company solely because she is a member, while every partner is an agent of the partnership.
LLC members have a full liability shield without making any filing beyond forming the LLC, while general partners need an LLP filing to get one.
A dissociated LLC member has no statutory right to be bought out, while a dissociated partner whose departure does not dissolve the firm does.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Compare ULLCA § 301(a) with RUPA § 301(1).
True. The LLC shield comes with formation (ULLCA § 304); general partners are personally liable unless the firm files to become an LLP (RUPA §§ 306(c), 901).
True. Compare ULLCA § 603(a)(3) (the departing member keeps only a transferee's interest) with RUPA § 701.
Incomplete. C is also an accurate distinction.
Correct. These are the key exam differences: no automatic agency, a shield without an LLP filing, and no mandatory buyout. (Oppression is also a ground for judicial dissolution of an LLC.)
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — LLC versus general partnership

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lupe and Marco agree to lease a vacant waterfront lot from its owner, Cora, for three summers to run weekend food festivals. Each puts up half the money. Marco manages the lot, books the vendors, and handles all dealings with Cora. They agree to split the festival profits equally, and they have no other business together. Near the end of the third summer, Cora offers Marco, alone, a ten-year lease of the lot together with the adjoining pier, at a much higher rent, for a year-round market. Marco signs the new lease in his own name without telling Lupe.

Lupe learns of the new lease and sues Marco. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Marco did nothing wrong, because Cora offered the new lease to him alone.
Marco did nothing wrong, because co-venturers owe each other only the morals of the marketplace.
Marco breached his duty of loyalty, because he had to disclose the offer to Lupe.
Marco breached only his duty of care, by failing to negotiate a lower rent.
None of the above.
oe: The offer came to Marco because he was the venture's manager; that is the reason he had to share it, not a defense.
Meinhard v. Salmon held the opposite: co-venturers owe "the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive."

Correct. As in Meinhard v. Salmon, the new lease was an extension of the venture's subject matter that came to the managing co-venturer because of his position, and he had to disclose it to his co-venturer.
The problem is that he took the opportunity for himself without disclosure, which is a loyalty issue.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — An opportunity from the venture (Meinhard)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lupe and Marco agree to lease a vacant waterfront lot from its owner, Cora, for three summers to run weekend food festivals. Each puts up half the money. Marco manages the lot, books the vendors, and handles all dealings with Cora. They agree to split the festival profits equally, and they have no other business together. Near the end of the third summer, Cora offers Marco, alone, a ten-year lease of the lot together with the adjoining pier, at a much higher rent, for a year-round market. Marco signs the new lease in his own name without telling Lupe.

Marco argues that the new lease is a different deal: it begins after the festival lease ends, covers the pier as well as the lot, and is for a year-round market rather than summer festivals. Which of the following statements is consistent with the majority opinion in Meinhard v. Salmon?
o: The argument succeeds, because the venture was ending, so Marco owed no further duty.
The argument fails, because the new lease grew out of the venture.
The argument succeeds, because adding the pier makes the new lease an entirely separate opportunity.
The argument fails only because Marco used venture funds to secure the new lease.
None of the above.
oe: That is closer to Judge Andrews's dissent, which saw the venture as a limited one that was ending.

Correct. Cardozo's majority treated the new lease as an extension and enlargement of the old one, coming to the manager while the venture was ongoing. That the new deal was bigger and started later did not free the manager from his duty.
In Meinhard, the new lease also covered more land (adjoining lots) and a bigger project, and the court still held it belonged in part to the venture.
Nothing suggests Marco used venture funds; the breach lies in taking the opportunity without disclosure.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — The new lease is different

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lupe and Marco agree to lease a vacant waterfront lot from its owner, Cora, for three summers to run weekend food festivals. Each puts up half the money. Marco manages the lot, books the vendors, and handles all dealings with Cora. They agree to split the festival profits equally, and they have no other business together. Near the end of the third summer, Cora offers Marco, alone, a ten-year lease of the lot together with the adjoining pier, at a much higher rent, for a year-round market. Marco signs the new lease in his own name without telling Lupe.

If Lupe wins, what is the most likely remedy?
o: An interest in the new lease, which Marco holds in trust for the venture, with Lupe sharing in it.
Nothing beyond her share of the third summer's profits, because the venture is over.
An order canceling the new lease and returning the lot to Cora.
Punitive damages only, because disgorgement is not available against a co-venturer.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In Meinhard, the court gave the wronged co-venturer a share of the new lease, held in trust (with one extra share left to Salmon so that he kept control as manager). The remedy captures the opportunity, not just damages.
The venture's opportunity is what Marco took, and equity reaches it.
The court does not undo the lease; it makes the fiduciary share it.
Disgorgement and constructive trust are the core remedies for a fiduciary's taking of an opportunity.
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Meinhard's remedy

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lupe and Marco agree to lease a vacant waterfront lot from its owner, Cora, for three summers to run weekend food festivals. Each puts up half the money. Marco manages the lot, books the vendors, and handles all dealings with Cora. They agree to split the festival profits equally, and they have no other business together. Near the end of the third summer, Cora offers Marco, alone, a ten-year lease of the lot together with the adjoining pier, at a much higher rent, for a year-round market. Marco signs the new lease in his own name without telling Lupe.

Assume instead that Lupe and Marco's written venture agreement said: "Each party may pursue any other real estate opportunity for his or her own account, even if it competes with the venture." Under Singer v. Singer, which of the following statements is true?
o: Marco still breached his duty of loyalty, because the duty to share opportunities cannot be varied by agreement.
Marco did not breach, so long as he took none of the venture's existing assets.
Marco did not breach, because a clause like this eliminates all fiduciary duties between the parties.
The clause is void as against public policy.
None of the above.
oe: Singer enforced a clause allowing partners to compete for opportunities; partners can contract around the opportunity doctrine (subject to RUPA § 105 limits).

Correct. In Singer v. Singer, a family partnership's agreement expressly allowed competition, and partners who bought a parcel the family had discussed did not breach; only taking existing partnership assets or funds would have.
The clause narrowed the duty not to take opportunities; it did not eliminate all duties, such as the duty not to take existing assets.
Singer upheld a similar clause.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — A clause permitting competition (Singer)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lupe and Marco agree to lease a vacant waterfront lot from its owner, Cora, for three summers to run weekend food festivals. Each puts up half the money. Marco manages the lot, books the vendors, and handles all dealings with Cora. They agree to split the festival profits equally, and they have no other business together. Near the end of the third summer, Cora offers Marco, alone, a ten-year lease of the lot together with the adjoining pier, at a much higher rent, for a year-round market. Marco signs the new lease in his own name without telling Lupe.

Which of the following steps would have protected Marco from liability for taking the new lease?
o: Fully disclosing Cora's offer to Lupe and taking the lease only after she declined to take part.
Offering Lupe an equal share of the new lease on the same terms.
Waiting until the festival lease expired before negotiating with Cora.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A fiduciary who fully discloses an opportunity and obtains the other's informed consent does not breach the duty of loyalty.
True. Sharing the opportunity with the co-venturer satisfies the duty; the breach in Meinhard was taking it secretly.
False. Waiting would not change the fact that the opportunity grew out of the venture and came to Marco as its manager.
Correct. Disclosure followed by Lupe's informed decision not to participate, or sharing the lease with her, would have satisfied Marco's duty.
C would not have protected him.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Harlow and Ines form Ridgecrest Apartments, L.P., which buys a 60-unit apartment complex. They properly file a certificate of limited partnership naming Harlow as the general partner and Ines as the limited partner. Ines contributes $900,000; Harlow contributes $100,000 and manages the property. Ridgecrest is governed by the Uniform Limited Partnership Act (ULPA) (2001) and has not elected to be a limited liability limited partnership. Ines also sits on an advisory committee that recommends rent levels each year; she is not otherwise involved in the business.

A contractor that renovated the complex is owed $200,000 that Ridgecrest cannot pay. The contractor sues Ines personally, arguing that by setting rents on the advisory committee she took part in controlling the business. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Ines is not personally liable, even though she took part in setting rents.
Ines is personally liable only up to the amount she would have earned as a manager.
Ines is personally liable, because she contributed most of the capital.
Ines is personally liable, because a limited partner who participates in control loses her limited liability.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under ULPA (2001) § 303, an obligation of a limited partnership is not the obligation of a limited partner, and a limited partner is not personally liable for it solely by reason of being a limited partner, even if she participates in the management and control of the LP.
No such measure exists. Either the shield applies or it does not.
The size of a limited partner's contribution does not affect her liability for the LP's obligations.
That was the old "control rule." ULPA (2001) § 303 largely eliminated it.
A is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — No control rule under ULPA (2001)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Harlow and Ines form Ridgecrest Apartments, L.P., which buys a 60-unit apartment complex. They properly file a certificate of limited partnership naming Harlow as the general partner and Ines as the limited partner. Ines contributes $900,000; Harlow contributes $100,000 and manages the property. Ridgecrest is governed by the Uniform Limited Partnership Act (ULPA) (2001) and has not elected to be a limited liability limited partnership. Ines also sits on an advisory committee that recommends rent levels each year; she is not otherwise involved in the business.

Ines buys a competing apartment complex across the street and runs it herself. Harlow sues her for breach of fiduciary duty. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Ines breached her duty of loyalty by competing with the partnership.
Ines breached her duty to disclose, because she had to tell Harlow before buying the complex.
Ines did not breach any duty, because she owes none merely as a limited partner.
Ines breached her duty of care, because her competing complex may lower Ridgecrest's profits.
None of the above.
oe: A limited partner does not owe the general partner's duty of loyalty.
Absent an agreement, a limited partner has no fiduciary duty to disclose her outside investments.

Correct. ULPA (2001) § 305 provides that a limited partner does not have any fiduciary duty to the LP or to any other partner solely by reason of being a limited partner. Unless the partnership agreement says otherwise, she may run a competing business.
Lawful competition is not a breach of care, and a limited partner owes no fiduciary duty of care by status.
C is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — A limited partner may compete

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Harlow and Ines form Ridgecrest Apartments, L.P., which buys a 60-unit apartment complex. They properly file a certificate of limited partnership naming Harlow as the general partner and Ines as the limited partner. Ines contributes $900,000; Harlow contributes $100,000 and manages the property. Ridgecrest is governed by the Uniform Limited Partnership Act (ULPA) (2001) and has not elected to be a limited liability limited partnership. Ines also sits on an advisory committee that recommends rent levels each year; she is not otherwise involved in the business.

Which of the following statements about Harlow's liability for the contractor's $200,000 claim is true?
o: Harlow is personally liable for the LP's obligations as its general partner.
Harlow could have avoided personal liability by having a corporation or LLC that he owned serve as the general partner.
Harlow could have avoided personal liability by having the LP elect to become a limited liability limited partnership (LLLP).
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A general partner of an LP that is not an LLLP is personally liable for the LP's obligations.
True. A corporate or LLC general partner gives the individuals behind it limited liability, which is why the structure is common in real estate (Frigidaire).
True. An LLLP shields its general partners as well as its limited partners.
Incomplete. The LLLP election would also have protected him.
Correct. Harlow is personally liable as general partner, and either a corporate general partner or an LLLP election would have avoided that.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — The general partner's exposure

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Harlow and Ines form Ridgecrest Apartments, L.P., which buys a 60-unit apartment complex. They properly file a certificate of limited partnership naming Harlow as the general partner and Ines as the limited partner. Ines contributes $900,000; Harlow contributes $100,000 and manages the property. Ridgecrest is governed by the Uniform Limited Partnership Act (ULPA) (2001) and has not elected to be a limited liability limited partnership. Ines also sits on an advisory committee that recommends rent levels each year; she is not otherwise involved in the business.

Ines grows unhappy with Harlow's management. Under ULPA (2001), which of the following is NOT one of her rights as a limited partner?
o: To share in the LP's profits and distributions according to the partnership agreement.
To inspect and copy required records of the partnership.
To sue the general partner for breach of his fiduciary duties.
To vote on ordinary business decisions, such as which contractors to hire.
To withhold her consent to an amendment of the partnership agreement.
oe: This is a right of a limited partner; limited partners are owners who share in profits.
Limited partners have information rights, including access to required records.
A limited partner may bring a direct or derivative action against the general partner.

Correct: this is not her right. Ordinary business decisions belong to the general partner; limited partners have no management role in daily operations (though they do vote on matters such as amendments).
This is a right. Under ULPA (2001), amending the partnership agreement requires the consent of all partners, limited partners included (§ 406(b)(1)).
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Not a limited partner's right

q: Ruiz tells his agent, Kim, in writing, "Sell my boat for $20,000." Ruiz meant to write $25,000. Kim, reasonably reading the instruction as written, sells the boat to a buyer for $20,000. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Ruiz is not bound, because he never intended to authorize a sale for $20,000.
Ruiz is bound only through apparent authority, because Kim had no actual authority.
Ruiz is bound, because Kim had express actual authority.
Ruiz is bound only if he later ratifies the sale.
None of the above.
oe: Actual authority turns on the agent's reasonable understanding of the principal's manifestation, not on the principal's unexpressed intent.
Kim did have actual authority; apparent authority is not needed.

Correct. Actual authority exists when the principal's manifestation would lead a reasonable agent to believe she is authorized (R3d §§ 2.01–2.02, 3.01). Express authority is effective even if the principal granted it by mistake.
Ratification is unnecessary when the agent acted with actual authority.
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Authority given by mistake

q: Under RUPA § 202(c)(3), a person who receives a share of a business's profits is presumed to be a partner unless the profits were received in one of several excepted capacities. Which of the following recipients would be presumed to be a partner?
o: A seller of equipment who is being paid the purchase price in installments equal to 5% of profits.
A store manager who receives 10% of profits as a bonus on top of a salary.
A landlord who receives 8% of the tenant's profits as rent.
The widow of a deceased partner who receives 3% of profits as a retirement annuity.
None of the above.
oe: Excepted: profits received in payment of a debt by installments or otherwise.
Excepted: profits received as wages or other compensation to an employee.
Excepted: profits received as rent.
Excepted: profits received as an annuity or other retirement or health benefit to a beneficiary or representative of a deceased or retired partner.

Correct. Each recipient falls within an exception to the presumption: debt repayment, wages, rent, and an annuity to a deceased partner's widow. (The other exceptions are interest on a loan, even if it varies with profits, and the price of goodwill or other property.)
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Profit-sharing presumption exceptions

q: Kay, Lev, and Mo are equal partners in a RUPA partnership that sells building supplies. Kay and Lev, over Mo's objection, write to Ridge Lumber: "Do not accept any orders from Mo; the partnership will not pay for them." Mo then orders $12,000 of lumber from Ridge, which ships it. Is the partnership bound?
o: Yes, because buying lumber is in the ordinary course of the partnership's business.
Yes, because a partner who objects is not a majority and cannot restrict a co-partner's authority, just as in National Biscuit v. Stroud.
No, because a majority of the partners restricted Mo's authority, and Ridge had notice of the restriction before it shipped.
No, because any one partner may revoke another partner's authority by notifying suppliers.
None of the above.
oe: Ordinary-course acts bind the partnership unless the partner lacked authority and the third party knew or had notice of that. Ridge had notice.
In Nabisco, one of two equal partners could not form a majority. Here two of three partners, a majority, restricted Mo's authority on an ordinary matter.

Correct. A majority may decide ordinary-course matters (RUPA § 401(k)), so Mo lacked actual authority, and because Ridge knew of the restriction, Mo's order does not bind the partnership under § 301(1).
One partner alone cannot strip another of authority on ordinary matters (that was Stroud's problem); a majority can.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Notice of a limit

q: A general partnership of architects files a statement of qualification and becomes a limited liability partnership (LLP). Which of the following statements is true?
o: A partner is not personally liable for partnership obligations incurred while the firm is an LLP solely by reason of being a partner.
A partner who personally designs a defective building remains liable for her own negligence.
Partners remain personally liable for partnership obligations incurred before the firm became an LLP.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. RUPA § 306(c): an obligation of a partnership incurred while it is an LLP is solely the obligation of the partnership.
True. The LLP shield protects a partner from liability for the partnership's obligations, not for her own torts.
True. The shield covers obligations incurred while the firm is an LLP; earlier obligations are unaffected.
Incomplete. C is also true.
Correct. The LLP shield covers only obligations incurred while the firm is an LLP, and it never protects a partner from liability for her own wrongful conduct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — What an LLP filing does and doesn't do

q: While still employed as the sales manager of Delta Tools, Ned plans to start a competing business. Which of the following is Ned permitted to do before he leaves?
o: Form an LLC for the new business and open its bank account.
Persuade Delta's top salespeople to quit and join his new business.
Sign a lease for office space for the new business.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Preparing to compete, such as forming an entity, is permitted if not otherwise wrongful (R3d § 8.04).
False. Using his position to recruit the principal's key employees while still employed is a breach (Bancroft-Whitney v. Glen).
True. Lining up space and financing is permitted preparation.
Correct. Forming the entity and leasing space are permitted preparations; soliciting Delta's employees while still its manager is not.
B is a breach of the duty of loyalty.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Preparing to compete

q: A partnership's buyout agreement requires it to buy the interest of any partner who dies. The partners worry that paying a large price in a lump sum would drain the firm's cash. Which provision best addresses that concern?
o: A clause requiring the estate to accept the deceased partner's capital account balance as the price.
A clause giving the surviving partners an option, rather than an obligation, to buy.
Installment payments with interest, funded partly by life insurance.
A clause requiring the partnership to dissolve and liquidate whenever a partner dies.
None of the above.
oe: That lowers the price (often unfairly, as in G & S v. Belman); it does not address how the price is paid.
An option lets the survivors refuse to buy at all, which leaves the estate without a market for the interest.
Correct. Buyout agreements address payment terms (lump sum versus installments with interest) and funding; life insurance is the standard way to fund a buyout triggered by death.
Liquidating the business is the opposite of what a buyout agreement is meant to accomplish.
C is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Payment terms

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Sela and Tobias are partners in Ostrander & Vale, a twelve-partner accounting firm organized as a general partnership under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). The firm has no fixed term, and its partnership agreement says nothing about what happens when a partner withdraws. Sela and Tobias decide to leave and start their own firm. While still partners, they (1) sign a lease for new office space and arrange a bank line of credit; (2) copy a confidential firm spreadsheet listing every staff accountant's salary and billing rate and give it to the recruiter for their new firm; (3) deny any plans to leave when the managing partner asks them directly; and (4) prepare letters on firm letterhead asking their clients to move their files to the new firm, which they mail the day they give notice.

Which of Sela and Tobias's actions, standing alone, is permissible preparation to compete?
o: Action (1) only.
Actions (1) and (3).
Actions (1) and (4).
Actions (1), (2), and (4).
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Signing a lease and arranging financing are permitted preparations. Copying confidential salary data (Gibbs v. Breed, Abbott & Morgan), lying to the managing partner, and using firm letterhead to solicit clients before notice (Meehan v. Shaughnessy) are breaches.
Denying their plans when asked directly was part of what made the departure unfair in Meehan.
Preparing client letters in secret and mailing them the moment notice is given is the unfair head start Meehan condemned.
Using confidential salary and billing data to recruit is a breach (Gibbs).
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Permitted preparation

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Sela and Tobias are partners in Ostrander & Vale, a twelve-partner accounting firm organized as a general partnership under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). The firm has no fixed term, and its partnership agreement says nothing about what happens when a partner withdraws. Sela and Tobias decide to leave and start their own firm. While still partners, they (1) sign a lease for new office space and arrange a bank line of credit; (2) copy a confidential firm spreadsheet listing every staff accountant's salary and billing rate and give it to the recruiter for their new firm; (3) deny any plans to leave when the managing partner asks them directly; and (4) prepare letters on firm letterhead asking their clients to move their files to the new firm, which they mail the day they give notice.

Which of the following statements about the salary spreadsheet is true?
o: Giving it to their new firm's recruiter was permissible, because partners may share information about their own colleagues.
Giving it to the recruiter was a breach only if the recruiter actually hired someone.
Giving it to the recruiter breached their duty of loyalty by misusing confidential information.
Giving it to the recruiter was permissible, because their duty not to compete had already ended when they decided to leave.
None of the above.
oe: The data was confidential firm information, and they used it to give their new firm a head start in recruiting.
The breach lies in misusing confidential information; the extent of the harm goes to remedy.

Correct. In Gibbs v. Breed, Abbott & Morgan, departing partners breached their duty by giving their new firm a confidential memo of staff salaries and billing rates; planning the move together was not a breach.
The duty of loyalty continues until dissociation, not until a partner privately decides to leave.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Confidential firm data (Gibbs)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Sela and Tobias are partners in Ostrander & Vale, a twelve-partner accounting firm organized as a general partnership under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). The firm has no fixed term, and its partnership agreement says nothing about what happens when a partner withdraws. Sela and Tobias decide to leave and start their own firm. While still partners, they (1) sign a lease for new office space and arrange a bank line of credit; (2) copy a confidential firm spreadsheet listing every staff accountant's salary and billing rate and give it to the recruiter for their new firm; (3) deny any plans to leave when the managing partner asks them directly; and (4) prepare letters on firm letterhead asking their clients to move their files to the new firm, which they mail the day they give notice.

After they leave, Sela and Tobias send a neutral announcement of their new firm to the public, including to Ostrander & Vale's clients. Which of the following statements is true?
o: They breach their duty of loyalty by contacting any client of their old firm.
They may compete for clients, but not with the firm's confidential information.
They may not contact any former client for two years, because a dissociated partner's power to bind lasts two years.
They may compete only if the remaining partners consent.
None of the above.
oe: After dissociation, the duty not to compete ends for matters arising after dissociation (RUPA § 603(b)(2)).

Correct. A partner's duties under § 409 end for matters arising after dissociation (§ 603(b)(2)), so former partners may compete fairly. They remain liable for breaches committed while partners and may not use confidential information.
The two-year period concerns a dissociated partner's lingering power to bind and liability to third parties (§§ 702–703), not a ban on competition.
No consent is needed to compete after leaving, absent a valid agreement restricting competition.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Competing after departure

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Sela and Tobias are partners in Ostrander & Vale, a twelve-partner accounting firm organized as a general partnership under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). The firm has no fixed term, and its partnership agreement says nothing about what happens when a partner withdraws. Sela and Tobias decide to leave and start their own firm. While still partners, they (1) sign a lease for new office space and arrange a bank line of credit; (2) copy a confidential firm spreadsheet listing every staff accountant's salary and billing rate and give it to the recruiter for their new firm; (3) deny any plans to leave when the managing partner asks them directly; and (4) prepare letters on firm letterhead asking their clients to move their files to the new firm, which they mail the day they give notice.

Sela and Tobias give written notice that they are withdrawing. Under the RUPA's default rules, what is the effect on Ostrander & Vale?
o: Nothing, because two of twelve partners cannot affect the firm.
Sela and Tobias are dissociated, and the firm continues and must buy them out.
The partnership is dissolved and must be wound up.
Their withdrawal is wrongful, and they owe the firm damages.
None of the above.
oe: Under the default rules, even one partner's express will to withdraw from an at-will partnership has consequences for the whole firm.
That is the result when a dissociation does not cause dissolution, for example in a term partnership.

Correct. In a partnership at will, the partnership's notice of a partner's express will to withdraw causes dissolution (RUPA § 801(1)). This is why professional firms' agreements usually provide that the firm continues, with a buyout, when a partner leaves.
Withdrawal from an at-will partnership is rightful unless it breaches an express term of the agreement (§ 602(b)).
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Withdrawal from an at-will firm

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Sela and Tobias are partners in Ostrander & Vale, a twelve-partner accounting firm organized as a general partnership under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). The firm has no fixed term, and its partnership agreement says nothing about what happens when a partner withdraws. Sela and Tobias decide to leave and start their own firm. While still partners, they (1) sign a lease for new office space and arrange a bank line of credit; (2) copy a confidential firm spreadsheet listing every staff accountant's salary and billing rate and give it to the recruiter for their new firm; (3) deny any plans to leave when the managing partner asks them directly; and (4) prepare letters on firm letterhead asking their clients to move their files to the new firm, which they mail the day they give notice.

The recruiter worked for the new firm, which knew the spreadsheet came from Ostrander & Vale's confidential files and used it to make offers to the firm's best staff. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The new firm may be liable to Ostrander & Vale for knowingly participating in the partners' breach of duty.
The new firm cannot be liable, because it owed Ostrander & Vale no fiduciary duty.
The new firm cannot be liable, because staff accountants are free to change jobs.
The new firm is liable only if it hired every accountant on the spreadsheet.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In Bancroft-Whitney Co. v. Glen, the competitor that knowingly cooperated in the president's breach was held liable along with him. A third party that knowingly participates in a fiduciary's breach can be liable.
A non-fiduciary that knowingly participates in a fiduciary's breach may be liable even though it owes no duty of its own.
Employees are free to move; the wrong here is the knowing use of confidential data obtained through a breach of duty.
The extent of hiring affects damages, not liability.
A is correct.
