q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Halcyon Realty, a brokerage, signs Vince, a licensed real estate agent, to a contract calling him an "independent contractor." Vince sets his own hours, drives his own car, pays his own expenses, and is paid only by commission. He must use Halcyon's forms, list properties under Halcyon's name, and follow Halcyon's written sales policies, which set a minimum listing commission of 6%. Vince has read the seller's disclosure form for a riverside house he is showing, which reports that the basement flooded twice. Halcyon's sales manager nevertheless tells Vince to tell buyers that the house "has never flooded."

While driving a buyer to a showing in his own car, Vince negligently runs a stop sign and injures a cyclist. The cyclist sues Halcyon. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Halcyon is vicariously liable, because Vince is its agent and was working on a Halcyon sale.
Halcyon is likely not vicariously liable, because it has no right to control how Vince drives.
Halcyon is liable, because the contract's "independent contractor" label is irrelevant.
Halcyon is liable, because a principal is liable for every tort an agent commits while acting on its business.
None of the above.
oe: Being an agent is not enough for vicarious liability for physical harm; respondeat superior requires an employee, one whose manner and means of work the principal controls or may control.

Correct. Under R3d § 7.07, respondeat superior applies to employees, those whose manner and means of work the principal controls or has the right to control. Vince sets his own hours, uses his own car, and pays his own expenses; Halcyon's forms and policies govern results, not the manner of his driving.
Labels are not controlling, but here the actual facts also show no control over the manner and means of Vince's work.
Liability for a nonemployee agent's physical torts generally requires more, such as the principal's own negligence.
B is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — A nonemployee agent's driving

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Halcyon Realty, a brokerage, signs Vince, a licensed real estate agent, to a contract calling him an "independent contractor." Vince sets his own hours, drives his own car, pays his own expenses, and is paid only by commission. He must use Halcyon's forms, list properties under Halcyon's name, and follow Halcyon's written sales policies, which set a minimum listing commission of 6%. Vince has read the seller's disclosure form for a riverside house he is showing, which reports that the basement flooded twice. Halcyon's sales manager nevertheless tells Vince to tell buyers that the house "has never flooded."

Following the manager's instruction, Vince tells a buyer, Wynn, that the house has never flooded. Wynn buys the house and suffers flood damage. Which theories could make Halcyon liable to Wynn?
o: Direct liability, because Halcyon instructed Vince to make the statement.
Vicarious liability, because Vince made the statement with apparent authority while acting for Halcyon.
Respondeat superior, which is the only route to holding Halcyon liable for Vince's conduct.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A principal is subject to direct liability when an agent acting with actual authority commits a tort (R3d § 7.03(1)(a)); the manager directed the false statement.
True. A principal is vicariously liable for an agent's tortious representations made with apparent authority (R3d § 7.08), even if the agent is not an employee.
False. Respondeat superior requires an employee, and it is not the only route: direct liability and apparent-authority liability reach a nonemployee agent's misrepresentations.
Correct. Halcyon may be directly liable because it authorized the statement, and vicariously liable because Vince made it with apparent authority. Neither theory requires that Vince be an employee.
C is false.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Misrepresentation by an agent

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Halcyon Realty, a brokerage, signs Vince, a licensed real estate agent, to a contract calling him an "independent contractor." Vince sets his own hours, drives his own car, pays his own expenses, and is paid only by commission. He must use Halcyon's forms, list properties under Halcyon's name, and follow Halcyon's written sales policies, which set a minimum listing commission of 6%. Vince has read the seller's disclosure form for a riverside house he is showing, which reports that the basement flooded twice. Halcyon's sales manager nevertheless tells Vince to tell buyers that the house "has never flooded."

Wynn also sues Vince, who argues that he only repeated what his sales manager told him to say. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Vince is liable, because an agent is subject to liability for his own torts even when acting on the principal's instructions.
Vince is not liable, because the principal, not the agent, answers for torts committed with actual authority.
Vince is not liable, because he is an independent contractor, and only Halcyon made the decision.
Vince is liable only if Halcyon cannot pay the judgment.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. An agent is liable to a third party harmed by the agent's tortious conduct, and acting with actual authority or at the principal's direction does not relieve him (R3d § 7.01). Vince knew of the floods from the disclosure form.
Both may be liable; the principal's liability does not displace the agent's.
Vince made the statement himself; status as an independent contractor does not excuse an actor's own torts.
The agent's liability is not secondary to the principal's.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Following orders is no defense

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Halcyon Realty, a brokerage, signs Vince, a licensed real estate agent, to a contract calling him an "independent contractor." Vince sets his own hours, drives his own car, pays his own expenses, and is paid only by commission. He must use Halcyon's forms, list properties under Halcyon's name, and follow Halcyon's written sales policies, which set a minimum listing commission of 6%. Vince has read the seller's disclosure form for a riverside house he is showing, which reports that the basement flooded twice. Halcyon's sales manager nevertheless tells Vince to tell buyers that the house "has never flooded."

On Halcyon's standard listing form, Vince signs a listing agreement with a seller, promising that Halcyon will accept a 4% commission. The seller has never heard of Halcyon's 6% minimum. Is Halcyon bound to the 4% rate?
o: No, because Vince is an independent contractor, and independent contractors can never bind the business that hires them.
No, because Vince lacked actual authority to agree to less than 6%.
Halcyon is bound only if it ratifies the 4% rate after learning of it.
Halcyon is bound only if Vince told the seller that he had authority to set the rate.
Yes, because Halcyon's own name and forms support Vince's apparent authority.
oe: A nonemployee agent can bind the principal in contract; employee status matters for vicarious tort liability, not for authority.
Lack of actual authority is not the end of the analysis.
Ratification is another route, but Halcyon may already be bound.
An agent's own statement cannot create apparent authority; the manifestation must come from the principal.

Correct. Halcyon's own manifestations (its name, its forms, its authorization to take listings) support apparent authority, and a secret internal limit does not bind a third party without notice (R3d § 3.03 cmt. b).
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — A nonemployee agent can bind the principal

q: Paul, an adult, authorizes his 16-year-old neighbor, Ty, to sell Paul's used snowblower for at least $400. Ty sells it to a buyer for $450. Paul later wants to undo the sale, arguing that Ty was too young to act for him. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Paul may undo the sale, because a minor lacks capacity to act as an agent.
Paul may undo the sale, because contracts made through a minor agent are voidable by either party.
The sale binds Paul only if Ty's parents consented to his acting as an agent.
The sale binds Paul, because an agent needs only minimal capacity, unlike a principal.
None of the above.
oe: An agent needs only minimal capacity; the contract is the principal's, not the agent's (R3d § 3.05).
The minority of the agent does not make the principal's contract voidable.
No parental consent is required for a minor to act as an agent.
Correct. The principal must have contractual capacity; the agent needs only the minimal (mental) capacity to act (R3d §§ 3.04–3.05). Paul's appointment of Ty and the sale bind Paul.
D is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — A minor as agent

q: A supplier wins a $70,000 judgment against both a RUPA partnership and its partner, Gail. The partnership still has a bank account and equipment. The supplier wants to levy at once on Gail's vacation house. Under RUPA § 307(d), which of the following statements is true?
o: The supplier may levy on Gail's house first, because partners are jointly and severally liable for partnership debts.
The supplier generally must first exhaust partnership assets, unless an exception applies.
The supplier may never reach Gail's personal assets, because only the partnership owes the debt.
The supplier may levy on Gail's house only if Gail personally signed the supply contract.
None of the above.
oe: Joint and several liability makes Gail liable, but the exhaustion rule governs the order of collection.

Correct. A judgment against a partner based on a partnership obligation generally may not be satisfied from the partner's assets until a judgment against the partnership has gone unsatisfied (§ 307(d)). Exceptions include the partnership's bankruptcy, the partner's agreement, a court order where partnership assets are clearly insufficient or exhaustion would be excessively burdensome, and liability imposed on the partner independently of the partnership.
Partners are personally liable for partnership obligations (§ 306(a)); the exhaustion rule only sets the order.
Liability for partnership obligations does not depend on which partner signed.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Exhaustion and its exceptions

q: Three founders form Lakeview Bikes, LLC under the ULLCA. Their operating agreement says, "Kim will handle the company's day-to-day operations," but it does not use the words "manager-managed" or anything similar. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The LLC is manager-managed, with Kim as its manager, because the agreement put her in charge of operations.
The LLC is manager-managed, and all three founders are its managers.
The LLC is member-managed; Kim's role is a delegation among the members.
The LLC has no valid management structure until the founders amend the agreement.
None of the above.
oe: An LLC is manager-managed only if the operating agreement expressly says so, using words such as "manager-managed," "managed by managers," or words of similar import (ULLCA § 407(a)).
Nothing in the agreement creates managers; this reverses the default.

Correct. An LLC is member-managed unless the operating agreement expressly provides that it is manager-managed (§ 407(a)). Assigning one member to run daily operations does not, by itself, make the company manager-managed.
The ULLCA supplies a default structure (member management) whenever the agreement does not choose one.
C is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Member-managed by default

q: Two potato distributors advance money to a group of growers, buy interests in their crops, and sign an agreement providing that profits and losses from the crops will be divided "between the partners." When the growers go bankrupt, the distributors file claims as creditors. Under Kaufman-Brown Potato Co. v. Long, which of the following statements is true?
o: The distributors were partners, because they shared losses as well as profits.
The distributors were creditors, because they did not manage the farms day to day.
The distributors were partners only for the crops they personally harvested.
The distributors were creditors, because advancing money to someone always creates a debt.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In Kaufman-Brown, sharing losses as well as profits, and dealing as co-owners, made the distributors partners. Contrast Martin v. Peyton, where the lenders shared no losses and could only veto, not initiate.
Daily management is not required for partnership; the distributors shared both profits and losses as co-owners.
No such limited partnership status exists; the court treated them as partners in the venture.
Advances can be capital contributions to a venture; the question is whether the parties were co-owners.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Sharing losses tips the balance (Kaufman-Brown)

q: A partnership agreement lets the surviving partners continue the business and buy a deceased partner's interest by formula. One partner, Yale, files suit asking a court to dissolve the partnership. Before the case is decided, Yale dies. His estate argues that his lawsuit dissolved the partnership, so the buyout clause does not apply. Under G & S Investments v. Belman, which of the following statements is true?
o: The estate is right, because filing a suit for dissolution dissolves a partnership on the day the suit is filed.
The estate is wrong; filing suit did not dissolve the partnership, so the buyout clause governs.
The estate is right, because a partner's death always dissolves the partnership whatever the agreement says.
The estate is wrong, but only because Yale's lawsuit was frivolous.
None of the above.
oe: G & S held that filing suit did not dissolve the partnership.
Correct. In G & S Investments v. Belman, the partner's suit for dissolution did not itself dissolve the partnership; when he died, the agreement's continuation and buyout provisions applied.
Partners may agree that the business continues after a death; the court enforced that agreement.
The merits of Yale's lawsuit were not the basis of the holding; filing it simply did not dissolve the firm.
B is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Suing for dissolution doesn't dissolve (G & S)

q: Lyle drives a tow truck for Ace Towing, whose rules forbid drivers to help stranded motorists except on dispatched calls. On his way back to the yard, Lyle stops to push a stranger's stalled car for a $20 tip, and the push causes a collision. The injured driver sues Ace. Under Brill v. Davajon, which of the following statements is true?
o: Ace is liable, because Lyle was driving Ace's truck during working hours.
Ace is liable, because forbidden acts are always within the scope of employment.
Ace is not liable; the push was outside the scope of employment.
Ace is not liable, because tow-truck drivers are independent contractors.
None of the above.
oe: Using the employer's vehicle during work hours does not make every act within scope; the purpose of the act matters.
Forbidden acts can be within scope (R2d § 230), but not when the employee departs from the employer's business to serve only himself.

Correct. In Brill v. Davajon, a cab driver who pushed a stalled car for $1, against company rules, was outside the scope of employment: the act served only his own purpose (R2d § 228(1)(c)). Contrast Bushey's enterprise-risk view.
Nothing suggests Lyle is an independent contractor; the issue is scope of employment.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — A side job for himself (Brill)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Dirk, Elsa, and Flynn, siblings, are partners in Hartwell Orchards, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says the partnership will last until December 31, 2040. For the past two years Dirk has threatened Elsa and Flynn ("You'll be sorry; I'll be the last one standing"), screamed at seasonal workers in front of customers, refused to sign routine loan renewals, and stalled the harvest. The orchard is otherwise profitable.

Elsa and Flynn ask a court to expel Dirk from the partnership. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The court may not expel Dirk, because a partner can be expelled only under the partnership agreement.
The court may expel Dirk, but only if he has committed a crime.
The court may expel Dirk, because his conduct makes partnership with him impracticable.
The court may expel Dirk only with the consent of all three partners, including Dirk.
None of the above.
oe: Expulsion under the agreement is one route; the RUPA also allows expulsion by judicial order (§ 601(5)).
Criminal conduct is not required; conduct making it not reasonably practicable to carry on the business with him suffices.

Correct. On application by the partnership or another partner, a court may expel a partner whose conduct relating to the partnership business makes it not reasonably practicable to carry on the business with him (§ 601(5)(C)). Giles v. Giles Land Co. expelled a family partner for threats and obstruction much like Dirk's.
Judicial expulsion is ordered over the expelled partner's objection.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Judicial expulsion (Giles)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Dirk, Elsa, and Flynn, siblings, are partners in Hartwell Orchards, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says the partnership will last until December 31, 2040. For the past two years Dirk has threatened Elsa and Flynn ("You'll be sorry; I'll be the last one standing"), screamed at seasonal workers in front of customers, refused to sign routine loan renewals, and stalled the harvest. The orchard is otherwise profitable.

Assume the court expels Dirk in 2027 and the orchard continues. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Dirk's dissociation is not wrongful, because he did not choose to leave.
Dirk is entitled to the full buyout price immediately, with no deductions.
Dirk's expulsion automatically dissolves the partnership, so the orchard must be sold.

Dirk's dissociation is wrongful; his buyout price is reduced by the damages he caused, and he may have to wait until the term ends in 2040 to be paid unless earlier payment would not cause the business undue hardship.
None of the above.
oe: Judicial expulsion before the end of a term is on the list of wrongful dissociations (§ 602(b)(2)(B)).
Damages caused by a wrongful dissociation are offset against the buyout price (§ 701(c)), and payment may be deferred (§ 701(h)).
Under the RUPA, a dissociation in a term partnership does not by itself dissolve it; the business may continue with a buyout.

Correct. In a term partnership, a judicial expulsion before the term ends is wrongful (§ 602(b)(2)(B)). Damages are offset against the buyout price (§ 701(c)), and a wrongful dissociator is not entitled to payment until the term expires unless he shows that earlier payment will not cause undue hardship; deferred payment must be secured and bear interest (§ 701(h)).
D is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Consequences of a judicial expulsion

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Dirk, Elsa, and Flynn, siblings, are partners in Hartwell Orchards, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says the partnership will last until December 31, 2040. For the past two years Dirk has threatened Elsa and Flynn ("You'll be sorry; I'll be the last one standing"), screamed at seasonal workers in front of customers, refused to sign routine loan renewals, and stalled the harvest. The orchard is otherwise profitable.

Why would Elsa and Flynn likely prefer to seek Dirk's judicial expulsion rather than a court-ordered dissolution of the partnership?
o: Expulsion lets the profitable orchard continue, with a buyout of Dirk, while dissolution would require winding up the business.
Expulsion relieves Dirk of all liability for partnership debts incurred while he was a partner.
Dissolution is not available when one partner's conduct is the problem.
Expulsion requires no court order, so it is faster.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The RUPA lets a court remove one partner (with a buyout) instead of dissolving the business (Giles), whereas a dissolution ordered under § 801(4) starts winding up. Under the UPA, by contrast, a misbehaving partner's case typically ended in dissolution (Owen v. Cohen).
Dissociation does not discharge a partner's existing liabilities (§ 603(c)).
Dissolution is available on the ground that another partner's conduct makes it not reasonably practicable to carry on the business with him (§ 801(4)(C)).
Here they need a court order, because the agreement has no expulsion clause.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Expulsion versus dissolution

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Dirk, Elsa, and Flynn, siblings, are partners in Hartwell Orchards, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says the partnership will last until December 31, 2040. For the past two years Dirk has threatened Elsa and Flynn ("You'll be sorry; I'll be the last one standing"), screamed at seasonal workers in front of customers, refused to sign routine loan renewals, and stalled the harvest. The orchard is otherwise profitable.

Before Elsa and Flynn act, Dirk himself asks a court to dissolve the partnership, arguing that the partners' conflicts make it not reasonably practicable to carry on. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The court must dissolve the partnership, because any partner may obtain dissolution when the partners cannot get along.
The court may dissolve the partnership on Dirk's application, and his misconduct is irrelevant to the outcome.
The court may deny Dirk's application, because he caused the problems.
Dirk cannot apply for dissolution, because only the partnership itself may file such an application.
None of the above.
oe: Judicial dissolution is discretionary and turns on the statutory grounds; it is not automatic for any partner.
A court may weigh the fact that the applicant caused the problem.

Correct. In Collins v. Lewis, the court denied dissolution to a partner whose own conduct caused the business's problems; he had the power to leave, but not the right to force a dissolution and profit from his own wrong.
§ 801(4) allows a partner to apply.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Profiting from your own misconduct (Collins)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Dirk, Elsa, and Flynn, siblings, are partners in Hartwell Orchards, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says the partnership will last until December 31, 2040. For the past two years Dirk has threatened Elsa and Flynn ("You'll be sorry; I'll be the last one standing"), screamed at seasonal workers in front of customers, refused to sign routine loan renewals, and stalled the harvest. The orchard is otherwise profitable.

Assume instead that, in 2026, Dirk simply announces that he is withdrawing, and the partnership does not dissolve. Sixty days later, Elsa decides that she, too, wants out and gives notice of her withdrawal. Is Elsa's withdrawal wrongful?
o: Yes, because any withdrawal from a term partnership before the term ends is wrongful.
Yes, because Elsa needs Flynn's consent to withdraw.
No, because a sibling partnership is always a partnership at will.
No, because she withdrew within 90 days after Dirk's wrongful dissociation.
None of the above.
oe: There is an exception for a partner who withdraws soon after another partner's wrongful dissociation.
No partner's consent is needed to withdraw; the only question is whether the withdrawal is wrongful.
The agreement sets a term ending in 2040, so this is a term partnership.

Correct. In a term partnership, withdrawal by express will before the end of the term is wrongful unless it follows, within 90 days, another partner's dissociation by death or similar event or a wrongful dissociation (§ 602(b)(2)(A)). Dirk's withdrawal was wrongful, so Elsa may leave rightfully within 90 days.
D is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Leaving within 90 days

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Northgate Tools, Inc. makes power tools and sells them to hardware chains. It names Rhea its regional sales manager and authorizes her to negotiate supply contracts with hardware chains in her region and to grant volume discounts of up to 10%. In the tool industry, regional sales managers commonly agree to two-year price locks for large chains. An internal memo from Northgate's vice president tells Rhea never to grant price locks. Rhea signs a supply contract with BuildRite, a hardware chain, that includes a two-year price lock. BuildRite knows that Rhea is Northgate's regional sales manager but knows nothing about the memo.

Did Rhea have actual authority to agree to the two-year price lock?
o: Yes, because price locks are customary in the industry, which gives her implied authority to grant them.
Yes, because she had express authority to negotiate supply contracts.
No, because the memo's express prohibition overrides any authority custom might give.
No, because a sales manager never has authority to agree to any contract term.
None of the above.
oe: Custom can support implied authority, but not when the principal has expressly told the agent not to do the act.
Express authority to negotiate contracts was limited by the express instruction never to grant price locks.

Correct. Actual authority turns on the agent's reasonable understanding of the principal's manifestations to her (R3d §§ 2.01–2.02). An express prohibition defeats any implied authority that custom might otherwise supply.
Rhea had express authority to negotiate contracts and grant discounts; she lacked authority only for price locks.
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Express prohibition, no actual authority

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Northgate Tools, Inc. makes power tools and sells them to hardware chains. It names Rhea its regional sales manager and authorizes her to negotiate supply contracts with hardware chains in her region and to grant volume discounts of up to 10%. In the tool industry, regional sales managers commonly agree to two-year price locks for large chains. An internal memo from Northgate's vice president tells Rhea never to grant price locks. Rhea signs a supply contract with BuildRite, a hardware chain, that includes a two-year price lock. BuildRite knows that Rhea is Northgate's regional sales manager but knows nothing about the memo.

BuildRite argues that Northgate is bound anyway. Which of the following statements best supports BuildRite's argument?
o: By naming Rhea its regional sales manager, a position whose holders customarily grant price locks, Northgate manifested to BuildRite that she had that authority, and BuildRite had no notice of the memo.
Rhea told BuildRite that she was authorized to grant the price lock.
BuildRite needed the price lock to make the contract profitable.
Northgate later accepted BuildRite's first payment without reading the contract.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A principal that places an agent in a position manifests that the agent has the authority customarily held there; a third party need not inquire into undisclosed limits (R3d § 3.03 cmt. b). That supports apparent authority.
An agent's own statements cannot create apparent authority.
The third party's business needs are not a manifestation by the principal.
Accepting benefits without knowledge of the material terms is not ratification (Ercanbrack).
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Apparent authority from the position

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Northgate Tools, Inc. makes power tools and sells them to hardware chains. It names Rhea its regional sales manager and authorizes her to negotiate supply contracts with hardware chains in her region and to grant volume discounts of up to 10%. In the tool industry, regional sales managers commonly agree to two-year price locks for large chains. An internal memo from Northgate's vice president tells Rhea never to grant price locks. Rhea signs a supply contract with BuildRite, a hardware chain, that includes a two-year price lock. BuildRite knows that Rhea is Northgate's regional sales manager but knows nothing about the memo.

Under Restatement (Second) of Agency § 161, as explained in Nogales Service Center v. Atlantic Richfield Co., which of the following statements is true?
o: Northgate is bound only if it made some manifestation to BuildRite about Rhea's authority.
A general agent of a disclosed principal can bind it to usual acts, even forbidden ones, if the third party reasonably believes she is authorized.
Inherent authority applies only to undisclosed principals, as in Watteau v. Fenwick.
Inherent authority binds a principal only if the principal later ratifies the agent's act.
None of the above.
oe: That describes apparent authority. Inherent authority does not depend on any manifestation by the principal.

Correct. R2d § 161 describes inherent agency power, which arises from the agency relationship itself rather than from the principal's manifestation. Nogales used it to distinguish inherent from apparent authority. (The Restatement (Third) dropped inherent authority and relies on apparent authority and § 2.06 instead.)
Watteau involved an undisclosed principal (R2d §§ 194–195), but § 161 extends inherent authority to general agents of disclosed principals.
Inherent authority binds without ratification.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Inherent authority (Nogales)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Northgate Tools, Inc. makes power tools and sells them to hardware chains. It names Rhea its regional sales manager and authorizes her to negotiate supply contracts with hardware chains in her region and to grant volume discounts of up to 10%. In the tool industry, regional sales managers commonly agree to two-year price locks for large chains. An internal memo from Northgate's vice president tells Rhea never to grant price locks. Rhea signs a supply contract with BuildRite, a hardware chain, that includes a two-year price lock. BuildRite knows that Rhea is Northgate's regional sales manager but knows nothing about the memo.

Assume Northgate is bound to the price lock and loses $300,000 when its costs rise. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Northgate is bound to BuildRite on the price lock.
Rhea is liable to Northgate for the loss caused by acting beyond her actual authority.
Rhea is personally liable to BuildRite for breach of the implied warranty of authority.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Rhea had apparent authority (and, under the R2d, inherent authority) to agree to it.
True. An agent who acts beyond actual authority, contrary to the principal's instructions, breaches her duty and is liable for the resulting loss (R3d § 8.09).
False. The implied warranty applies only when the principal is not bound; here Northgate is bound, so BuildRite has suffered no loss from any lack of authority.
Correct. Northgate is bound to BuildRite, and Rhea must answer to Northgate for disobeying its instruction.
C is false, because Northgate is bound.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — The agent who exceeds her authority

q: For weeks, a man in an apron matching those worn by Brightway Hardware's staff has been taking cash "deposits" from customers for special orders. Brightway's managers have seen him and suspected he was not an employee, but did nothing. A customer, Pia, pays him $600 and never receives her order. Which of the following statements best describes Pia's claim against Brightway?
o: Pia can recover on apparent authority, because the man looked like a Brightway salesperson.
Pia may recover on estoppel, but not on apparent authority.
Pia cannot recover, because a principal is never liable for the acts of a person who is not its agent.
Pia can recover only if Brightway ratifies the impostor's sale.
None of the above.
oe: Apparent authority must rest on the principal's manifestation; an impostor's own appearance and conduct cannot create it (Hoddeson v. Koos Bros.).

Correct. In Hoddeson, the court rejected apparent authority but allowed an estoppel claim: a store must use reasonable care to keep impostors from posing as staff. Brightway's managers knew of the risk and did nothing (R3d § 2.05).
Estoppel can make a person liable even when no agency exists, if its intentional or careless conduct caused the third party's belief.
Ratification requires an act done on the principal's behalf and the principal's affirmance; Brightway is not going to ratify, and Pia need not rely on it.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — An impostor and the store's carelessness (Hoddeson)

q: Ana and her brother Ben co-own a lake cabin. Without consulting Ben, Ana signs a five-year lease of the whole cabin to Cole, with an option to buy, signing only her own name. Ben knows Cole is staying at the cabin and accepts a few rent checks Ana forwards to him, but he does not know about the option. When Cole tries to exercise the option, Ben refuses to sell his half. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Ben is not bound, because Ana was not his agent and he did not knowingly ratify the lease.
Ben is bound, because accepting rent checks ratified the entire lease, including the option.
Ben is bound, because co-owners of property are each other's agents for leasing it.
Ben is bound to the lease but not to the option, because he may ratify part of the transaction.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. As in Botticello v. Stefanovicz, co-ownership (or a family tie) does not make one owner the other's agent. Ratification requires knowledge of all material facts, and one can ratify only an act done or purportedly done on one's behalf.
Accepting some benefits without knowledge of material terms such as the option is not ratification.
There is no such rule; agency must be proved.
There is no partial ratification (R3d § 4.07); and here Ben did not ratify at all.
A is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Co-ownership isn't agency (Botticello)

q: Vale Construction's division manager, Will, secretly owns a scaffolding company that wins $1.2 million of Vale subcontracts he helped award, even after Vale starts its own scaffolding business. Will's written employment contract expired a year earlier, but he kept working in the same role. Vale sues him for breach of fiduciary duty. Under Rash v. J.V. Intermediate, Ltd., which of the following statements is true?
o: Will is not liable, because his fiduciary duties ended when his employment contract expired.
Will is not liable, unless Vale proves it paid more than market prices for the scaffolding.
Will breached his duty of loyalty, because he contracted with his principal through his own company without full disclosure.
Will breached only his contractual duties, which expired with the contract.
None of the above.
oe: Fiduciary duties arise from the agency relationship, which continued after the contract lapsed.
A secret conflict breaches loyalty whether or not the prices were fair.

Correct. In Rash, a manager who secretly owned a company that won subcontracts he helped award breached his fiduciary duty as a matter of law; an agent must disclose matters affecting the principal's business, and the fiduciary claim did not depend on the lapsed employment contract.
The claim is for breach of fiduciary duty, which does not depend on the contract.
C is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Undisclosed self-dealing (Rash)

q: A large firm's partnership agreement puts all real power in a self-perpetuating executive committee. The firm demotes 30 partners who share profits, have capital at risk, and are personally liable for firm debts, but who have no voice in firm management. A federal agency investigates whether the demotions were age discrimination. Under EEOC v. Sidley Austin Brown & Wood, which of the following statements is true?
o: The agency must drop the matter, because people who are partners under state law can never be employees under federal law.
The demoted partners are employees, because anyone who can be demoted is an employee.
The agency may pursue the matter, because the demoted partners are employees under federal law if they have no real control over the firm.
The agency may investigate whether the demoted partners are really employees.
None of the above.
oe: Sidley held that state-law partner status does not settle federal coverage.
The court did not decide the question that way; it allowed the agency to investigate whether the partners lacked real control.
Too strong. Sidley allowed the inquiry to go forward; whether these partners were employees required more facts (and the concurrence thought they were bona fide partners).

Correct. In EEOC v. Sidley Austin Brown & Wood, Judge Posner allowed the agency's subpoena: profit sharing, capital at risk, and liability did not settle the question when a committee held all the power. Compare Clackamas, which also looks to control.
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Partners as employees for federal law (Sidley)

q: Under the RUPA, Abe and Cy run a landscaping business as partners. Abe borrows $8,000 from his aunt, buys a dump truck titled in the partnership's name, and uses it only in the business. Later, Cy files for personal bankruptcy, and Cy's trustee claims a half interest in the truck. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The truck is partnership property, because it was acquired in the partnership's name.
Abe's purchase of the truck counts as his capital contribution to the partnership.
Cy's trustee reaches only Cy's partnership interest, not the truck itself.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Property acquired in the name of the partnership is partnership property (RUPA § 204(a)); the purpose and the parties' intent at acquisition confirm it.
True. In In re Fulton, the partner's purchase of the trailer for the business, titled in the business's name, was treated as his capital contribution.
True. A partner has no interest in specific partnership property that can be transferred (§ 501); Cy's estate takes his transferable interest.
Incomplete. B is also true.

Correct. As in In re Fulton, title, purpose, and intent made the vehicle partnership property, the purchase was the buying partner's capital contribution, and the bankrupt partner's estate got only his partnership interest.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Property bought for the firm (Fulton)

q: Under the UPA (1914), two partners open a bowling alley. One of them, Ned, tries to dominate the business, humiliates his partner in front of customers, refuses to work, and takes partnership money without consent. The other partner, who lent the partnership $6,000, asks a court to dissolve it. Under Owen v. Cohen, which of the following statements is true?
o: The court must deny relief, because petty quarrels between partners are not grounds for dissolution.
The court may dissolve the partnership only if Ned has committed a crime.
The court may order dissolution, and the lending partner's loan is repaid before profits.
The court may dissolve the partnership, but the loan must be treated as a capital contribution and repaid last.
None of the above.
oe: Minor disagreements are not enough, but Ned's persistent misconduct destroyed the cooperation the business needed.
No crime is required; misconduct that makes it impracticable to carry on the business together suffices (UPA § 32).

Correct. In Owen v. Cohen, the court affirmed a decree of dissolution for persistent misconduct that destroyed the partners' cooperation (now RUPA § 801(4)), and the complaining partner's loan was repaid first from the proceeds.
A partner's loan is repaid before capital and profits (UPA § 40(b)).
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Judicial dissolution under the UPA (Owen v. Cohen)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lyle, Mei, Nate, and Olga are partners in Kestrel Architects, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Their buyout agreement provides that when a partner dies, becomes disabled, retires, or is expelled, the partnership "shall purchase" the partner's interest for "the balance of the partner's capital account on the firm's books." The agreement says nothing about a partner who simply withdraws. The firm's office building, bought twenty years ago, is carried on its books at cost, far below its market value.

Lyle dies. His capital account shows $90,000, but his estate shows that, because of the office building's market value, a quarter of the firm is worth $1.2 million. The estate asks the court to pay it a fair share of market value. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The estate receives $90,000, because the court will enforce the buyout formula as written.
The estate receives $300,000, a quarter of the firm's book value.
The estate receives the default RUPA buyout price, because a capital-account formula is unenforceable.
The estate receives $1.2 million, because courts interpret "capital account" to mean fair market value.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In G & S Investments v. Belman, "capital account" meant the book figure, not market value, and the court enforced the formula even though the result was harsh. A buyout clause is a bargain the partners made in advance.
The agreement uses Lyle's capital account, not a share of book value of the whole firm.
The default § 701 price applies only if the agreement does not provide otherwise; the formula is enforceable.
Courts read "capital account" as the book figure; it is kept at cost, not market value.
A is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Book value means book value (G & S)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lyle, Mei, Nate, and Olga are partners in Kestrel Architects, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Their buyout agreement provides that when a partner dies, becomes disabled, retires, or is expelled, the partnership "shall purchase" the partner's interest for "the balance of the partner's capital account on the firm's books." The agreement says nothing about a partner who simply withdraws. The firm's office building, bought twenty years ago, is carried on its books at cost, far below its market value.

Nate contributed $60,000 when he joined Kestrel. Since then, his share of the firm's profits has totaled $520,000, his share of losses $40,000, and his draws $470,000. What is the balance of Nate's capital account?
o: None of the above.
oe: That is only his original contribution; profits, losses, and draws change the balance.
That figure ignores his share of the losses.
That figure ignores both his losses and his draws.
Correct. Capital account = contributions + share of profits − share of losses − draws: $60,000 + $520,000 − $40,000 − $470,000 = $70,000.
D is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Computing a capital account

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lyle, Mei, Nate, and Olga are partners in Kestrel Architects, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Their buyout agreement provides that when a partner dies, becomes disabled, retires, or is expelled, the partnership "shall purchase" the partner's interest for "the balance of the partner's capital account on the firm's books." The agreement says nothing about a partner who simply withdraws. The firm's office building, bought twenty years ago, is carried on its books at cost, far below its market value.

Mei retires. Two months later, the partners sell the firm to a national design company at a price that would have made Mei's quarter worth ten times her capital account. Mei claims that the other partners breached the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing by letting the buyout clause apply when they knew a sale was possible. Under Nemec v. Shrader, which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Mei wins, because the implied covenant forbids applying any contract term in a way that disadvantages a partner.
Mei loses, because the implied covenant cannot override conduct the agreement expressly allows, and a later sale was a foreseeable event the parties could have addressed.
Mei wins, because partners owe a fiduciary duty that always overrides the terms of a buyout agreement.
Mei loses, because a retired partner has no rights at all against the firm.
None of the above.
oe: The implied covenant does not override terms the parties expressly agreed to.

Correct. In Nemec v. Shrader, the Delaware Supreme Court held that redeeming retired officers' stock at book value weeks before a lucrative sale did not breach the implied covenant: the contract expressly allowed it, and the possibility of a sale was foreseeable. The dissent would have required that the power serve a legitimate company interest.
Where a contract governs the matter, the fiduciary claim may be displaced; Nemec held the parties to their bargain.
Mei has contract rights under the buyout clause; she just received what it provided.
B is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Timing a buyout before a sale (Nemec)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lyle, Mei, Nate, and Olga are partners in Kestrel Architects, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Their buyout agreement provides that when a partner dies, becomes disabled, retires, or is expelled, the partnership "shall purchase" the partner's interest for "the balance of the partner's capital account on the firm's books." The agreement says nothing about a partner who simply withdraws. The firm's office building, bought twenty years ago, is carried on its books at cost, far below its market value.

Olga does not die, retire, or become disabled; she simply gives notice that she is withdrawing to join another firm. Under the RUPA's default rules, what is the most likely result?
o: The partnership must buy Olga's interest at her capital account balance under the buyout agreement.
Olga's withdrawal has no effect, because the agreement does not list withdrawal as a way to leave.
The partnership dissolves and must be wound up, because the agreement does not cover withdrawal.
Olga's withdrawal is wrongful, and she forfeits her entire interest.
None of the above.
oe: The agreement's triggers do not include withdrawal, so its formula does not apply to Olga's departure.
A partner always has the power to dissociate by express will (§ 602(a)).

Correct. In a partnership at will, a partner's express will to withdraw causes dissolution (§ 801(1)) unless the agreement provides otherwise. The missing trigger is a drafting gap: a well-drafted buyout agreement covers withdrawal too.
Withdrawal from an at-will partnership is not wrongful unless it breaches an express term, and nothing in the RUPA forfeits a partner's interest.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — A trigger the agreement left out

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lyle, Mei, Nate, and Olga are partners in Kestrel Architects, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Their buyout agreement provides that when a partner dies, becomes disabled, retires, or is expelled, the partnership "shall purchase" the partner's interest for "the balance of the partner's capital account on the firm's books." The agreement says nothing about a partner who simply withdraws. The firm's office building, bought twenty years ago, is carried on its books at cost, far below its market value.

Which of the following are purposes that a buyout agreement like Kestrel's serves?
o: Providing for an orderly transfer of a departing partner's interest.
Letting the remaining partners keep control and choose who becomes an owner.
Creating a market for the interest of a partner who leaves or of a deceased partner's estate.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Orderly transfer is a core purpose of a buyout agreement.
True. A buyout agreement keeps an interest from passing to someone the remaining owners do not want.
True. Partnership interests are hard to sell; a buyout agreement creates a buyer.
Incomplete. C is also a purpose.
Correct. Buyout agreements provide orderly transfers, preserve control over who the owners are, and create a market for the interests of inactive or departed owners (and their estates).
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Why have a buyout agreement

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Rosa and Sid are equal partners in R&S Properties, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) whose only business is owning and leasing a warehouse. They have no written agreement. The warehouse is leased, on a month-to-month basis, to SidCo, Inc., a corporation that Sid owns and runs. The rent is now well below market. Rosa wants to raise it; Sid refuses.

Rosa sends SidCo a notice raising its rent to market, signing for the partnership. Sid, for the partnership, tells SidCo to ignore it. As between the partners, which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Rosa's notice is effective, because any partner may decide ordinary matters.
Sid's instruction controls, because he is the partner closest to the tenant.
Rosa's notice is effective, because Sid has a conflict of interest and so loses his vote.
With equal partners evenly divided, neither may impose the increase on the other.
None of the above.
oe: Ordinary matters are decided by a majority (§ 401(k)); with two equal partners divided, there is no majority.
Neither partner's view controls when they are evenly divided.
The RUPA has no automatic vote-stripping rule; Sid's conflict raises loyalty issues, but it does not give Rosa a majority.

Correct. As in Covalt v. High, when partners are evenly divided on a matter, the partnership's power to act on it is suspended as between the partners (though not as to third parties, as National Biscuit shows).
D is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Evenly divided partners (Covalt v. High)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Rosa and Sid are equal partners in R&S Properties, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) whose only business is owning and leasing a warehouse. They have no written agreement. The warehouse is leased, on a month-to-month basis, to SidCo, Inc., a corporation that Sid owns and runs. The rent is now well below market. Rosa wants to raise it; Sid refuses.

Rosa sues Sid, claiming that by keeping SidCo's rent below market he breached his duty of loyalty. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Sid cannot have breached any duty, because he is entitled to vote his own interest on any partnership matter.
Sid's role implicates his duty not to deal for an adverse party; fairness or Rosa's informed consent is his defense.
Sid breached his duty of care, because a below-market rent is grossly negligent.
Sid breached no duty, because the lease was signed before the dispute began.
None of the above.
oe: A partner may further his own interest (§ 409(e)), but dealing with the partnership on behalf of an adverse party implicates the duty of loyalty.

Correct. Acting for SidCo, a tenant whose interest is adverse to the partnership's, falls within § 409(b)(2). Fairness to the partnership is a defense (§ 409(g)), and Rosa's informed consent after full disclosure would authorize it (§ 409(f)).
The issue is loyalty, not care; the duty of care is limited to gross negligence and worse.
A continuing month-to-month rent with the partner's own company remains a conflict transaction.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — A partner on both sides

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Rosa and Sid are equal partners in R&S Properties, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) whose only business is owning and leasing a warehouse. They have no written agreement. The warehouse is leased, on a month-to-month basis, to SidCo, Inc., a corporation that Sid owns and runs. The rent is now well below market. Rosa wants to raise it; Sid refuses.

Without Sid's consent, Rosa signs a one-year lease of the warehouse, starting next month, to Tidewater Freight at a market rent. Tidewater knows nothing of the dispute. Sid insists the partnership is not bound. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The partnership is bound, because Tidewater had no notice of any limit.
The partnership is not bound, because the partners were evenly divided, so Rosa had no authority.
The partnership is not bound, because Tidewater should have asked Sid before signing.
The partnership is bound only if Sid later ratifies the lease.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under RUPA § 301(1), a partner's ordinary-course act binds the partnership unless the partner lacked authority and the third party knew or had notice of that. Leasing space is this partnership's ordinary business, and, as in National Biscuit v. Stroud, an even split between the partners does not protect the firm against outsiders.
The deadlock limits authority as between the partners; it does not bind an outsider who has no notice of it.
Third parties have no duty to inquire into a partner's authority (RNR Investments).
No ratification is needed; Rosa's apparent authority binds the partnership.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Binding outsiders despite the deadlock

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Rosa and Sid are equal partners in R&S Properties, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) whose only business is owning and leasing a warehouse. They have no written agreement. The warehouse is leased, on a month-to-month basis, to SidCo, Inc., a corporation that Sid owns and runs. The rent is now well below market. Rosa wants to raise it; Sid refuses.

Rosa wants to end the stalemate. Under the RUPA, which of the following options does she have?
o: Ask a court to dissolve the partnership on the ground that it is not reasonably practicable to carry on the business in conformity with the partnership agreement.
Withdraw by express will, which, in this at-will partnership, dissolves it and starts winding up.
Expel Sid on her own, because he has a conflict of interest.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A court may order dissolution when it is otherwise not reasonably practicable to carry on the business in conformity with the partnership agreement (§ 801(4)(D)), and a lasting deadlock between two equal partners is a classic case.
True. In a partnership at will, a partner's express will to withdraw causes dissolution (§ 801(1)).
False. With no expulsion clause, one partner cannot expel another; expulsion would require a court order (§ 601(5)) or the unanimous vote of the others in narrow cases (§ 601(4)).
Correct. Rosa may seek judicial dissolution or simply withdraw from the at-will partnership, which dissolves it. She cannot expel Sid by herself.
C is wrong.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Breaking a deadlock

q: Kleen Team, a house-cleaning service, built its customer list through months of costly cold calls; the list is not public, and most households turned the company down. Three of its employees quit, form a competing service, and solicit only Kleen Team's customers, using names they remember from work. Under Town & Country House & Home Service, Inc. v. Newbery, which of the following statements is true?
o: The former employees may solicit any customers they remember, because memory is not a trade secret.
Kleen Team may enjoin solicitation of its customers and recover damages.
The former employees may not open any competing cleaning service at all.
Kleen Team has no remedy, because the employees' duties ended when they quit.
None of the above.
oe: Town & Country protected a list developed through costly effort, even though the employees did not take a written copy.

Correct. In Town & Country, the court treated a customer list developed through costly cold calls as a trade secret, enjoined the former employees from soliciting those customers, and awarded damages, while leaving them free to compete for other business. Contrast Corroon & Black, where widely accessible lists of shoppers were not secret.
Without a non-compete, former employees may compete; they may not exploit the confidential list.
The duty not to use the former principal's trade secrets and confidential information survives the end of the agency.
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Customer lists as trade secrets (Town & Country)

q: A public limited partnership's agreement allows its general partner to propose converting the LP into a corporation, subject to approval by two-thirds of the unitholders. The general partner proposes a conversion that would give it a large share of the new company's stock. A unitholder sues, claiming the general partner breached its fiduciary duty of loyalty. Under Sonet v. Plum Creek Timber Co., L.P., how would a Delaware court likely rule?
o: It would apply the entire-fairness standard, because the general partner stands on both sides of the deal.
It would enjoin the conversion, because general partners may never benefit from a transaction they propose.
It would dismiss the claim, because the agreement's voting procedure displaces default fiduciary duties.
It would require the general partner to give up its stock in the new company.
None of the above.
oe: Sonet held that a clear partnership agreement displaced the default fiduciary standard.
Nothing in Sonet bars a general partner from benefiting; the agreement set a voting procedure for approval.

Correct. In Sonet v. Plum Creek, the Court of Chancery held that where a clear partnership agreement governs the transaction, it displaces default fiduciary duties: the unitholders' protection was "the ballot box, not the courthouse." Contrast Jerman v. O'Leary, where the court read fiduciary duties into a permissive clause.
The court enforced the agreement's procedure; it ordered no such remedy.
C is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — The ballot box, not the courthouse (Sonet)

q: An LP's agreement forbids its general partner to borrow more than $250,000 without the limited partners' consent. The general partner borrows $900,000 from a bank that never saw the agreement, and the LP defaults. Under RNR Investments Ltd. Partnership v. Peoples First Community Bank, which step would most clearly have protected the limited partners from being bound to the loan?
o: Notifying the bank directly, before the loan, that the general partner could not borrow more than $250,000 without their consent.
Including the borrowing cap in the partnership agreement, which binds anyone dealing with the partnership.
Requiring the general partner to sign the loan in his own name.
Relying on the bank's duty to investigate a borrower's partnership agreement before lending.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A partner's ordinary-course act binds the partnership unless the third party knew or had notice of the partner's lack of authority. Telling the lender directly gives it knowledge. Lenders have no duty to read partnership agreements, and a filed statement limiting authority is generally not notice to outsiders (except for recorded limits on transferring real property).
That is what the LP did. A private agreement does not bind a third party without notice of it.
That would make the general partner personally liable but would not stop the LP from being bound by an authorized-looking loan.
RNR held that the bank had no duty to inquire into the agreement.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Protecting against an overreaching partner (RNR)

q: Which of the following statements about forming a general partnership under the RUPA is true?
o: No written agreement or filing is required.
The parties need not intend to form a partnership.
A clause stating "we are not partners" does not prevent a partnership from forming if the parties carry on a business as co-owners for profit.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A general partnership needs no writing and no filing; it arises from the parties' conduct.
True. A partnership forms "whether or not the persons intend to form a partnership" (§ 202(a)).
True. Labels and disclaimers do not control when the parties do the things that make a partnership (compare Fenwick and Zajac).
Incomplete. C is also true.

Correct. Formation requires only an association of two or more persons to carry on as co-owners a business for profit. No writing, filing, or subjective intent to be partners is needed, and disclaimers do not control.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Forming a partnership

q: A pizza franchisor's 300-page operations manual dictates how franchisees hire and train drivers, the routes and time limits for deliveries, and the procedures drivers must follow, and the franchisor audits compliance. A franchisee's driver, rushing to meet the time limit, causes a crash. The trial court grants the franchisor summary judgment. Under Parker v. Domino's Pizza, which of the following statements is true?
o: Summary judgment was proper, because a franchisor is never vicariously liable for a franchisee's employees.
Summary judgment was proper, because the franchise agreement called the franchisee an independent contractor.
Summary judgment should be reversed, because a jury could find the franchisor had the right to control delivery.
Summary judgment should be reversed, because a franchisor is strictly liable for every accident involving its brand.
None of the above.
oe: Franchisors are not immune; pervasive control can make one a principal.
Labels do not control; the right to control does.

Correct. In Parker, the franchise agreement and a "veritable bible" of an operations manual controlled nearly every detail of the operation, so whether the franchisor had the right to control the means of operation was a jury question. Contrast Murphy v. Holiday Inns.
There is no strict liability for franchisors; the question is the right to control.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Pervasive controls (Parker v. Domino's)

q: Opal became a member of Riverbend Outfitters, LLC in March 2026. She learns that in 2025, the LLC's manager sold company property to his own company at a steep discount. She wants to bring a derivative action against the manager. Under the ULLCA, which of the following statements is true?
o: Opal may sue derivatively, because any current member may enforce the company's rights.
Opal may not sue derivatively, because she was not a member when the conduct occurred.
Opal may sue directly instead, because the injury to the company is an injury to her.
Opal may sue derivatively without making any demand, because the manager is interested.
None of the above.
oe: A derivative plaintiff must generally have been a member when the conduct occurred, not just when suit is brought (§ 803).

Correct. A derivative action may be maintained only by a person who is a member when the action is commenced and who was a member when the conduct occurred, or whose status as a member devolved on her by operation of law or under the operating agreement from such a person (ULLCA § 803).
A direct action requires an injury not solely resulting from an injury to the company (§ 801(b)).
Futility may excuse demand (§ 802), but it does not cure Opal's lack of standing under § 803.
B is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Who may sue derivatively

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Wynn, Xia, and Yuri are equal partners in Saltmarsh Surf Shop, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term and no written agreement. On May 1, Wynn gives his partners written notice that he is withdrawing, and the partners begin winding up the business. On May 10, Xia, who knows the shop is winding up, orders $25,000 of next season's surfboards from Crest Boards, a regular supplier that knows nothing of the dissolution. On May 20, Yuri sells the shop's remaining inventory to a liquidator. On June 1, the partnership files a statement of dissolution.

Xia and Yuri tell Wynn that, because he caused the dissolution, he may not take part in winding up the business. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Wynn may participate in winding up, because his dissociation was not wrongful.
Wynn may not participate, because a partner who causes a dissolution forfeits his management rights.
Wynn may participate only if a court appoints him.
Wynn may not participate, because he is no longer a partner and is now only a transferee.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A person whose dissociation resulted in dissolution may participate in winding up as if still a partner, unless the dissociation was wrongful (RUPA § 802(c)). Withdrawing from an at-will partnership is not wrongful.
Only a wrongful dissociator is excluded from winding up (§ 802(c)).
No court appointment is needed; the statute gives him the right.
§ 802(c) lets him participate "as if still a partner."
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Who winds up

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Wynn, Xia, and Yuri are equal partners in Saltmarsh Surf Shop, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term and no written agreement. On May 1, Wynn gives his partners written notice that he is withdrawing, and the partners begin winding up the business. On May 10, Xia, who knows the shop is winding up, orders $25,000 of next season's surfboards from Crest Boards, a regular supplier that knows nothing of the dissolution. On May 20, Yuri sells the shop's remaining inventory to a liquidator. On June 1, the partnership files a statement of dissolution.

Crest Boards ships the $25,000 of surfboards Xia ordered on May 10. Is the partnership bound to pay?
o: No, because after dissolution a partner has no power to bind the partnership to new business.
No, because Xia knew the partnership was winding up.
Yes, because Crest had no notice of the dissolution.
Yes, because ordering inventory is always appropriate for winding up.
None of the above.
oe: After dissolution, a partner lacks actual authority for new business, but the partnership may still be bound to a third party without notice of the dissolution (§ 804(a)(2)).
Xia's knowledge makes her liable to her partners; it does not protect the partnership against a third party who lacked notice.

Correct. After dissolution, a partnership is bound by a partner's act that would have bound it under § 301 before dissolution if the other party does not know or have notice of the dissolution (RUPA § 804(a)(2)). The statement of dissolution was not filed until June 1, and even then outsiders are not deemed to have notice of it for 90 days (§ 103(d)).
Ordering next season's inventory is new business, not winding up.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Authority after dissolution

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Wynn, Xia, and Yuri are equal partners in Saltmarsh Surf Shop, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term and no written agreement. On May 1, Wynn gives his partners written notice that he is withdrawing, and the partners begin winding up the business. On May 10, Xia, who knows the shop is winding up, orders $25,000 of next season's surfboards from Crest Boards, a regular supplier that knows nothing of the dissolution. On May 20, Yuri sells the shop's remaining inventory to a liquidator. On June 1, the partnership files a statement of dissolution.

Assume the partnership must pay Crest for the surfboards, which it can sell only at a loss. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The loss is shared equally by the three partners, because it is a partnership obligation.
Xia is liable to the partnership and her partners for the damage, because she knowingly bound the partnership to business that was not appropriate for winding up.
Xia is liable only if she acted in bad faith.
Crest must bear the loss, because it should have checked whether the partnership was winding up.
None of the above.
oe: As to outsiders it is a partnership obligation, but the statute shifts the resulting loss, as among the partners, to Xia.

Correct. A partner who, with knowledge of the dissolution, causes the partnership to incur an obligation by an act not appropriate for winding up is liable to the partnership, and to other partners who are liable for the obligation, for the resulting damage (RUPA § 805(a)).
§ 805(a) turns on her knowledge of the dissolution and the nature of the act, not on bad faith.
Crest had no notice and no duty to inquire; the partnership is bound to it.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Liability for new business after dissolution

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Wynn, Xia, and Yuri are equal partners in Saltmarsh Surf Shop, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term and no written agreement. On May 1, Wynn gives his partners written notice that he is withdrawing, and the partners begin winding up the business. On May 10, Xia, who knows the shop is winding up, orders $25,000 of next season's surfboards from Crest Boards, a regular supplier that knows nothing of the dissolution. On May 20, Yuri sells the shop's remaining inventory to a liquidator. On June 1, the partnership files a statement of dissolution.

Which of the following acts bind Saltmarsh Surf Shop?
o: Yuri's May 20 sale of the remaining inventory to the liquidator.
Xia's May 10 order from Crest Boards.
An order of new wetsuits that Xia places on October 1 with a supplier that has not actually heard of the dissolution.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A partner's act that is appropriate for winding up binds the partnership after dissolution (§ 804(a)(1)).
True. It would have bound the partnership before dissolution, and Crest had no knowledge or notice of the dissolution (§ 804(a)(2)).
False. By October 1, more than 90 days after the June 1 filing, the supplier is deemed to have notice of the statement of dissolution (§ 103(d)), so the order does not bind the partnership.

Correct. An act appropriate for winding up binds the partnership; so does a pre-dissolution-type act with a third party lacking notice. Once a statement of dissolution has been on file for 90 days, third parties are deemed to have notice.
C does not bind the partnership.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Which acts bind the partnership

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Wynn, Xia, and Yuri are equal partners in Saltmarsh Surf Shop, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term and no written agreement. On May 1, Wynn gives his partners written notice that he is withdrawing, and the partners begin winding up the business. On May 10, Xia, who knows the shop is winding up, orders $25,000 of next season's surfboards from Crest Boards, a regular supplier that knows nothing of the dissolution. On May 20, Yuri sells the shop's remaining inventory to a liquidator. On June 1, the partnership files a statement of dissolution.

After the business is wound up, the partnership still owes outside creditors $15,000 that its assets could not pay. All of the debts were incurred before the dissolution. Yuri has no money. Under RUPA § 806, which of the following statements is true?
o: Each partner must contribute $5,000, and if Yuri cannot pay, Wynn and Xia must contribute his share and may recover it from him later.
The creditors must absorb the $15,000 loss, because the partnership has been wound up.
Wynn owes nothing, because he withdrew before the debts went unpaid.
Wynn and Xia owe $5,000 each, and Yuri's share is simply forgiven.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Each person who was a partner when an obligation was incurred must contribute in proportion to his share of distributions ($5,000 each). If one does not contribute, the others must make additional contributions in the same proportion, and they may recover the additional amounts from the partner who failed to pay (§ 806(c), (d)).
Partners must contribute to enable the partnership to pay its creditors (§ 806(c)).
The debts were incurred while Wynn was a partner, so he must contribute toward them.
The others must cover the defaulting partner's share, with a right of recovery against him.
A is correct.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Summit Peak Resort, Inc. runs a ski area and houses many of its seasonal workers in a dormitory on the mountain. It also runs a staff bar near the dormitory. Bo, a lift operator, finishes his shift at 6 p.m., drinks heavily at the staff bar, and, walking back to the dormitory across resort property, starts playing with the controls of a snow-making machine for fun. The machine sprays water that freezes on a neighbor's roof and driveway, causing $80,000 in damage.

The neighbor sues Summit Peak for the damage Bo caused. Under Restatement (Second) of Agency § 228, what is the resort's strongest argument that Bo acted outside the scope of his employment?
o: Bo's job as a lift operator did not include running snow-making machines.
Bo was on resort property when he caused the damage.
Bo was not acting, even in part, to serve the resort.
The resort had a written rule against touching the snow-making machines.
None of the above.
oe: Conduct not authorized can still be within scope if it is of the same general nature or incidental to authorized conduct (§ 229); this is not the resort's strongest point.
That fact helps the neighbor, not the resort.

Correct. Under § 228(1)(c), conduct is within scope only if it is actuated, at least in part, by a purpose to serve the master. Off-duty horseplay for one's own amusement serves no purpose of the employer.
Forbidden conduct can still be within scope (§ 230); a rule is not decisive.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — The purpose prong (R2d § 228)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Summit Peak Resort, Inc. runs a ski area and houses many of its seasonal workers in a dormitory on the mountain. It also runs a staff bar near the dormitory. Bo, a lift operator, finishes his shift at 6 p.m., drinks heavily at the staff bar, and, walking back to the dormitory across resort property, starts playing with the controls of a snow-making machine for fun. The machine sprays water that freezes on a neighbor's roof and driveway, causing $80,000 in damage.

The neighbor relies on Ira S. Bushey & Sons, Inc. v. United States. Which of the following statements best states the neighbor's argument under that case?
o: The resort is liable because Bo intended to benefit the resort.
The resort is liable because it is always strictly liable for anything its employees do on its property.
The resort is liable only if it negligently supervised Bo.
The resort may be liable because the harm arose from risks characteristic of its activities, such as housing and serving alcohol to workers on a mountain full of equipment.
None of the above.
oe: Bushey imposed liability even though the sailor had no purpose to serve his employer; motive was not the test.
Bushey did not impose liability for everything; purely personal acts, such as the sailor shooting his wife's lover, would fall outside it.
Negligent supervision is a different theory (direct liability); Bushey concerned vicarious liability without fault.

Correct. Judge Friendly held that an enterprise must answer for risks "characteristic of its activities": a drunken sailor returning to his ship was a foreseeable risk of operating a ship at a drydock. The neighbor would argue that a worker returning drunk to the on-site dormitory and tampering with equipment is a comparable risk.
D is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Enterprise risk (Bushey)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Summit Peak Resort, Inc. runs a ski area and houses many of its seasonal workers in a dormitory on the mountain. It also runs a staff bar near the dormitory. Bo, a lift operator, finishes his shift at 6 p.m., drinks heavily at the staff bar, and, walking back to the dormitory across resort property, starts playing with the controls of a snow-making machine for fun. The machine sprays water that freezes on a neighbor's roof and driveway, causing $80,000 in damage.

Earlier that day, a skier cut the lift line, shoved Bo, and cursed him. Bo punched the skier, breaking his nose. The resort's liability policy excludes injuries "expected or intended by the insured." Under Lamkin v. Brooks, which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The resort may be vicariously liable, because the attack was closely connected to Bo's work, though its insurer may escape coverage under the intentional-acts exclusion.
Neither the resort nor its insurer is liable, because a punch is an intentional tort outside the scope of employment.
Both the resort and its insurer must pay, because an insurer must cover whatever its insured is liable for.
Only Bo is liable, because the skier provoked the attack.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In Lamkin, the town was vicariously liable for its officer's punch because it was closely connected in time, place, and causation to his duties, but the insurer was not liable because of the intentional-acts exclusion. Liability and coverage are separate questions.
Intentional torts can be within scope when they are rooted in the employment.
Coverage depends on the policy's terms; an intentional-acts exclusion can defeat it even when the employer is vicariously liable.
Provocation by the plaintiff, while relevant to the claim against Bo, does not take job-related violence outside the scope of employment.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Job-rooted violence and insurance (Lamkin)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Summit Peak Resort, Inc. runs a ski area and houses many of its seasonal workers in a dormitory on the mountain. It also runs a staff bar near the dormitory. Bo, a lift operator, finishes his shift at 6 p.m., drinks heavily at the staff bar, and, walking back to the dormitory across resort property, starts playing with the controls of a snow-making machine for fun. The machine sprays water that freezes on a neighbor's roof and driveway, causing $80,000 in damage.

Which of the following theories could support the neighbor's claim against Summit Peak for the snow-machine damage?
o: Vicarious liability under Bushey's enterprise-risk reasoning.
Direct liability for negligently supervising its staff bar and its workers, if the resort overserved workers it knew would walk past unsecured equipment.
Liability for leaving its snow-making controls unsecured where foreseeable misuse could harm neighbors.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A court following Bushey could find the harm characteristic of the resort's activities.
True. A principal is directly liable for harm caused by its own negligence in supervising or controlling its agents (R3d § 7.05), whether or not the act was within scope.
True. A landowner's own negligence in securing dangerous equipment is a basis for direct liability that does not depend on agency.
Incomplete. C is also a possible theory.

Correct. Even if Bo acted outside the scope of employment under R2d § 228 or R3d § 7.07, the neighbor can argue enterprise risk (Bushey) and the resort's own negligence in supervision and in securing its equipment.
