q: Rex is president of a musicians' union local and also a trustee of its pension fund. Only the fund's board may settle claims for unpaid contributions. Over a year, Rex signs a dozen settlements with Stagecraft, Inc., each stating that it binds the fund, and the fund cashes every settlement check that arrives with them without objecting. Later the fund sues Stagecraft for the full amounts, and Stagecraft only then learns of the board's exclusive power. Which theories support holding the fund to the settlements?
o: Apparent authority, because the fund's conduct led Stagecraft reasonably to believe that Rex could settle, until Stagecraft learned otherwise.
Ratification, because the fund accepted the settlement money with knowledge of the settlements.
Estoppel, because the fund's silence and acceptance of payments induced Stagecraft to change its position by paying.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. As in Trustees of the American Federation of Musicians v. Steven Scott Enterprises, the fund's conduct gave Rex apparent authority until the employer learned of the board's exclusive power.
True. Knowingly accepting the benefits of an unauthorized transaction ratifies it.
True. A principal that knows of a third party's belief and fails to correct it is estopped to deny the transaction against one who relied to its detriment (R3d § 2.05).
Incomplete. Estoppel also applies.
Correct. The AFM case is the course's example of a single fact pattern supporting apparent authority, estoppel, and ratification, and of how notice of the real limits ends reasonable reliance.

q: Gulfway Oil owns a service station and its equipment, sets the station's hours, pays most of its utilities, may end its arrangement with the operator at will, and may assign the operator "other duties" as it sees fit. Their contract calls the operator an independent "commission agent." A car left for service rolls out of the station and injures a pedestrian. Under Humble Oil & Refining Co. v. Martin, which of the following statements is true?
o: Gulfway is not liable, because the contract describes the operator as independent.
Gulfway is liable, because it had the right to control the station's daily operations.
Gulfway is not liable, because a supplier of branded fuel is never liable for a station's negligence.
Gulfway is liable only if it trained the operator negligently.
None of the above.
oe: Labels do not control; the right to control the station's operations does.

Correct. In Humble Oil v. Martin, the oil company owned the station and products, set the hours, paid most utilities, could end the arrangement at will, and could assign other duties, which made the operator its servant despite the contract's label. Contrast Hoover v. Sun Oil, where the dealer set his own hours, hired his own staff, and bore his own profit and loss.
Liability depends on control; an oil company that keeps the right to control daily operations answers for them.
Vicarious liability for a servant's negligence does not depend on the master's own fault.
B is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — An oil company's servant (Humble Oil)

q: Lou is a partner in Bayside Bakery, a RUPA partnership with no agreement on competition. While the partnership continues, Lou opens a second bakery of his own two blocks away and lures some of Bayside's customers. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Lou did nothing wrong, because a partner may pursue his own interests (§ 409(e)).
Lou did nothing wrong, unless the partnership agreement expressly forbade competition.
Lou breached his duty of loyalty, which includes refraining from competing with the partnership before its dissolution.
Lou breached only his duty of care, because competition is a form of mismanagement.
None of the above.
oe: § 409(e) protects conduct merely because it furthers a partner's own interest; it does not permit competing with the partnership.
The duty not to compete is a statutory default; no express clause is needed.

Correct. A partner's duty of loyalty includes refraining from competing with the partnership in the conduct of its business before dissolution (RUPA § 409(b)(3)). The agreement may, if not manifestly unreasonable, identify permitted activities, but this one does not.
Competing with the partnership is a loyalty problem.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Competing before dissolution

q: Which of the following correctly contrasts the payout order on liquidation under the UPA (1914) and the RUPA (1997)?
o: Both statutes pay partners' capital before any creditor.
The UPA pays partners' loans together with outside creditors, while the RUPA ranks partners' loans after outside creditors.
Both statutes pay partners' profits before returning their capital.
The UPA pays outside creditors before partners' loans; the RUPA pays them together.
None of the above.
oe: Both statutes pay creditors first.
That reverses the two statutes.
Both return capital (unreturned contributions) before distributing profits or surplus.

Correct. UPA § 40(b) ranks (1) outside creditors, (2) partners' loans, (3) capital, and (4) profits. RUPA § 806(a) applies assets to creditors, including partners that are creditors, and then returns unreturned contributions before distributing the surplus.
D is correct.

q: A restaurant's owners sign a contract calling Zane an "outside consultant." In practice, Zane sets the menu and prices, hires and fires staff, sets budgets, and signs checks. While doing so, he secretly helps a celebrity chef plan a competing restaurant nearby and recruits the owners' investors and staff for it. The owners sue Zane for breach of fiduciary duty. Under MJ & Partners Restaurant LP v. Zadikoff, which of the following statements is true?
o: The claim may proceed, because Zane's actual practices, not the contract's label, show he may have been the owners' agent, owing them loyalty.
The claim fails, because a consultant owes only the duties stated in his contract.
The claim fails, because Zane never signed a non-compete agreement.
The claim may proceed only if the owners prove Zane used their trade secrets.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In MJ & Partners v. Zadikoff, the breach-of-fiduciary-duty claim survived dismissal because agency turns on the parties' actual practices, the right to control and the power to bind, not on a "consultant" label. As an agent, he could not build a competitor while managing the restaurant.
The contract's label does not prevent the law from treating him as an agent, with an agent's duties.
An agent's duty not to compete during the agency does not depend on a non-compete.
Competing and recruiting the principal's investors and staff while serving as its agent is enough to state a loyalty claim.
A is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Labels don't decide agency (MJ & Partners)

q: One founder of a software partnership contributed licenses to her patents for the firm's use. The partners are drafting a buyout agreement. In light of cases such as Pav-Saver Corp. v. Vasso Corp., which provision is most important to include?
o: A clause stating that the partnership is "permanent."
A clause requiring all disputes to be resolved by the managing partner.
A clause valuing each partner's interest at book value.
A clause governing the contributed patents when she leaves.
None of the above.
oe: Pav-Saver's agreement called the partnership permanent, which only made the dissolution wrongful; it did not settle what happened to the patents.
That does not address what happens to the contributed patents when the founder leaves.
Book value says nothing about who keeps the right to use contributed intellectual property.

Correct. A buyout agreement's drafting checklist includes the treatment of contributed intellectual property. Pav-Saver shows the fight that results when the agreement does not clearly say whether the business may keep using a departing partner's patents.
D is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Contributed property in a buyout plan

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Maple Leaf Cider Works is a general partnership of Ike and Jen, governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). After a bad harvest, it borrows $500,000 from Orchard Capital, LLC. The loan agreement gives Orchard 30% of the cidery's profits until Orchard has received $750,000; the right to inspect the books monthly; a veto over any capital expenditure above $50,000; and an option to buy a one-third interest in the partnership within five years. Orchard cannot initiate any transaction or sign for the cidery, and it bears no share of any losses. Ike and Jen also give Orchard signed letters resigning from the business, to be used only if they default.

A creditor of the cidery sues Orchard, claiming that Orchard is a partner. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Orchard is a partner, because it receives 30% of the cidery's profits.
Orchard is likely a lender rather than a partner, because each of its rights is a reasonable protection for a large, risky loan, and it can veto but not initiate or bind.
Orchard is a partner, because its option to buy a one-third interest makes it a co-owner now.
Orchard is a partner, because the resignation letters give it control of the business.
None of the above.
oe: Profit sharing raises a presumption only if the profits are not received in an excepted capacity, such as interest on a loan.

Correct. As in Martin v. Peyton, profit-based repayment, information rights, a veto over major spending, an option to buy in, and resignations held as security were each reasonable protections for a risky loan, and the lender could not initiate transactions or bind the firm. Enough such terms together could cross the line, but these do not.
An option to become a partner in the future is not present co-ownership.
The resignations were security to be used only on default, as in Martin v. Peyton; they are not present control.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Lender, not partner (Martin v. Peyton)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Maple Leaf Cider Works is a general partnership of Ike and Jen, governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). After a bad harvest, it borrows $500,000 from Orchard Capital, LLC. The loan agreement gives Orchard 30% of the cidery's profits until Orchard has received $750,000; the right to inspect the books monthly; a veto over any capital expenditure above $50,000; and an option to buy a one-third interest in the partnership within five years. Orchard cannot initiate any transaction or sign for the cidery, and it bears no share of any losses. Ike and Jen also give Orchard signed letters resigning from the business, to be used only if they default.

Under RUPA § 202(c)(3), does Orchard's 30% share of profits raise a presumption that it is a partner?
o: Yes, because any share of a business's net profits raises an irrebuttable presumption of partnership.
Yes, because the share is capped at $750,000, which makes it a return on an investment.
No, because Orchard does not share in the cidery's gross receipts.
No, because profits paid as interest on a loan, even if they vary, are excepted.
None of the above.
oe: The presumption is rebuttable, and it does not arise at all for profits received in an excepted capacity.
A cap on the total payable is typical of a loan, not of co-ownership.
The statute is concerned with sharing net profits; gross receipts do not raise a presumption at all (§ 202(c)(2)).
Correct. One of § 202(c)(3)'s exceptions covers profits received in payment of interest or other charges on a loan, even if the amount varies with the profits of the business.
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Interest that varies with profits

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Maple Leaf Cider Works is a general partnership of Ike and Jen, governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). After a bad harvest, it borrows $500,000 from Orchard Capital, LLC. The loan agreement gives Orchard 30% of the cidery's profits until Orchard has received $750,000; the right to inspect the books monthly; a veto over any capital expenditure above $50,000; and an option to buy a one-third interest in the partnership within five years. Orchard cannot initiate any transaction or sign for the cidery, and it bears no share of any losses. Ike and Jen also give Orchard signed letters resigning from the business, to be used only if they default.

Which additional term would most likely turn Orchard from a lender into a partner?
o: A right to receive monthly financial statements instead of inspecting the books.
An increase in Orchard's profit share from 30% to 40%.
An agreement that Orchard will bear 30% of any losses and may direct which orchards the cidery buys fruit from.
A requirement that Ike and Jen carry insurance on the cider press.
None of the above.
oe: More information is still a lender's protection.
A larger share of profits paid as a loan charge is still within the loan exception.

Correct. Sharing losses and having the power to initiate business decisions are marks of co-ownership. In Kaufman-Brown Potato Co. v. Long, sharing losses as well as profits and acting as co-owners made the distributors partners; in Martin v. Peyton, the lenders bore no losses and could only veto.
Insurance requirements are standard protections for a lender's collateral.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Crossing the line (Kaufman-Brown)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Maple Leaf Cider Works is a general partnership of Ike and Jen, governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). After a bad harvest, it borrows $500,000 from Orchard Capital, LLC. The loan agreement gives Orchard 30% of the cidery's profits until Orchard has received $750,000; the right to inspect the books monthly; a veto over any capital expenditure above $50,000; and an option to buy a one-third interest in the partnership within five years. Orchard cannot initiate any transaction or sign for the cidery, and it bears no share of any losses. Ike and Jen also give Orchard signed letters resigning from the business, to be used only if they default.

Which of the following facts, if added, would support a claim that Orchard had become the cidery's principal under A. Gay Jenson Farms Co. v. Cargill, Inc.?
o: An Orchard officer gives Ike and Jen daily instructions on which customers to supply and at what prices.
Orchard must approve every contract the cidery signs and has its own employee run the cidery's production schedule.
Orchard inspects the cidery's books every month.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Daily direction of the debtor's business is the kind of de facto control that made Cargill a principal.
True. Approving all contracts and running operations go beyond protecting a loan (Cargill's control factors).
False. Information rights are a lender's ordinary protection (Martin v. Peyton).
Correct. A creditor that takes over management of the debtor's business can become a principal liable for the debtor's obligations (R2d § 14O); inspection rights alone do not do that.
C is an ordinary lender protection.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Maple Leaf Cider Works is a general partnership of Ike and Jen, governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). After a bad harvest, it borrows $500,000 from Orchard Capital, LLC. The loan agreement gives Orchard 30% of the cidery's profits until Orchard has received $750,000; the right to inspect the books monthly; a veto over any capital expenditure above $50,000; and an option to buy a one-third interest in the partnership within five years. Orchard cannot initiate any transaction or sign for the cidery, and it bears no share of any losses. Ike and Jen also give Orchard signed letters resigning from the business, to be used only if they default.

Orchard issues a press release announcing that "Orchard Capital is now a partner in Maple Leaf Cider Works." Relying on the release, a bottle supplier sells the cidery $40,000 of bottles on credit, which go unpaid. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Orchard is not liable, because it is not actually a partner.
Orchard is liable to the supplier as a purported partner, because it represented itself as a partner and the supplier relied on that representation in extending credit.
Orchard is liable to every creditor of the cidery, whether or not they saw the press release.
Orchard is liable only if Ike and Jen consented to the press release.
None of the above.
oe: Liability as a purported partner does not depend on actual partnership.

Correct. A person who purports to be a partner is liable to a person who enters into a transaction with the partnership in reliance on the representation; a representation made publicly can reach anyone who relies on it (RUPA § 308(a)). Compare Young v. Jones, where no one relied.
Even a public representation creates liability only to those who relied on it.
Orchard made the representation itself; the partners' consent is not required for Orchard's own liability.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — A public representation (§ 308)

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Three nurses, Kay, Lin, and Mae, form CareHome Partners, LLC, a member-managed home-health business, by filing a certificate of organization under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). Each contributes $5,000. They never adopt a written operating agreement. They keep the LLC's money in Kay's personal checking account, pay their own personal bills from it, and carry almost no liability insurance, although home-health work carries a high risk of injury claims.

An employee of CareHome negligently injures a patient, who wins a $400,000 judgment against the LLC. The LLC has $20,000 in assets. The patient seeks to collect the rest from Kay, Lin, and Mae personally. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The members are personally liable, because they never adopted a written operating agreement.
The members can never be personally liable for an LLC judgment, because the shield is absolute.
Members are not liable merely as members, but a court may pierce the veil here.
The members are liable only up to their $5,000 contributions.
None of the above.
oe: An operating agreement need not be written, and failing to observe formalities is not a ground for member liability (ULLCA § 304(b)).
Veil piercing remains the main exception to the LLC shield.

Correct. The LLC's debts are its own, and members are not liable solely by reason of membership (§ 304(a)). But veil piercing is the main exception, and commingling funds and gross undercapitalization are classic grounds for it. Informality alone is not a ground (§ 304(b)).
If the veil is pierced, members' liability is not capped at their contributions; if it is not, they are not liable at all.
C is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Piercing the LLC veil

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Three nurses, Kay, Lin, and Mae, form CareHome Partners, LLC, a member-managed home-health business, by filing a certificate of organization under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). Each contributes $5,000. They never adopt a written operating agreement. They keep the LLC's money in Kay's personal checking account, pay their own personal bills from it, and carry almost no liability insurance, although home-health work carries a high risk of injury claims.

Suppose instead that Lin herself was the nurse who negligently injured the patient during a home visit. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Lin is shielded from personal liability by the LLC, like Kay and Mae.
Lin is personally liable for her own negligence, whether or not the veil is pierced.
Lin is liable only if the LLC cannot pay the judgment.
Lin is liable, and Kay and Mae are also personally liable because they are her co-members.
None of the above.
oe: The LLC shield covers liability for the company's obligations; it does not protect a member from liability for her own torts.

Correct. A member's status does not shield her from liability for her own wrongful conduct; ULLCA § 304 protects members only from liability for the company's obligations "solely by reason of" membership.
Lin's liability for her own tort is direct, not secondary to the LLC's.
Kay and Mae are not liable for Lin's tort merely because they are members (§ 304(a)), absent veil piercing.
B is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Members' own torts

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Three nurses, Kay, Lin, and Mae, form CareHome Partners, LLC, a member-managed home-health business, by filing a certificate of organization under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). Each contributes $5,000. They never adopt a written operating agreement. They keep the LLC's money in Kay's personal checking account, pay their own personal bills from it, and carry almost no liability insurance, although home-health work carries a high risk of injury claims.

While still a member, Mae opens her own home-health agency and steers several CareHome patients to it. Kay and Lin sue her. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Mae breached her duty of loyalty, because a member of a member-managed LLC must refrain from competing with the company before its dissolution.
Mae did nothing wrong, because LLC members owe no fiduciary duties.
Mae did nothing wrong, because the LLC never adopted a written operating agreement forbidding competition.
Mae breached only her duty of care.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In a member-managed LLC, members owe the company and the other members the duties of loyalty and care, including the duty to refrain from competing with the company before dissolution (ULLCA § 409(b)(3)).
Members of a member-managed LLC owe fiduciary duties (§ 409(a)); in a manager-managed LLC, it is the managers who owe them.
The duty not to compete is a statutory default.
Competing with the company is a loyalty problem.
A is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Members' duties in a member-managed LLC

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Three nurses, Kay, Lin, and Mae, form CareHome Partners, LLC, a member-managed home-health business, by filing a certificate of organization under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). Each contributes $5,000. They never adopt a written operating agreement. They keep the LLC's money in Kay's personal checking account, pay their own personal bills from it, and carry almost no liability insurance, although home-health work carries a high risk of injury claims.

Suppose the three nurses had simply started working together without forming an LLC, so that the business was a general partnership under the RUPA. Which of the following would be different?
o: Each nurse would be personally liable for the business's obligations, including those arising from the others' torts in the ordinary course.
Each nurse would be an agent of the business for ordinary-course matters solely by being a partner.
A nurse who left, without causing a dissolution, would be entitled to have her interest bought out.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Partners are jointly and severally liable for partnership obligations (RUPA §§ 305, 306(a)), with no LLC shield.
True. Each partner is an agent of the partnership (RUPA § 301(1)); an LLC member is not an agent solely by being a member (ULLCA § 301(a)).
True. RUPA § 701 requires a buyout of a dissociated partner when the business continues; an LLC has no mandatory buyout (ULLCA § 603(a)(3)).
Incomplete. C is also a difference.
Correct. Unlimited personal liability, automatic agency, and a statutory buyout right are three of the main differences between a general partnership and an LLC.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — If they had formed a general partnership
